P2-Q12a:
## Introduction

By the mid-1960s successive monsoon failures had left India dependent on concessional American wheat under PL-480 — food security had become a foreign-policy vulnerability. The New Agricultural Strategy adopted from 1966–67, associated with M.S. Swaminathan and B.P. Pal and delivered through the Intensive Agricultural District Programme, combined high-yielding varieties with assured irrigation, fertiliser, credit and price support. Within two decades India became self-sufficient in wheat and rice. The critical question is what that transformation cost, and who paid.

## Components — A Package, Not a Seed
- High-yielding varieties. Semi-dwarf wheats (Sonora-64, Lerma Rojo, later Kalyan Sona and Sonalika) and rice IR-8 were bred for short, stiff straw that would not lodge under heavy grain load. This is the essential mechanism: the dwarfing gene allowed the plant to respond to nitrogen instead of falling over — which is why HYV seed without fertiliser and water yields little, and why the package had to move as a package.
- Assured irrigation. Tube wells, canal expansion and rural electrification supplied controlled water; HYVs are far less drought-tolerant than the tall indigenous landraces they replaced, so irrigation was a precondition, not an enhancement.
- Chemical inputs and mechanisation. Nitrogenous fertiliser, pesticide and herbicide backed by domestic capacity and subsidy; tractors, threshers, pump-sets, roads and warehousing shortened turnaround between harvests and made double-cropping physically feasible.
- Institutional scaffolding. Minimum Support Price and the Agricultural Prices Commission (1965), the Food Corporation of India (1965), subsidised credit and the ICAR agricultural-university system — without an assured buyer, no farmer would have carried the risk of a purchased-input crop.

## Positive Impacts
- Food self-sufficiency. Wheat output rose from roughly 12 million tonnes in the mid-1960s to over 75 million tonnes by the 1990s; foodgrain production reached a record 3,577.32 lakh tonnes in 2024–25, with kharif alone estimated at 1,733.30 lakh tonnes in 2025–26. Famine was eliminated from Indian experience — the single largest welfare gain of independent India.
- Commercialisation and poverty reduction in the adopting belts. Marketable surplus turned subsistence cultivators into commercial farmers, generating agro-processing, transport and repair demand; higher productivity lifted both farm incomes and agricultural wages, and buffer stocks made the later PDS and food-security legislation logistically possible.
- Andhra’s delta case. The Godavari and Krishna deltas absorbed HYV paddy readily because Cotton’s nineteenth-century canal network already supplied assured water — which is precisely why the deltas gained and rain-fed Rayalaseema did not. Andhra Pradesh retains the title “Rice Bowl of India” on the strength of that inheritance.

## Negative Impacts
- Regional divergence. Because the package required assured irrigation, it went where irrigation already existed — Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh, and within states to the canal commands. Rain-fed eastern India and the dry interiors were structurally excluded, so a national programme widened inter-regional inequality. Within Andhra Pradesh the same logic divided the deltas from Rayalaseema.
- Intra-regional inequality. Purchased inputs favour the farmer with credit access and holding size; smallholders adopted late, at higher unit cost, and often through informal debt, deepening rural differentiation and indebtedness.
- Ecological cost. Continuous cereal monoculture depleted micronutrients, nitrogen-phosphorus-potassium ratios grew badly skewed, and canal commands developed waterlogging and salinity. Groundwater tables fell steeply in Punjab and Haryana — an achievement financed by drawing down a natural asset.
- Loss of genetic and dietary diversity. HYV wheat and rice displaced coarse cereals and landraces, narrowing the genetic base just as climate volatility makes breadth most valuable, and shifting diets from millet-based to cereal-based with micronutrient consequences.
- Health and social distress. Agro-chemical exposure carried occupational health costs, pest resistance raised the dose required, and rising cultivation costs against stagnating yields underlie the agrarian distress of the Punjab cotton and Vidarbha belts.

## Conclusion

The Green Revolution solved the problem it was designed to solve and created the problems it was not designed to consider. Its achievement was absolute; its distribution was not. The task now is a second transformation with inverted priorities — varieties bred for heat and water stress rather than for fertiliser response, procurement widened beyond rice and wheat, and the rain-fed districts the first revolution bypassed placed at the centre rather than the margin.

## Value addition
- The 2025–26 architecture reads as a deliberate correction: PM Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana targets the 100 districts with low productivity, low cropping intensity and low credit penetration — that is, the districts the first revolution bypassed — at Rs.24,000 crore a year for six years through convergence of 36 schemes across 11 ministries.
- Diversification missions attack the monoculture directly: Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses (tur, urad, masoor with climate-resilient seed and assured procurement) and the National Mission on High Yielding Seeds; the International Year of Millets, 2023 and the Shree Anna push restore the coarse cereals the first revolution displaced.
- Andhra Pradesh offers the alternative model: APCNF has moved 17.7 lakh farmers across 9.2 lakh hectares to chemical-free cultivation with verified income gains of 38–66 per cent, water savings up to 50 per cent and GHG reductions up to 46 per cent per acre — evidence that yield and input reduction are not necessarily opposed.
- Useful framing line for the conclusion: the first revolution raised output per hectare; the second must raise output per drop and per unit of nitrogen, since land is no longer the scarce factor.
P2-Q12b:
## Introduction

Fisheries are now the fastest-growing segment of Indian agriculture and its highest-value export. India is the world’s second-largest fish producer, contributing about 8 per cent of global output, second in aquaculture and first in shrimp production and export. Output has more than doubled from 95.79 lakh tonnes in 2013–14 to 197.75 lakh tonnes in 2024–25, and the sector now accounts for 7.43 per cent of agricultural Gross Value Added — the highest share among all allied sectors — while supporting around three crore fishers and fish farmers.

## Institutional and Policy Framework
- A dedicated ministry. A separate Department of Fisheries under the Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying gave the sector budgetary visibility it lacked as an appendage of agriculture; the Union Budget 2026–27 carries the highest-ever support of Rs.2,761.80 crore.
- Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana. Launched 10 September 2020 with an investment size of Rs.20,050 crore for 2020–21 to 2024–25 and now extended to 2025–26; projects worth Rs.21,274.16 crore had been approved by July 2025. PMMSY funds harbours, landing centres, cold chain, cages, hatcheries and insurance.
- PM-MKSSY (Cabinet, February 2024; Rs.6,000 crore, 2023–24 to 2026–27) addresses the sector’s informality directly — bringing unregistered fishers onto a national register so that credit and insurance can reach them.
- FIDF and KCC. The Fisheries and Aquaculture Infrastructure Development Fund gives interest subvention for infrastructure; the Kisan Credit Card, extended to fishers from 2018–19, has reached 4.39 lakh fishers, with insurance covering 33 lakh beneficiaries. NFDB, Hyderabad is the nodal implementing body.

## Management and Conservation — the Regulatory Side
- Seasonal fishing ban. A 61-day monsoon ban on mechanised fishing — observed from 15 April on the east coast and 1 June on the west — protects the spawning season. Its logic is that a closed season is cheaper to enforce than a catch quota across a dispersed artisanal fleet.
- Gear and effort regulation. Mesh-size limits, a ban on destructive bull and pair trawling in several states, and vessel registration under state Marine Fishing Regulation Acts, which govern within the 12-nautical-mile territorial waters.
- Habitat protection. Marine protected areas and mangrove conservation — Coringa in Andhra Pradesh is a critical nursery for the Godavari estuarine fishery.
- Traceability. MPEDA-administered antibiotic-residue monitoring and HACCP compliance now function as management instruments, since export rejection disciplines pond practice more sharply than domestic regulation.

## Development — Where the Growth Has Come From
- Inland aquaculture, not the sea, is the engine. Marine capture is near its sustainable ceiling; almost all growth has come from culture fisheries. Average aquaculture productivity has risen to roughly 4.7 tonnes per hectare from about 3 tonnes before PMMSY, and aquaculture now supplies 62 per cent of export value.
- Exports. Seafood exports reached an all-time high of Rs.62,408 crore (about US$7.45 billion) in 2024–25, covering over 350 products to 130 countries; GST on key fish products was cut from 12 to 5 per cent in 2025, improving both domestic affordability and export competitiveness.
- Diversification. Cage culture in reservoirs, recirculating aquaculture systems, seaweed and ornamental fisheries, and

17 notified production and processing clusters reduce dependence on a single export species.

## Andhra Pradesh — the Country’s Leading Producer
- Andhra Pradesh ranks first in India in total fish and shrimp production, contributing roughly 30 per cent of national output, and accounts for a dominant share of India’s vannamei shrimp — the Kolleru belt in West Godavari and Eluru is the largest inland aquaculture cluster in the country.
- Infrastructure under construction: four Phase-I fishing harbours at Juvvaladinne, Nizampatnam, Machilipatnam and Uppada (Rs.1,522.80 crore), at 97.98, 81.61, 71.45 and 84.29 per cent physical progress respectively as of October 2025; five more in Phase-II at Rs.1,977.77 crore, plus six fish landing centres at Rs.126.91 crore.
- The sustainability counterpoint: Kolleru’s encroachment by fish tanks and the resulting Operation Kolleru demolitions, effluent discharge and salinisation of adjoining paddy land show that aquaculture growth carries an ecological bill that management has yet to fully settle.

## Conclusion

India’s rise to second place in global fish production has been driven almost entirely by aquaculture, while marine capture sits close to its biological ceiling. The sector’s next phase therefore depends less on raising output than on securing it — species diversification away from vannamei dependence, disease and residue management, and formalising the artisanal fisher so that credit and insurance actually reach the household most exposed to a bad season.

## Value addition
- Numbers worth memorising: India second globally, about 8 per cent of world output; production 197.75 lakh tonnes (2024–25) against 95.79 lakh tonnes (2013–14), a 106 per cent rise; fisheries 7.43 per cent of agricultural GVA; exports Rs.62,408 crore; per capita fish consumption up from 5–6 kg to 12–13 kg.
- Scheme shorthand: PMMSY (2020, Rs.20,050 crore, extended to 2025–26); PM-MKSSY (2024, Rs.6,000 crore, formalisation); FIDF (2018–19, infrastructure with interest subvention); KCC for fishers (4.39 lakh reached); NFDB as nodal agency; Blue Revolution as the predecessor umbrella.
- Fisheries sit inside the Blue Economy agenda — Sagarmala has completed 11 fishing harbour projects worth Rs.1,057 crore benefiting over 30,000 fishermen, and Andhra Pradesh projects a US$20 billion Blue Economy by 2035 on its 1,053.07 km coastline.
- Andhra-specific institutions: MPEDA field offices including the new Kakinada office, NaCSA headquarters and RGCA facilities in the state, and subsidised power at Rs.1.50 per unit for aqua farmers in notified aqua zones.
P2-Q13a:
## Introduction

At the 2011 Census, Andhra Pradesh had 495.77 lakh people, of whom 70.53 per cent lived in rural areas and 29.47 per cent in urban areas — slightly less urbanised than India's 31.14 per cent. The decade's significance lies less in the level than in the movement: the urban share climbed from 24.13 per cent in 2001 to 29.47 per cent in 2011, a gain of over five percentage points and the sharpest urban transition the residuary state has recorded. The 2011 data therefore captures Andhra Pradesh at an inflection point, still predominantly rural but urbanising faster than the national average.

1. The rural segment: still the demographic majority

- About 3.50 crore people, roughly seven in ten, were rural. The concentration follows the irrigated deltas, where the Krishna and Godavari canal systems support a dense agrarian population — rural population here is a function of cropping intensity, not of isolation from cities.
- Srikakulam (16.16 per cent urban) and Prakasam (19.56 per cent urban) were the least urbanised districts. Their economies rest on rainfed agriculture, cashew and tobacco processing, and marine fishing — activities that generate seasonal rather than year-round wage employment, which is why both are major sending areas for out-migration.
- The occupational structure explains the vulnerability: agriculture and allied activities absorb the bulk of the rural workforce, and a substantial share of workers are recorded as marginal workers — employed for under six months in the year. This is the statistical signature of disguised unemployment, and it is what MGNREGS was designed to address.
- Rural poverty stood at 10.96 per cent against urban 5.81 per cent in 2011–12 (Planning Commission, Tendulkar methodology), a gap of nearly double. NITI Aayog's later National Multidimensional Poverty Index confirms that Andhra Pradesh has since moved into the group of states with the lowest deprivation headcounts.

2. The urban segment: balanced, coastal, and industrially anchored

- The urban population was about 1.46 crore. Critically, the state has no primate city: after Hyderabad passed to Telangana in 2014, the urban system rests on two million-plus centres — Visakhapatnam and Vijayawada — with a well-graded second tier of Guntur, Nellore, Kurnool, Rajahmundry, Tirupati and Kakinada. This spreads urban opportunity more evenly than in most states, but also means no single city commands the agglomeration economies of a Chennai or Bengaluru.
- Visakhapatnam (47.45 per cent) and Krishna (40.81 per cent) were the most urbanised districts.

Visakhapatnam's position rests on port-led heavy industry — steel, refining, shipbuilding, pharmaceuticals and the Eastern Naval Command; Krishna's on the Vijayawada–Machilipatnam commercial and transport nexus at the delta head.

- Urbanisation is corridor-aligned rather than dispersed. The Visakhapatnam–Chennai Industrial Corridor — India's first coastal economic corridor and the opening phase of the East Coast Economic Corridor — runs along the NH-16 spine, reinforcing exactly the coastal belt that was already urbanising. The Sri City–Tirupati industrial belt performs the same role in the south.
- Urban literacy and service employment exceed rural levels across the board, against a state literacy rate of 67.35 per cent (male 74.77, female 59.96). The rural–urban education gap is the principal mechanism by which urbanisation translates into income divergence.

## What the 2011 baseline means in 2026
- The 28-district reorganisation of 31 December 2025 has stretched the rural–urban contrast to its extreme. Visakhapatnam district now returns an urban share of 89.69 per cent with a density of 1,870 per sq km; the new Polavaram district returns 2.84 per cent urban at 54 per sq km. These two figures, quoted together, are the most current evidence available on this question.
- Correspondingly, Visakhapatnam leads in literacy at 79.05 per cent while Alluri Sitharama Raju trails at 44.67 per cent — a 34-point spread that maps directly onto the urban–agency divide.

## Conclusion

Census 2011 captures Andhra Pradesh as a state still rural in weight but decisively urbanising in direction, with a balanced multi-city system that is a genuine planning advantage. The policy task that follows from the data is twofold: to raise rural productivity in the rainfed districts that supply the migrant streams, and to build absorptive capacity — housing, water, transport — in the coastal corridor that receives them. With Census 2027 enumeration due in February 2027, this fifteen-year-old baseline is finally about to be refreshed, and Andhra Pradesh's urban share will almost certainly be found to have crossed a third.

## Value addition
- Core AP figures (Census 2011, as recorded in the AP Socio-Economic Survey 2025–26): population 495.77 lakh; tenth most populous state; 4.09 per cent of India's population; decadal growth 9.21 per cent against 17.72 per cent nationally; density 304 against 382; sex ratio 997 against 943; literacy 67.35 per cent against 72.98 per cent.
- Sex ratio is the state's standout indicator — it rose from 983 in 2001 to 997 in 2011, well above the national 943, helped by better female survival, high female work participation in agriculture and heavy male out-migration.
- Post-reorganisation extremes (28 districts): SPSR Nellore most populous at 24.17 lakh, Polavaram least at 3.49 lakh; Polavaram records the highest sex ratio at 1,051 and Markapuram the lowest at 962.
- Andhra Pradesh's urban strategy is deliberately multi-nodal — Amaravati as capital, Visakhapatnam as financial capital, Kurnool as the judicial centre — an approach that consciously avoids creating a primate city.
- Census 2027: Phase I Houselisting April–September 2026; Phase II Population Enumeration February 2027 (reference date 1 March 2027); outlay Rs. 11,718.24 crore; first digital census, first with self-enumeration, first caste count since 1931.

## Introduction

Andhra Pradesh's Scheduled Tribe population stood at about 27.4 lakh, or 5.53 per cent of the state, at the 2011 Census — well below the national figure of 8.6 per cent, with 34 communities notified for the state. The number is modest, but the geography is not: tribal communities occupy the forested Eastern Ghats and the Nallamala, tracts that hold the state's forest wealth, its major reservoir sites and its mineral belt. The tribal question in Andhra Pradesh is therefore less a question of numbers than of the collision between resource development and constitutionally protected habitats.

## Demographic profile
- Share and size: about 27.4 lakh persons, 5.53 per cent of the state, against 8.6 per cent for India.
- Literacy is the starkest deficit: ST literacy stood at 49.2 per cent against a state figure of 67.35 per cent, and ST female literacy at only 40.1 per cent. The gap of eighteen percentage points is the single most quotable indicator of tribal marginalisation, and it is driven by distance to school, language of instruction and secondary-stage drop-out in the agency.
- Work participation is high but low-productivity — concentrated in cultivation, agricultural labour and the collection of minor forest produce, which is seasonal and price-volatile.

2. Spatial distribution: four tribal regions

## (a) The Godavari region
- Koya, Konda Reddi, Konda Kammara and Valmiki in Alluri Sitharama Raju, Eluru, the new Polavaram district and the East and West Godavari agency. This is the region where the Polavaram project's submergence and rehabilitation makes displacement a live issue rather than a historical one.

## (b) The north-eastern hill region
- Savara, Jatapu, Gadaba, Konda Dora, Khond, Porja, Bagata and Mukha Dora in Srikakulam, Parvathipuram Manyam, Vizianagaram and the Visakhapatnam agency. Linguistically this is the state's most diverse tract, combining Dravidian, Austro-Asiatic (Munda) and Indo-Aryan language families — Savara and Gadaba belong to the Munda group, an unusual survival this far south.

## (c) The Nallamala region
- The Chenchu, a classic hunter-gatherer PVTG, across Nandyal, Kurnool, Prakasam and YSR Kadapa. Their habitat lies inside a tiger reserve landscape, which places forest-rights recognition and conservation regulation in direct tension.

## (d) The plains
- Yanadi, Yerukula, Sugali or Lambada and Nakkala across Nellore, Prakasam, Chittoor and Anantapuram. These communities live outside the Scheduled Areas and therefore outside the Fifth Schedule's protection — a distinction candidates almost always miss, and one that carries a real policy consequence for land security.

## Institutional and constitutional architecture
- The agency tracts are Scheduled Areas under the Fifth Schedule (Article 244), restricting transfer of land to non-tribals and vesting the Governor with power to modify the application of central and state laws.
- Integrated Tribal Development Agencies at Paderu, Seethampeta, Parvathipuram, Rampachodavaram, K. R. Puram (Chintoor) and Srisailam are the delivery arms, while the Girijan Cooperative Corporation handles procurement and marketing of minor forest produce, insulating collectors from exploitative middlemen.
- PESA 1996 extends Panchayat self-rule to Scheduled Areas with the Gram Sabha as gatekeeper; the Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises individual and community forest rights; and the Samatha judgment (1997) — an Andhra Pradesh case — held that government land in Scheduled Areas cannot be leased to private mining companies.

## Persisting challenges
- Land alienation and podu insecurity: shifting cultivation on unrecorded forest land leaves households without title, and therefore without access to credit or compensation.
- Health burden: malnutrition, malaria in the agency and a significant sickle cell disease load — the last now addressed through the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission.
- Displacement from irrigation and mining projects remains the sharpest grievance, Polavaram being the current instance.

## Conclusion

Numerically a small minority, Andhra Pradesh's tribal population occupies the ecologically and strategically most sensitive fifth of the state, which is why its development question is disproportionately important. The literacy gap of eighteen percentage points and the persistence of land insecurity show that welfare transfers alone have not closed the distance. Durable progress requires that rights recognition under FRA and PESA move at the same pace as the saturation missions — because amenities delivered onto land a household does not securely own will not by themselves convert into lasting economic mobility.

## Introduction

Project Tiger, launched in April 1973 from Jim Corbett with nine reserves, was conceived not merely as species rescue but as the protection of the ecosystems the tiger sits atop — on the logic that securing an apex predator secures the entire prey base, forest and catchment beneath it. The All India Tiger Estimation 2018 was the programme's most-cited validation: 2,967 tigers, up from 1,411 in 2006, 1,706 in 2010 and 2,226 in 2014, with India holding roughly 70% of the world's wild tigers. Evaluated critically, however, the 2018 report revealed as much about the unevenness of that recovery as about its scale.

## Achievements — Population Recovery
- The trajectory from 1,411 (2006) to 2,967 (2018) and onward to 3,682 (2022, range 3,167–3,925) represents a sustained 6.1% annual increase — a rare instance of a large carnivore recovering at national scale anywhere in the world.
- Madhya Pradesh regained "Tiger State" status with 526 tigers in 2018 and led again in 2022 with 785, showing that concentrated protection and prey-base management can reverse decline within a single estimation cycle.

## Achievements — Institutional and Legal Deepening
- The 2005 Sariska crisis, where a reserve was found to hold no tigers, forced the 2006 amendment to the Wild Life (Protection) Act. This created the National Tiger Conservation Authority and the concept of Critical Tiger Habitat, converting a scheme into a statutory regime under Sections 38L–38X.
- Section 38V mandates a Tiger Conservation Plan for every reserve, and Section 38W bars de-notification without NTCA and National Board for Wildlife approval — a genuine safeguard against political reversal of protected status.
- Management Effectiveness Evaluation, conducted jointly by NTCA and the Wildlife Institute of India, and Conservation Assured | Tiger Standards accreditation, introduced audited performance where earlier there was only headcount.

## Achievements — Technology and Landscape Planning
- The 2018 cycle deployed camera traps at unprecedented density and used the M-STrIPES application for patrol logging, making individual tigers identifiable by stripe pattern and patrol effort auditable. This is why the 2018 count is treated as a census rather than an estimate.
- 32 tiger corridors have been identified by NTCA and WII, shifting planning from reserve boundaries to landscapes — necessary because a viable tiger population needs genetic exchange across reserves, not isolation within them.

## Limitations — Read Critically from the Data
- Recovery is spatially uneven. The 2022 cycle recorded localised decline in the Western Ghats even as Central India and the Shivalik–Gangetic landscape gained. National totals therefore mask regional failure — the single most important critical point in this answer.
- Source–sink dependence. A few reserves carry disproportionate numbers — Corbett alone held 260 tigers in 2022, against reserves such as Buxa with virtually no confirmed presence. Saturation in the best reserves pushes tigers into fringe areas and multiplies conflict.
- Human–wildlife conflict and relocation. Voluntary village relocation from Critical Tiger Habitats remains slow and contested, and sits in unresolved tension with community forest rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006. Inviolate space cannot be created faster than consent and compensation allow.
- Poaching, electrocution and disease. Deaths from snaring and illegal power-line electrocution continue in and around reserves, and rising tiger density raises the risk of zoonotic transmission — a threat the earlier decades did not face.

## The Andhra Pradesh Dimension
- The Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam Tiger Reserve, declared in 1983 and now shared with Telangana, is India's largest tiger reserve, yet carries relatively low tiger density — a consequence of rugged Nallamala terrain, historic disturbance and a thin prey base. It illustrates that reserve area alone does not produce tigers.
- Gundla Brahmeswaram Wildlife Sanctuary functions as extended core, and the Seshachalam–Sri Venkateswara landscape to the south offers potential connectivity — making corridor management, rather than further notification, AP's priority.

## The Current Response (2025–26)
- During Wildlife Week 2025 the Ministry launched a Centre of Excellence for Human– Wildlife Conflict Management and a project on "Tigers Outside Tiger Reserves" — a direct acknowledgement that a third of India's tigers now live beyond reserve boundaries.
- State and district committees now review ex-gratia relief, with payment mandated within 24 hours in cases of death or injury — conflict management as social policy, not only ecology.

## Conclusion

Judged against its founding objective, Project Tiger has succeeded: the tiger has been pulled back from the brink and India now holds the majority of the world's wild population within a statutory, audited, landscape-planned system. Judged against ecological sufficiency, the verdict is qualified. Numbers are concentrated in a minority of reserves, the Western Ghats are losing ground, and a growing share of tigers lives outside protected boundaries where neither law nor infrastructure was designed for them. The programme's next phase must therefore move from counting tigers to securing corridors, from relocating people to co-existing with them, and from reserve-level protection to landscape-level governance. On present evidence, the recovery is real but not yet self-sustaining.

## Value addition
- Estimation series to memorise: 1,411 (2006), 1,706 (2010), 2,226 (2014), 2,967 (2018), 3,682 (2022; minimum 3,167, upper 3,925). The 6th cycle has commenced and will cover 58 reserves.
- Reserve network: 9 reserves in 1973, 46 in 2014, 58 in 2025 over about 85,000 sq km — Madhav (MP, March 2025) is the 58th, Ratapani (MP, December 2024) the 57th, Guru Ghasidas–Tamor Pingla the 56th and Dholpur–Karauli the 55th.
- Statutory architecture: Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972; the 2006 amendment created the NTCA and Critical Tiger Habitats; Section 38V mandates Tiger Conservation Plans; Section 38W governs de-notification.
- International: India leads the International Big Cat Alliance, whose framework agreement entered into force on 23 January 2025 with membership expanding to 18 countries, covering seven big cat species.
- Wider species programmes for comparison: Project Elephant (33 Elephant Reserves, 150 corridors across 15 States), Project Cheetah (30 cheetahs as of December 2025, including 19 cubs born in India), Snow Leopard assessment (718 individuals), Project Dolphin (6,327 riverine dolphins).
- AP anchor: NSTR — declared 1983, India's largest tiger reserve, shared with Telangana, encompassing the Srisailam and Nagarjunasagar reservoirs and the Nagarjunakonda Buddhist landscape.

## Introduction

Andhra Pradesh has three National Parks — Papikonda, Sri Venkateswara and Rajiv Gandhi (Rameswaram) — and their significance lies in how little they overlap. Between them they cover moist deciduous river-valley forest on the Godavari, dry and moist deciduous hill forest on the Seshachalam, and tropical dry deciduous scrub on the sand dunes of the Penna. Together with 13 Wildlife Sanctuaries they form a protected estate of 7,311.08 sq km, about 4.49% of the State. Their flora and fauna are, in effect, a cross-section of the Eastern Ghats and Deccan transition.

## Papikonda National Park — the Godavari River-Valley Forest
- Setting: 1,012.86 sq km in the Papi Hills of the northern Eastern Ghats, straddling the Godavari, with altitude from roughly 20 to 850 metres. That altitudinal spread, plus permanent river water, is why it is the most species-rich of the three and an identified Important Bird and Biodiversity Area.
- Flora: moist and dry deciduous forest with Terminalia arjuna along watercourses, Pterocarpus marsupium (Indian kino), teak and extensive bamboo brakes.
- Fauna: Bengal tiger, leopard, Indian gaur, sloth bear, sambar and chausingha (four-horned antelope); avifauna includes the Indian peafowl and red jungle fowl.
- Distinguishing feature: the Godavari acts as a biogeographic divide, so the park is one of very few places hosting both the Rhesus macaque (north of the river) and the Bonnet macaque (south of it) — a textbook illustration of a riverine barrier to species distribution.
- Threat: partial submergence from the Polavaram project, along with podu cultivation on the slopes.

## Sri Venkateswara National Park — the Seshachalam Hill Forest
- Setting: 353.62 sq km across the Seshachalam and Tirumala hills in the Tirupati– Annamayya belt, notified in 1989 as AP's first National Park and forming the ecological heart of the Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve (2010).
- Flora: dry and moist deciduous with dry evergreen patches, and above all Red Sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus) — endemic to this belt, listed in CITES Appendix II, and the single most valuable plant species in the State. The hills also carry a rich medicinal plant assemblage.
- Fauna: the Grey Slender Loris, leopard, sloth bear, Indian giant squirrel, mouse deer and chausingha. Birds include the Indian grey hornbill and pied kingfisher; the reptile of note is the Indian Golden Gecko, an Eastern Ghats endemic rediscovered here after a century.
- Threat and response: quarrying, pilgrim-driven construction pressure and Red Sanders smuggling. In November 2025 the National Biodiversity Authority released ₹39.84 crore to AP for Red Sanders protection and scientific management.

## Rajiv Gandhi (Rameswaram) National Park — the Penna Dune Ecosystem
- Setting: about 2.4 sq km at Rameswaram in Kadapa district, on the north bank of the Penna — among the smallest National Parks in India, notified in 2005, with a 500-metre eco-sensitive zone added in 2017.
- Flora: tropical dry deciduous woodland on sandy dune soil, with over twenty-five recorded plant species including Dalbergia sissoo, Grewia villosa and the medicinal Gymnema sylvestre.
- Fauna: spotted deer (chital), common mongoose and black-naped hare; roughly fifty bird species including little egrets, parakeets and peafowl; reptiles include Russell's viper, the earth boa and John's earth boa.
- Why it matters despite its size: it is the only formally protected riverine-dune ecosystem in the State. Small parks like this test whether India's conservation model can protect micro-habitats and not merely charismatic megafauna landscapes.

## Shared Ecological Pressures
- Fire is the common threat: FSI classifies 4.26% of AP's forest as extremely fire-prone and 13.04% as very highly fire-prone, monitored through the Forest Survey of India's satellite alert system.
- Invasive species — Lantana camara, Chromolaena odorata and Prosopis juliflora — are documented across AP's recorded forest area and suppress native regeneration in exactly the open, disturbed edges these parks contain.

Sketch an outline map of Andhra Pradesh and plot three dots, north to south: Papikonda (Godavari), Rajiv Gandhi (Penna, Kadapa) and Sri Venkateswara (Tirupati). Beside each dot write two lines only — area, and one signature species (gaur / chital / Red Sanders). Below the map draw a size ladder: 1,012.86 → 353.62 → 2.4 sq km, labelled "moist deciduous → dry evergreen hill → dune scrub" to show habitat complementarity at a glance.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh's three National Parks are small in aggregate but strategically distributed, capturing the State's three principal terrestrial systems — the Godavari valley, the Seshachalam hills and the Penna dunes — and with them their endemic Red Sanders, Golden Gecko and Slender Loris. Their real vulnerability is not internal but external: Polavaram submergence, quarrying, pilgrim pressure and invasive spread all originate at the boundary.

Securing their flora and fauna therefore depends less on tighter rules inside the parks than on eco-sensitive zone enforcement, corridor protection and community stewardship in the landscape that surrounds them.

## Introduction

Environmental pollution is the introduction into air, water, soil or the acoustic environment of substances or energy at rates exceeding the environment's capacity to disperse, dilute, degrade or absorb them, resulting in harm to human health and ecosystems. The distinction that organises the whole answer is between natural sources — volcanic emission, forest fire, dust storms, pollen — which are episodic and locally absorbable, and anthropogenic sources, which are continuous, spatially concentrated and increasingly synthetic, and which account for almost the entire pollution burden of concern to policy.

## Industrial Activity
- Industry concentrates emissions and effluent at a point source, so even a modest total load can overwhelm the local receiving medium. Where siting, effluent treatment or storage safety is inadequate, the result is acute rather than chronic damage.
- AP illustration: the LG Polymers styrene leak at Visakhapatnam on 7 May 2020 — a storage-and-monitoring failure that killed residents, hospitalised hundreds and drew a ₹50 crore interim environmental compensation direction from the NGT. The Visakhapatnam petrochemical and pharmaceutical belt remains the State's principal industrial pollution hotspot; nationally, the Bhopal Gas Tragedy of 1984 remains the reference case.

## Vehicular Emissions
- Transport is a low-level, dispersed source, which makes it harder to control than industry: emissions occur at breathing height in the middle of dense population, so exposure per unit emitted is far higher. Growth in the vehicle fleet routinely outpaces gains from cleaner fuel standards.
- AP illustration: the Socio-Economic Survey 2025–26 records about 1.90 crore registered motor vehicles in the State as on 31 December 2025, a 5.12% increase over the previous year — so absolute emissions rise even as per-vehicle emissions fall

under BS-VI. This is why thirteen AP cities are non-attainment cities under the National Clean Air Programme.

## Agricultural Practices
- Excess nitrogenous fertiliser and pesticide leach into groundwater and run off into surface water, causing nitrate contamination and eutrophication — algal blooms that deoxygenate water and kill fish. Residue burning adds particulate matter and carbon monoxide.
- Correction to note:stubble burning in north-west India occurs after the kharif paddy harvest in October–November, immediately before rabi wheat sowing — not "during the rabi season" as the source booklet states. The narrow turnaround between harvest and sowing is precisely why farmers burn.
- AP illustration:Kolleru Lake, India's largest freshwater lake and a Ramsar site since 2002, has suffered severe eutrophication from aquaculture feed and fertiliser runoff, along with encroachment by fish ponds — a case where agricultural intensification directly degraded a wetland of international importance.

## Waste Generation and Disposal
- Untreated sewage and unsegregated municipal solid waste are the largest single source of surface-water pollution in India, because the volume is enormous and the treatment gap persistent. Open dumpsites generate leachate that contaminates groundwater and methane that contributes to warming.
- AP illustration: the State treats roughly 693.5 MLD of sewage through about twenty treatment plants, leaving a substantial gap against generation in fast-growing urban centres such as Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada and Tirupati; nationally the Ganga and Yamuna remain the standard examples.

## Deforestation, Mining and Urbanisation
- Removing vegetation eliminates a carbon and particulate sink, exposes soil to wind and water erosion, and replaces evaporative cooling surfaces with heat-absorbing concrete, producing urban heat islands. Construction and quarrying generate the coarse particulate load that dominates PM10 in Indian cities.
- AP illustration: sand mining in the Godavari and Krishna beds, quarrying pressure in the Nallamala and Seshachalam tracts, and rapid built-up expansion around Visakhapatnam and Vijayawada; road dust suppression is accordingly the core intervention in most AP city action plans under NCAP.

## The Underlying Multipliers
- Population growth, rising per-capita consumption and energy intensity multiply every factor above — the relationship captured by the IPAT identity, Impact = Population × Affluence × Technology. Technology is the only term policy can improve quickly, which is why the emphasis falls on cleaner fuels, treatment infrastructure and circular-economy rules rather than on restraining the other two.

## Conclusion

Environmental pollution in India is not the by-product of any single sector but the cumulative outcome of an industrialising, motorising and urbanising economy whose waste and emission infrastructure has lagged behind its growth. The factors are therefore developmental rather than accidental, and the remedy lies in sequencing — enforcing existing standards through adequately resourced pollution control boards, closing the sewage and solid-waste treatment gap before expanding cities further, and shifting the energy and transport base. Andhra Pradesh's own trajectory, with a large clean-energy build-out alongside a growing petrochemical belt, will test whether that sequencing can be achieved in practice.

## Value addition
- Classification of pollutants — two axes worth reproducing. By occurrence in nature: quantitative pollutants are naturally present substances that become pollutants only when concentration rises through human activity, such as carbon dioxide; qualitative pollutants do not occur naturally at all and are wholly man-made, such as organochlorine insecticides. By form on release: primary pollutants are emitted directly, such as sulphur dioxide, oxides of nitrogen and particulate matter; secondary pollutants form in the atmosphere by reaction, such as ground-level ozone, peroxyacetyl nitrate and photochemical smog. A third axis is degradability — biodegradable versus non-biodegradable and persistent organic pollutants.
- Legal and programmatic framework: Water Act, 1974; Air Act, 1981; Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986 setting emission and effluent standards; Solid Waste, Plastic Waste, E-Waste, Bio-Medical Waste and Hazardous Waste Management Rules; National Ambient Air Quality Standards; National Clean Air Programme; Swachh Bharat Mission; Namami Gange; Extended Producer Responsibility.
- Measurement vocabulary: the Air Quality Index bands — Good 0–50, Satisfactory 51– 100, Moderate 101–200, Poor 201–300, Very Poor 301–400, Severe above 400 — computed on eight pollutants including PM2.5, PM10, SO2, NO2, CO and O3; and Biochemical

Oxygen Demand as the standard indicator of organic water pollution.

- AP anchors for any pollution question: LG Polymers, Visakhapatnam (2020); Kolleru Lake eutrophication; thirteen NCAP non-attainment cities; about 1.90 crore registered vehicles as on 31 December 2025; roughly 693.5 MLD of sewage treatment capacity; and the Integrated Clean Energy Policy, 2024 with its net-zero-by-2047 target as the mitigation counterweight.

## Introduction

Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs — the formulation given by the World Commission on Environment and Development in Our Common Future (the Brundtland Report, 1987). It was operationalised globally through the 2030 Agenda and its 17 Sustainable Development Goals, adopted in 2015. In India the idea is not merely aspirational: Article 48A directs the State to protect the environment, and Article 51A(g) makes it a fundamental duty of every citizen, while the Supreme Court has read the precautionary principle and the polluter-pays principle into Article 21.

## The Concept — Three Pillars and Two Equities
- Economic sustainability requires that growth be decoupled from resource depletion, so that today's output does not draw down tomorrow's natural capital. The test is whether the resource base is intact after the growth, not merely whether GDP rose.
- Environmental sustainability requires that the rate of resource use stay within the regenerative capacity of ecosystems and that waste stay within their absorptive capacity — the "safe operating space" idea.
- Social sustainability requires that the benefits of growth reach the poorest, since a development path that concentrates gains generates the very inequality that destabilises it.
- Inter-generational equity protects the unborn; intra-generational equity protects the presently poor. Sustainable development is distinctive precisely because it insists on both at once, refusing the trade-off between poverty reduction and conservation.

## Importance — Ecological Security
- It converts conservation from a cost into an insurance asset. The restored mangroves of the Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary in the Godavari estuary — the second-largest mangrove formation of mainland India — measurably attenuate storm surge along the Konaseema

coast, which is why mangrove restoration is now treated in Andhra Pradesh as disaster-risk-reduction expenditure rather than as forestry spending.

- It reverses degradation at scale. Andhra Pradesh Community Managed Natural Farming (APCNF), among the world's largest agro-ecological programmes, cuts chemical input costs and rebuilds soil organic carbon, addressing farm distress and land degradation with a single intervention.

## Importance — Economic Transition
- It reprices the energy path. Under the Andhra Pradesh Integrated Clean Energy Policy, 2024 (G.O.Ms.No.37, 30 October 2024), the State targets over 160 GW of renewable and storage capacity and roughly ₹10 lakh crore of investment, aiming at net zero by 2047. Installed renewable capacity had already risen from 1.3 GW in 2014 to about 9.5 GW by August 2024, concentrated in the Anantapuramu–Kurnool–Kadapa solar belt — showing that a drought-prone region's very handicap, high insolation and low cropping intensity, can become its economic asset.

## Importance — Social Equity and Measurable Governance
- It ties welfare delivery to measurable outcomes. India's composite score on NITI Aayog's SDG India Index 2023-24 rose to 71, from 66 in 2020-21 and 57 in the 2018 baseline, with the number of Front-Runner States and UTs rising to 32. Andhra Pradesh is in the Front-Runner category.
- Goal 13 (Climate Action) recorded the sharpest gain, from 54 to 67, followed by Goal 1 (No Poverty), 60 to 72 — evidence that targeted public investment, not growth alone, moves these indicators.
- Behavioural change completes the policy loop: Mission LiFE shifts the burden from regulation of producers alone to demand-side restraint by consumers.

## Conclusion

Sustainable development is best understood not as an environmental constraint on growth but as a redefinition of what counts as growth. Its Indian test is whether a State such as Andhra Pradesh can raise incomes on a cyclone-exposed coast and a drought-prone interior without exhausting the soil, aquifer and mangrove that make that coast and interior habitable. The instruments now exist — natural farming, the clean-energy transition, SDG-linked budgeting. The remaining gap is one of delivery and of measurement at the district level, and closing it is the essential task of the coming decade.

## Value addition
- UN Sustainable Development Goals Report 2025: a decade into the 2030 Agenda, only about 35% of targets with trend data are on track or moderately progressing; nearly half are advancing too slowly; and roughly 18% have regressed. Conflict, climate change, inequality and financing gaps are identified as the principal brakes.
- Institutional chain to quote: Brundtland Report (1987) → Rio Earth Summit (1992), Agenda 21 → Rio+20 (2012) → 2030 Agenda and the 17 SDGs (2015) → Paris Agreement (2015) → India's updated NDC and Panchamrit commitments → NITI Aayog SDG India Index and State SDG Cells.
- Classification worth naming: "Weak sustainability" permits natural capital to be substituted by man-made capital; "strong sustainability" holds critical natural capital — aquifers, mangroves, topsoil — to be non-substitutable. Indian environmental jurisprudence leans towards the latter for critical assets.
- AP anchors: Coringa mangroves; APCNF; ICE Policy 2024 and net zero by 2047; the Anantapuramu–Kurnool solar corridor; Kolleru (Ramsar, 2002) and Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve (2010) as conservation assets inside a development landscape.

## Introduction
The Constitution of India, framed by the Constituent Assembly (1946–1949) under Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's Drafting Committee, is the lengthiest written constitution in the world.

## Merits
- **Comprehensive**: detailed provisions for a diverse society.
- **Fundamental Rights and DPSP**: balance liberty with social justice.
- **Federal with unitary bias**: suited to India's unity in diversity.
- **Independent judiciary** and judicial review.
- **Universal adult franchise** and secular, democratic republic.
- **Flexible yet rigid** amendment procedure.

## Criticisms
- Borrowed heavily from other constitutions ('bag of borrowings').
- Too lengthy and complex.
- Dominated by lawyers; unrepresentative of masses (partially indirect election).
- Strong centre criticised as weakening federalism.

## Balanced view
- Despite criticism, it has proven resilient, adaptable and democratic over decades.

## Conclusion
The Constituent Assembly produced a living document that balances rights and duties, unity and diversity, stability and change—a remarkable achievement that has stood the test of time.

## Introduction

Judicial review is the power of the judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders of the Union and the States, and to declare them void where they are ultra vires the Constitution. Unlike the United States, where the doctrine was inferred by Chief Justice John Marshall in Marbury v. Madison (1803), in India it is expressly conferred – by Articles 13, 32, 131 to 136, 143, 226, 227, 246, 251, 254 and 372. Since Kesavananda Bharati (1973) it has been part of the basic structure, and L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held that Articles 32 and 226 are themselves basic features that cannot be excluded even by amendment.

## Justice Syed Shah Mohamed Quadri’s Three-Fold Classification
- **Category** — What is reviewed and on what test · Landmark illustrations
- **I. Judicial review of constitutional amendments** — An amendment under Article 368 is tested against the basic structure doctrine. The Court does not ask whether the amendment is wise, only whether it damages an essential feature. · Kesavananda Bharati (1973); Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), striking down Clause 4 of the 39th Amendment; Minerva Mills (1980), striking down Articles 368(4) and (5) inserted by the 42nd Amendment; NJAC case (2015), voiding the 99th Amendment.
- **II. Judicial review of legislation of Parliament and State legislatures, and of subordinate legislation** — Under Article 13, a law is tested for (a) legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule, (b) violation of Part III, and (c) manifest arbitrariness (Shayara Bano, 2017). Delegated legislation is additionally tested against the parent Act. · Mineral Area Development Authority v. SAIL (nine judges, July 2024) on the States’ power to tax mineral rights – federal umpiring; Madras Bar Association v. Union of India (19 November 2025), striking down key provisions of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 as a legislative override of binding judgments.
- **III. Judicial review of administrative action of the Union, the States and authorities under the State** — Executive and quasi-judicial action is tested for illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety and proportionality. The reach of “authorities under the State” is set by Article 12, so statutory bodies and instrumentalities are covered. · Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978); Tata Cellular v. Union of India (1994). AP: Kaka Ramakrishna v. State of Andhra Pradesh (AP High Court, 12 May 2023) quashing G.O. Rt. No. 1 of 2 January 2023, which restricted meetings on roads, as arbitrary, excessive and disproportionate under Articles 19(1)(a), 19(1)(b) and 21.

2. Importance of Judicial Review – Four Distinct Functions IIt enforces constitutional supremacy. In a written Constitution with a distributed and limited grant of power, some organ must have the last word on the boundaries. Minerva Mills (1980) put it precisely: limited amending power is itself a basic feature, and a Parliament that could destroy the Constitution would cease to be a creature of it.

- It umpires the federal division. Because the Seventh Schedule cannot anticipate every overlap, the Court resolves competence disputes – as in MADA v. SAIL (2024), where nine judges upheld the States’ power to levy taxes on mineral rights, a ruling of direct fiscal consequence for mineral-bearing States including Andhra Pradesh. IIt protects fundamental rights against the tide of the moment. The trajectory from A.K. Gopalan (1950) through Maneka Gandhi (1978) to K.S. Puttaswamy (2017), which expressly overruled ADM Jabalpur (1976), shows judicial review correcting its own worst failure. IIt sustains the rule of law over administrative discretion. Every executive act must trace to a lawful source and survive a test of reasonableness, so that discretion does not become arbitrariness (E.P. Royappa, 1974).

3. Scope – and Its Self-Imposed Limits IWide in India because of a written Constitution, a justiciable Part III, an integrated judiciary and the breadth of Article 226, which lies not only for fundamental rights but “for any other purpose”. It extends to constitutional amendments, primary and delegated legislation, administrative and quasi-judicial action, and the conduct of constitutional functionaries. IBut it is review, not appeal. In Tata Cellular v. Union of India (1994) the Court held that it examines the decision-making process, not the merits of the decision – a boundary reaffirmed in the advisory opinion in Special Reference No. 1 of 2025 (2025 INSC 1333, 20 November 2025), where a five-judge bench held that courts cannot deem assent to Bills or fix timelines for the Governor and President, though inaction remains reviewable for mala fides. ITextual and prudential bars: Articles 122 and 212 shield legislative proceedings from review on grounds of irregularity, Article 74(2) shields ministerial advice, and the “political thicket” doctrine counsels restraint in matters of pure policy.

## Conclusion

Judicial review in India is not a residual judicial habit but an express constitutional design, and Justice Quadri’s classification is valuable precisely because it separates three different exercises with three different standards – the basic structure test for amendments, the Article 13 test for legislation, and the administrative-law grounds for executive action. Its scope is among the widest in the democratic world. Its legitimacy, however, rests on restraint: the Court is the guardian of constitutional boundaries, not a substitute legislature or executive, and the advisory opinion of November 2025 is a recent reminder that the judiciary is willing to police that boundary against itself.

## Value addition
- Justice Syed Shah Mohamed Quadri – an Andhra Pradesh jurist worth naming. He served as Government Pleader in the High Court of Andhra Pradesh, was elevated as a Judge of that Court in July 1986, was Dean of the Faculty of Law at Kakatiya University, Executive Chairman of the AP State Legal Services Authority, and Acting Chief Justice of the AP High Court in November–December 1997, before serving on the Supreme Court until his retirement on 5 April 2003. Naming this AP connection is a low-cost, high-return addition in an APPSC answer. ITextual sources to cite verbatim: Article 13 (laws inconsistent with Part III are void), Articles 32 and 226 (writ jurisdiction), Article 227 (superintendence over subordinate courts and tribunals), Articles 131–136, Article 143 (advisory jurisdiction), Articles 246, 251 and 254 (legislative competence and repugnancy), and Article 372 (continuance of pre-Constitution laws). IArticle 13(3)(a) defines “law” expansively to include ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, customs and usages – which is what brings delegated legislation and executive instructions within review. IAllied doctrines to deploy: severability, eclipse, prospective overruling (introduced in Golaknath, 1967), reading down, and the presumption of constitutionality – the last being why the burden lies on the challenger. IL. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997): tribunals under Articles 323A and 323B may act as courts of first instance but cannot oust the supervisory jurisdiction of High Courts under Articles 226 and 227 – tribunals supplement judicial review, they do not supplant it.
P3-Q2a:
## Introduction

India adopted a ‘Union of States’ (Article 1) — federal in structure but with a strong Centre — to manage partition-era instability, princely-state integration and the developmental urgency of a newly independent, diverse nation. The framers, wary of disintegration, deliberately tilted power toward New Delhi while retaining a federal division of subjects — what K.C. Wheare termed ‘quasi-federalism.’

## Reasons for a strong Centre
- National unity post-Partition and integration of over 560 princely states demanded decisive central authority.
- Administrative uniformity was essential across a linguistically and socially diverse Union.
- Uniform protection of Fundamental Rights required supra-State authority.
- Coordinated national economic planning enabled redistribution toward backward regions.

## Key constitutional provisions
- Legislative: Union List primacy and residuary power (Art. 248); Emergency provisions (Arts. 352, 356, 360) let Parliament legislate on State subjects.
- Financial: Articles 268–281 give the Union control of major revenue sources; conditional grants flow under Article 282.
- Executive: Governors (Arts. 153–156) as central appointees; All-India Services (IAS/IPS/IFS) ensure administrative uniformity across States.

Counter-balancing / cooperative mechanisms The Planning Commission's top-down model was replaced on 1 January 2015 by NITI Aayog, which ‘fosters cooperative federalism through structured support and continuous engagement’ with States (NITI Aayog, Annual Report 2025-26); its 10th Governing Council met on 24 May 2025 with 24 States and 7 UTs. The GST Council (Art. 279A) requires a three-fourths weighted vote — Centre 1/3, States 2/3 — giving States a collective veto, a genuine check on central dominance. Fiscal federalism is periodically recalibrated: the 16th Finance Commission (Chair: Dr. Arvind Panagariya) tabled its report in Parliament on 1 February 2026, retaining States' share of the divisible pool at 41% for 2026-31; Andhra Pradesh, still absorbing 2014 bifurcation costs, sought a higher devolution share and support for Amaravati's capital construction before the Commission.

## Conclusion

India's strong-Centre federalism was a calculated response to 1947's fragility, not an accident of drafting. Institutions like the Finance Commission, GST Council and NITI Aayog now provide the negotiated space that pure central dominance would deny States, so India functions as neither a loose confederation nor a unitary state, but a resilient, evolving cooperative federation.

## Value addition
- NITI Aayog was constituted on 1 January 2015, replacing the Planning Commission, and works on a ‘bottom-up,’ States-first model instead of top-down Five-Year Plans.
- The Aspirational Districts Programme and indices such as the SDG India Index promote competitive federalism among States (NITI Aayog).
- Special Category Status, earlier granted through the Planning Commission, has no institutional mechanism post-NITI Aayog; States now negotiate compensatory special-assistance packages instead.
- Article 280 mandates a Finance Commission every five years; the 16th FC's award governs devolution for 2026-31.
P3-Q2b:
## Introduction
Parliamentary/legislative privileges are special rights enjoyed by legislatures and their members to function effectively.

## Definition
Privileges of the state legislature are the rights, immunities and exemptions enjoyed by the House collectively and by members individually, without which they cannot discharge their functions.

## Two broad categories
- **Collective privileges** (of the House): right to publish proceedings, exclude strangers, punish for breach of privilege and contempt, regulate internal proceedings.
- **Individual privileges** (of members): freedom of speech in the House (Article 194), immunity from legal proceedings for anything said or voted, and exemption from arrest in civil cases during sessions.

## Significance
- Ensure independence, dignity and autonomy of the legislature.

## Conclusion
Legislative privileges, both collective and individual, safeguard the effective and independent functioning of the legislature, though they must be balanced with citizens' rights.
P3-Q3a:
## Introduction

The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts (1992–93) are twin pillars of Indian democratic decentralisation. Together they inserted Parts IX and IXA and the 11th and 12th Schedules into the Constitution, converting rural Panchayats and urban local bodies from statutory creations of State legislatures into constitutionally mandated, judicially enforceable institutions of self-government.

Reproduce this side-by-side comparison table in the answer sheet for quick recall:

- **Feature** — 73rd Amendment, 1992 (Rural) · 74th Amendment, 1993 (Urban)
- **Constitutional Part** — Part IX (Arts. 243–243O) · Part IXA (Arts. 243P–243ZG)
- **Schedule** — 11th Schedule — 29 subjects · 12th Schedule — 18 subjects
- **Structure** — 3-tier: Village, Intermediate, Zilla Parishad · Nagar Panchayat, Municipal Council, Municipal Corporation
- **Reservation** — 1/3 for women; SC/ST proportionate; later extended to OBC · Same formula applied to Urban Local Bodies
- **Tenure/Elections** — 5 years; elections via State Election Commission (Art. 243K) · 5 years; elections via State Election Commission (Art. 243ZA)
- **Finance** — State Finance Commission (Art. 243I) · State Finance Commission (Art. 243Y)
- **Planning Body** — District Planning Committee (Art. 243ZD) · Metropolitan Planning Committee for cities >10 lakh (Art. 243ZE)

Beyond structure, both amendments made regular elections mandatory (dissolution cannot exceed six months without fresh elections), created Gram Sabhas/Ward Committees as deliberative forums, and empowered State legislatures to devolve powers “as may be necessary to enable them to function as institutions of self-government” (Arts. 243G, 243W). Fiscally, both tiers now draw structured devolution: the 16th Finance Commission alone recommended Rs. 4,35,236 crore for Rural Local Bodies for 2026–31 (PIB, 2025), up nearly seven-fold from the 13th Finance Commission's Rs. 65,160 crore — showing how these “features” have matured into real fiscal architecture over three decades.

## Conclusion

The 73rd and 74th Amendments share a common DNA — constitutional recognition, mandatory elections, reservation, and fiscal devolution machinery — while addressing the distinct rural and urban contexts. Their principal achievement is converting local government from a matter of State discretion into an enforceable constitutional right, even though functional devolution of the “3 Fs” remains uneven across States.

## Value addition
- Articles 243ZD/243ZE: DPC/MPC consolidate Panchayat and Municipal plans into a coherent district/metropolitan development plan — often the weakest-implemented provision in practice.
- Article 243V: disqualification grounds for municipal members mirror those for State legislature members.
- The 73rd/74th Amendments operationalise Article 40 (DPSP) — a rare instance of a Directive Principle converted into a justiciable constitutional obligation.
- Two-track fiscal federalism: both tiers now receive tied and untied grants recommended by successive Central Finance Commissions, in addition to State Finance Commission devolution — a feature unique to local government.
P3-Q3b:
## Introduction

Appointed by the President under Article 155, the Governor is both the constitutional head of a State and a channel of Union oversight. Part VI (Articles 153–167) vests the office with executive, legislative, discretionary and emergency-related functions. While largely a nominal head bound by ministerial advice, litigation running from Tamil Nadu to the 2025 Presidential Reference has sharply increased judicial scrutiny of how these powers are actually exercised.

Executive & ceremonial powers: Appoints the Chief Minister, Council of Ministers and Advocate General; acts as Chancellor of State universities in most States; issues notifications for judicial and commission appointments. Legislative powers: Under Article 200, may assent, withhold-and-return (first proviso), or reserve a Bill for the President; can promulgate ordinances under Article 213 during recess; summons, prorogues or dissolves the Assembly. Discretionary powers: Selecting the Chief Minister in a hung House by constitutional convention; recommending President's Rule under Article 356 (misuse curtailed post S.R. Bommai, 1994); Article 163 discretion is the exception, not the rule. Emergency & financial powers: Central role under Articles 356 and 365 in reporting constitutional breakdown; can authorise expenditure when the Assembly is not in session (Article 353). 2025 judicial developments: In State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu (8 April 2025), the SC held the Governor's years-long inaction on 10 Bills “illegal” and used Article 142 to deem them assented, holding discretion under Article 200 to be limited and reviewable. Following President Murmu's Article 143 reference, a five-judge Bench (20 November 2025, Special Reference No. 1 of 2025; newsonair.gov.in) held that no textual basis exists for courts to impose fixed timelines on the Governor or President, though prolonged, unexplained inaction remains open to limited judicial review.

Suggested exam diagram – a four-box classification table:

- **Category of Power** — Constitutional Basis · Illustration
- **Executive** — Art. 154, 163, 166 · Appoints CM & Council of Ministers; Chancellor of State universities
- **Legislative** — Art. 200, 213 · Assent/withhold/reserve Bills; ordinances during recess
- **Discretionary** — Art. 163(2) · CM choice in hung House; recommending Art. 356
- **Emergency/Financial** — Art. 356, 365, 353 · Reports constitutional breakdown; sanctions expenditure

## Conclusion

The Governor's role spans ceremonial, legislative, discretionary and emergency domains meant to balance State autonomy with constitutional stability. The 2025 rulings – first expansive, then recalibrated by the Presidential Reference – show the judiciary drawing a careful line: Governors cannot indefinitely stall elected legislatures, but courts will not rewrite Articles 200/201 by prescribing deadlines the text itself does not contain.

## Value addition
- Article 163(3): whether ministerial advice was in fact given is itself non-justiciable, insulating the process even where the outcome remains reviewable.
- S.R. Bommai (1994): declared federalism part of the basic structure and subjected Article 356 to judicial review.
- Sarkaria Commission (1988): Governor's discretion should be used sparingly, “as a matter of last resort”.
- Andhra Pradesh's current Governor also held additional charge of Telangana until 2019, illustrating post-bifurcation transitional gubernatorial arrangements under the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014.
- Andhra Pradesh is one of only a handful of States with a bicameral legislature (Art. 168) – the AP Legislative Council – adding a further Governor-related procedural layer to State law-making there.
P3-Q4a:
## Introduction

Article 79 constitutes Parliament as the President together with two Houses. The Lok Sabha, with a maximum strength of 550 under Article 81, is directly elected on universal adult franchise; the Rajya Sabha, capped at 250 under Article 80, has 238 members elected by the elected members of State and Union Territory legislatures through proportional representation with a single transferable vote, plus 12 nominated for distinction in literature, science, art and social service. Andhra Pradesh returns 25 members to the Lok Sabha and 11 to the Rajya Sabha. The asymmetry between the two Houses is deliberate: it reflects the difference between a chamber that speaks for the people and one that speaks for the States.

- Draw two overlapping circles. The overlap holds equal powers – ordinary bills, constitutional amendments, election and impeachment of the President, removal of judges and the CAG, approval of Emergency. The left-only segment carries the Lok Sabha’s exclusive powers, the right-only segment the Rajya Sabha’s. This single diagram answers both halves of the question.

## Parameter One — Functions
- **Function** — Lok Sabha · Rajya Sabha
- **Legislative** — Ordinary bills may originate here; in a joint sitting under Article 108 its greater numbers ordinarily prevail. · Equal power on ordinary bills and, importantly, fully co-equal on constitutional amendments under Article 368, where there is no joint sitting.
- **Financial** — Money bills originate only here (Article 110); the Budget and Demands for Grants are voted only here (Article 113); the Speaker’s certificate under Article 110(3) is final and not questionable in any court. · May only make recommendations on a money bill within 14 days, which the Lok Sabha is free to reject (Article 109).
- **Executive accountability** — The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to it alone (Article 75(3)); a no-confidence motion under Rule 198 can bring down the Government. · May question, debate, censure an individual Minister and reject a bill, but cannot remove the Government.

- **Function** — Lok Sabha · Rajya Sabha
- **Emergency** — Approval of a Proclamation under Article 352 requires both Houses, but if the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the Proclamation survives on Rajya Sabha approval only until 30 days after the new House first sits (Article 352(6)); the Lok Sabha alone can force revocation by a simple-majority resolution on notice of one-tenth of its members. · Can approve a Proclamation but cannot compel its revocation.
- **Federal / special** — No corresponding power. · Exclusive: Article 249 – by a two-thirds resolution, enables Parliament to legislate on a State List entry in the national interest for one year; Article 312 – creation of a new All-India Service.

## Parameter Two — Control Over Elections
- How each House is itself constituted. The Lok Sabha is elected directly under Article 326 from territorial constituencies delimited on population, giving each member an individual popular mandate. The Rajya Sabha is elected indirectly by State legislators, is a permanent body never subject to dissolution, and renews one-third of its membership every two years – a design meant to secure continuity and federal representation rather than popular responsiveness.
- Role in electing constitutional functionaries. Both Houses form part of the electoral college for the President under Article 54, along with elected members of State Assemblies; for the Vice-President the electoral college is confined to the members of both Houses. Shri C.P. Radhakrishnan was elected on 9 September 2025 and assumed office as the 15th Vice-President and ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha on 12 September 2025 (Vice-President’s Secretariat, September 2025).
- Role in removal. Impeachment of the President under Article 61 may be initiated in either House. The removal of the Vice-President, however, is asymmetric: the resolution must originate in the Rajya Sabha and be agreed to by the Lok Sabha (Article 67(b)). Conversely, only the members of the Lok Sabha elect and can remove their Speaker and Deputy Speaker under Articles 93 and 94(c).
- A federal caution: the requirement that a Rajya Sabha candidate be ordinarily resident in the State concerned was removed by an amendment to the Representation of the People Act in 2003 and the change was upheld in Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006). The Council of States has consequently become less territorial in composition than the framers envisaged – a point worth making critically.

## Powers Exercised Only by the Lok Sabha — And Why
- Origination and final say on money bills. Rooted in the principle of no taxation without representation: only the House whose members are directly answerable to the taxpayer may impose a levy. This is why the Finance Bill, 2026 was passed by the Lok Sabha on 25 March 2026 and merely returned by the Rajya Sabha on 27 March 2026 (PIB, 18 April 2026) – the Upper House had no power to reject or amend it.
- Voting on Demands for Grants. Article 113 confines the power of assent to expenditure to the Lok Sabha; in 2026 it discussed and voted the Demands of the Ministries of Railways and of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare individually before the remainder were guillotined on 18 March.
- Removal of the Government. Because Article 75(3) fixes collective responsibility on the Lok Sabha alone, only it can pass a no-confidence motion. A Government defeated in the Rajya Sabha does not fall; a Government defeated in the Lok Sabha must resign. This is the structural heart of responsible parliamentary government.
- Election and removal of its own presiding officers, and the Speaker’s finality on money bills. The resolution for removal of the Speaker moved on 10 March 2026 and negatived after a two-day debate (PIB, April 2026) illustrates that this is an exclusively Lok Sabha proceeding in which the Rajya Sabha has no locus.
- The underlying reason in one line: direct election confers democratic legitimacy, democratic legitimacy justifies control over the purse, and control over the purse sustains responsible government. The Lok Sabha’s exclusive powers are all corollaries of that chain.

## The Rajya Sabha’s Compensating Value — Evidence, Not Assertion
- Its worth lies in deliberation and continuity rather than in power. In the Budget Session 2026 the Rajya Sabha recorded roughly 110 per cent productivity against the Lok Sabha’s 93 per cent, and gave the Motion of Thanks 17 hours 20 minutes with 81 speakers where the Lok Sabha managed 2 hours 46 minutes with 6 (PIB, 18 April 2026). A revising chamber that actually revises is not a superfluous one.
- Andhra Pradesh instance of co-equal ordinary legislation: the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2026, granting Amaravati statutory status as the sole capital, was introduced and passed by the Lok Sabha on 1 April 2026 and passed by the Rajya Sabha on 2 April 2026 – on an ordinary bill affecting a State, neither House can act without the other.

## Conclusion

The two Houses are unequal in power but complementary in purpose. The Lok Sabha’s primacy in finance and in sustaining the executive follows inescapably from its direct mandate; the Rajya Sabha’s permanence, its exclusive powers under Articles 249 and 312, and its co-equal role in constitutional amendment give the States and the long view a voice that a five-year electoral cycle cannot supply. As the Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions both observed, popular sovereignty and federal representation are not competing claims but the two supports on which Indian bicameralism rests.

## Value addition
- Composition at a glance: Lok Sabha – maximum 550 (530 States + 20 Union Territories), present strength 543, term five years, extendable by one year at a time during a National Emergency. Rajya Sabha – maximum 250 (238 elected + 12 nominated under Article 80(3)), present strength 245, members serve six years with one-third retiring biennially. The nomination of members from the Anglo-Indian community was discontinued by the 104th Amendment (2019).
- Joint sitting (Article 108): summoned by the President for ordinary and financial bills only – never for money bills or constitutional amendment bills; presided over by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha. It has been used three times: the Dowry Prohibition Bill (1961), the Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill (1978) and the Prevention of Terrorism Bill (2002).
- Money bill definition and litigation: Article 110(1) lists the six matters; the Speaker’s certificate is conclusive under Article 110(3). The scope of this power was questioned in Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank (2019), which referred the correctness of the money-bill reasoning in Puttaswamy (Aadhaar) to a larger Bench – a live constitutional issue worth flagging.
- Equal powers, worth listing: introduction and passage of ordinary bills, constitutional amendment under Article 368, election and impeachment of the President, election of the Vice-President, removal of judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, of the CAG, the Chief Election Commissioner and the Chairman and members of the UPSC, approval of Ordinances and of Proclamations under Articles 352, 356 and 360, and consideration of reports of constitutional bodies such as the Finance Commission, NHRC and the National Commissions for SCs and STs.
- Andhra Pradesh perspective: the State has a bicameral legislature of its own – a 175-member Legislative Assembly and a Legislative Council under Article 169 – making it one of only a handful of States where the Lok Sabha–Rajya Sabha analogy can be extended directly to the State level in an answer.
