impacted the income levels of farmers? (APPSC, 2020)

Sectoral growth and farmer income are related but not identical. Output can rise while incomes stagnate if prices fall, costs rise, or the gains accrue to those who own rather than those who cultivate. Andhra Pradesh’s experience illustrates both sides: agriculture and allied sectors have grown strongly, and incomes have risen — but unevenly, and not in proportion to output.

Channels through which growth has raised incomes

- Allied sectors have delivered the largest gains Nationally, livestock grew 7.1% and fisheries 8.8% a decade (FY16-FY25), against crops at 3.5%. In Andhra Pradesh, aquaculture returns per hectare are several times those from paddy, which is why large areas of delta paddy land have been converted to fish and shrimp ponds. For the farmer who made that shift successfully, income multiplied.
- Horticulture raised value per hectare Chillies, oil palm, cocoa, mango and banana yield far higher returns than cereals on the same land — decisive where average holdings are below one hectare.
- Regular income replaced seasonal income Dairy, poultry and fisheries generate weekly or monthly receipts rather than one payment a year. This transformed household cash flow, reduced dependence on the moneylender between harvests, and improved the ability to service formal credit.
- Irrigation converted risk into certainty Jalayagnam, HNSS and Polavaram brought assured water to previously rain-fed tracts, raising both yield and cropping intensity — two crops where there had been one.
- Input cost reduction through natural farming APCNF, covering over 17.7 lakh farmers across 0.92 million hectares, has produced verified income gains of 38% to 66% — achieved primarily by eliminating purchased inputs rather than by raising prices. It also delivered water savings up to 50%.
- Direct income support PM-KISAN (₹6,000 a year) and Annadata Sukhibhava (₹20,000 a year, explicitly covering tenant farmers) supplement farm income directly, and NTR Bharosa pensions support older farm households.
- Better price realisation Rythu Bharosa Kendras with direct e-payment, e-NAM integration (now 1,656 mandis nationally with cumulative trade of ₹4.84 lakh crore), and e-NWR warehouse receipts allowing storage instead of distress sale.
- Employment and wages Aquaculture, horticulture and processing are labour-intensive, raising agricultural wage rates — which benefits the landless labourer, the poorest group in the rural economy.

But the impact has been uneven — the critical part of the answer

- **Tenants captured little of the gain** — With among India’s highest tenancy incidence, almost all of it oral, the tenant pays rent that absorbs much of the productivity gain, while the owner captures the residual. The tenant also cannot access institutional credit, insurance or compensation
- **Rising input costs offset higher output** — Feed, seed, fertiliser, fuel and labour costs rose alongside output; net income grew far more slowly than gross output
- **Price volatility** — Shrimp, chillies and cotton are export-linked; a single price crash can wipe out a year’s income. Capital-intensive aquaculture means failure produces debt, not merely a poor season
- **Concentration of gains** — The delta districts and larger farmers benefited most; Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra lagged
- **Debt** — Agriculture’s GNPA stands at 6.0% across scheduled commercial banks — the highest of any sector — evidence that output growth has not universally produced repayment capacity
- **Ecological cost** — Salinisation of paddy land adjoining aquaculture ponds, and groundwater depletion, impose future income losses on neighbours

The national evidence on the gap

The NSS Situation Assessment Survey recorded average monthly income of an agricultural household rising from

₹6,426 (2012-13) to ₹10,218 (2018-19) — about 59% in nominal terms, and far less in real terms. Crucially, the growth came disproportionately from wages and animal husbandry rather than from crop cultivation — confirming that where farm incomes rose, allied activities and non-farm work did the work.

## Conclusion

Growth in Andhra Pradesh’s agriculture and allied sectors has raised farmer incomes substantially, but selectively — most for those who diversified into aquaculture and horticulture, who owned their land, and who farmed in the irrigated delta. It has done least for tenants, rain-fed farmers in Rayalaseema and the landless. Converting sectoral growth into broad-based income growth therefore requires recognising tenancy so the cultivator captures the gain, expanding processing so value is retained locally, insuring against price volatility, and scaling low-cost natural farming — which raises income by cutting costs, the one route available to the smallest farmer.

## Value addition
- The decisive evidence: APCNF’s verified income gains of 38-66% came primarily from cost elimination, not price premiums — the most replicable income model for small farmers.
- Sectoral growth rates (FY16-FY25): livestock 7.1%, fisheries and aquaculture 8.8%, crops 3.5%; overall agricultural growth 4.45%, the highest of any decade.
- AP income support: Annadata Sukhibhava ₹20,000 a year covering tenant farmers; PM-KISAN ₹6,000; NTR Bharosa pensions of ₹4,000-₹15,000 with over ₹58,000 crore disbursed in 19 months.
- The structural constraint: per capita GSDP of ₹2,70,295 (2023-24) is above the national average, yet about half the workforce remains in a sector producing 37% of value — the productivity gap that caps farm incomes.

Keyword discipline: “Contrast” requires a point-by-point comparison, ideally in a table, with the philosophical difference stated explicitly. Two separate descriptions placed side by side will not score as a contrast.

The Industrial Policy Statement of 1980 and the New Industrial Policy of 1991 represent opposed philosophies toward small enterprise. The 1980 policy sought to protect small units from competition through reservation and preference; the 1991 policy sought to make them competitive by removing protection and easing constraints. The contrast is therefore not one of degree but of direction.

The essential contrast

- **Underlying philosophy** — Protection — shelter small units from large-firm competition · Competition — expose them to it, while removing constraints on their growth
- **Core instrument** — Reservation of products exclusively for small-scale manufacture (the list expanded to over 800 items) · Dereservation initiated; the list progressively pruned, and fully abolished by 2015
- **Approach to size** — Keep units small to retain benefits — creating a “dwarfism” incentive · Allow units to grow; investment limits raised and later replaced by composite criteria
- **Equity participation** — Restricted — a small unit lost its status if a large firm held equity · Up to 24% equity by other industrial undertakings permitted, opening access to capital and technology
- **Relationship with large industry** — Ancillarisation — small units as captive suppliers to designated “nucleus plants” · Market-based subcontracting — partnership by choice, not by administrative direction
- **Licensing** — Industrial licensing retained for large industry, indirectly sheltering small units · Delicensing for all but a handful of industries — removing the shelter along with the restriction
- **Trade regime** — Import substitution, high tariffs, quantitative restrictions · Tariff reduction, removal of quantitative restrictions, exposure to import competition
- **Regional dimension** — “Economic federalism” — dispersal of industry to backward areas through District Industries Centres and nucleus plants · Market-determined location, with fiscal incentives rather than administrative direction
- **Public sector** — Central to the industrial structure · Role reduced; disinvestment begun; reserved areas cut from 17 to a handful
- **Technology** — Restricted foreign technology access · Automatic approval for foreign technology agreements and FDI in specified sectors
- **Credit and support** — Priority sector lending, subsidised credit, reservation in government purchase · PSL retained, but subsidy replaced progressively by credit guarantee and market access support
- **Implicit view of the small firm** — A social objective — an instrument of employment and dispersal, deserving protection · An economic agent — capable of competing if constraints are removed

Assessing the 1980 approach

What it achieved: the small-scale sector expanded substantially in units, output and employment; industry dispersed somewhat into smaller towns; and employment per unit of capital was high.

Why it failed: 1. It created an incentive not to grow. A firm crossing the investment ceiling lost reservation, credit and procurement benefits — so firms deliberately stayed small or split into multiple units. This is the origin of India’s “missing middle”: many micro firms, a few large ones, and too few mid-sized firms, which is where employment growth typically occurs. 2. Reservation protected inefficiency. Sheltered from competition, many units had no incentive to modernise or improve quality. 3. Ancillarisation created dependence rather than capability — the small unit served one buyer on the buyer’s terms. 4. Technological stagnation followed from restricted access to foreign technology and equity. 5. Export weakness — protected units could not meet global quality standards.

Assessing the 1991 approach

What it achieved: access to capital, technology and partnership; the emergence of globally competitive small and medium firms in auto components, pharmaceuticals, engineering goods and IT services; and integration into supply chains as suppliers by capability rather than by direction.

Its costs: 1. Transitional casualties — many protected units, unable to compete once dereserved and exposed to imports, closed. 2. Credit constraints persisted — dereservation removed protection faster than reforms delivered finance. 3. Employment displacement in traditional sectors such as handlooms and small textiles. 4. The “missing middle” was not resolved — the incentive to stay small persisted through other size-linked provisions, notably in labour and tax law.

Where policy now stands

The direction set in 1991 has been carried through and refined: - Reservation fully abolished by 2015. - Revised MSME classification (1 April 2025) — micro up to ₹2.5 crore investment and ₹10 crore turnover; small ₹25 crore /

₹100 crore; medium ₹125 crore / ₹500 crore — explicitly designed so that firms can grow without losing benefits, addressing the dwarfism problem directly. - Support shifted from protection to capability: CGTMSE credit guarantee, PSB Credit Assessment Model, Udyam registration, TReDS bill discounting, Samadhaan for delayed payments, PM Vishwakarma and PMEGP (which offers a 35% margin money subsidy in rural areas for special-category entrepreneurs), and 7.5% priority sector lending sub-target for micro enterprises. - Formalisation and access replaced reservation as the operative instrument.

## Conclusion

The contrast is between protecting small firms and enabling them. The 1980 policy assumed the small enterprise could survive only if sheltered, and in doing so rewarded staying small — producing a sector large in number and weak in capability. The 1991 policy assumed it could compete if constraints were removed, and delivered access to capital, technology and markets at the cost of transitional closures. Contemporary policy vindicates 1991’s direction while addressing its gap: the 2025 MSME reclassification allows growth without loss of benefits, which is the reform 1980 made necessary and 1991 left incomplete.

- The 1980 instruments to name: nucleus plants, ancillarisation, District Industries Centres, and the concept of “economic federalism” for regional dispersal.
- The 1991 instruments to name: delicensing (industries requiring licence cut to a handful); MRTP asset limits abolished; public sector reserved areas reduced from 17; automatic FDI approval up to 51% in specified industries; 24% equity participation by other industrial undertakings permitted in small units.
- The structural problem both left unresolved: the “missing middle” — the unincorporated sector alone employs

12.9 crore persons, while 42% of formal manufacturing workers are contractual.

## Introduction

Keyword discipline: the question asks what must be addressed before implementation. Organise the answer as a set of preconditions, not as a general critique of disinvestment.

Disinvestment is irreversible: once control passes, it cannot be recovered without repurchase at market cost. The issues

below must therefore be settled before a transaction, not resolved through litigation after it.

- Clarity of objective — the first question

Is the purpose fiscal or efficiency? If the aim is to bridge the deficit, the temptation is to sell profitable enterprises in a strong market. If the aim is efficiency, the priority is loss-making or non-strategic units regardless of market conditions.

The two objectives point in opposite directions, and confusing them produces poor sequencing — selling good assets while retaining bad ones. DIPAM’s repositioning in 2016 from “disinvestment” to “investment and public asset management” was an attempt to settle this in favour of efficiency.

- Strategic versus non-strategic classification

Which sectors must the State remain in? The New PSE Policy, 2021 answered this by defining four strategic sectors — atomic energy, space and defence; transport and telecommunications; power, petroleum, coal and minerals; and banking, insurance and financial services — with a bare minimum CPSE presence, and privatisation or closure elsewhere. Without such a prior classification, every transaction becomes an individual political controversy.

- Valuation — the most litigated issue
- Asset valuation is genuinely difficult where CPSEs hold large tracts of land acquired decades ago at nominal cost. Under-valuation invites CAG criticism and allegations of favouritism; over-valuation deters bidders.
- Methodology must be settled in advance — discounted cash flow, asset value, comparable transactions — and independently verified.
- Market timing matters: selling in a depressed market realises poor value, which is the substance of the “family silver” criticism.
- Land should ideally be separated from the operating business, since bidders often value the land rather than the enterprise.
- Employment and worker interests
- Job security — will the buyer retain employees, and for how long?
- Voluntary Retirement Scheme terms, funding and pension liabilities must be settled before sale.
- Reservation in employment for SC, ST and OBC candidates applies to public but not private employers — a genuine social cost that must be acknowledged rather than ignored.
- Union consultation in advance reduces the resistance that has delayed several transactions.
- Protecting the public interest embedded in the enterprise

Many CPSEs perform functions the market will not: supplying remote regions, maintaining strategic reserves, sustaining regional employment, cross-subsidising social objectives. These must be identified and either priced into the transaction or provided for separately — for instance through universal service obligations written into the sale agreement.

- Regulatory framework — the precondition most often neglected

Privatising a natural monopoly without an effective regulator simply converts a public monopoly into a private one, which is worse for the consumer. Electricity, ports, airports, gas and telecom therefore require an independent, adequately staffed regulator with tariff-setting powers in place before, not after, the transaction.

- Process transparency and competition
- A competitive, multi-stage process — Expression of Interest followed by financial bids — with adequate bidder participation.
- Conflict-of-interest safeguards for advisers and valuers.
- Disclosure of the basis of decision, to withstand CAG and parliamentary scrutiny.
- Avoiding transactions with only one or two bidders, where price discovery fails.
- Use of proceeds — the fiscal discipline question

Disinvestment is a one-time capital receipt. Using it to finance revenue expenditure converts a permanent asset into a temporary cushion and leaves the balance sheet worse. Proceeds should be earmarked for capital formation or debt reduction — a principle India has adopted in stated policy but not always in practice.

- Post-sale monitoring

Commitments on investment, employment, service obligations and land use must be enforceable and monitored, with penalties for breach. Several past transactions have suffered from weak post-sale enforcement.

- Political consensus and communication

Disinvestment fails more often for political than economic reasons. Several announced privatisations, including BPCL, have been deferred. Building a case in advance — explaining what is being sold, why, and what safeguards apply — is a precondition rather than an afterthought.

- Alternatives must be considered first

Before selling, the question should be asked whether professionalisation of the board, operational restructuring, listing without control transfer, or asset monetisation would achieve the objective. Asset monetisation — leasing operating rights while retaining ownership, under the National Monetisation Pipeline (₹6 lakh crore, 2021-25; NMP 2.0 of ₹10 lakh crore for 2025-30) — has become the preferred route precisely because it is politically feasible and reversible.

## Conclusion

The critical issues form a sequence, not a checklist: settle the objective, classify the sector, establish the valuation method and the regulator, provide for employees and public-service obligations, run a transparent competitive process, and commit the proceeds to capital formation. Disinvestment undertaken without these preconditions realises poor value, attracts litigation and generates political reversal — which is why India’s record shows targets missed more often for process failure than for lack of intent.

## Value addition
- The governing framework: New Public Sector Enterprise Policy, 2021, defining four strategic sectors with a bare minimum CPSE presence and privatisation or closure elsewhere.
- Institutional oversight: DIPAM (Ministry of Finance); NITI Aayog recommends candidates for strategic disinvestment; the Core Group of Secretaries on Disinvestment; CAG audit and Parliamentary scrutiny.
- Landmark precedents: Air India to the Tata Group (January 2022); Neelachal Ispat (2022); the LIC IPO (2022), India’s largest; earlier, VSNL, Hindustan Zinc, BALCO and Maruti.
- Current position: disinvestment target of ₹80,000 crore in Budget 2026-27 — the first increase in six years.

- **Export concentration in a few commodities** — APEX Policy 2022-27 with the PUSH strategy and District Export Action Plans

Which strategies are working — and which are not

Working - Procedural reform — the Single Desk and its deemed-approval provision gave AP a genuine and externally verified advantage in ease of doing business. - Port-led development — plays to a real comparative advantage rather than an invented one. - Clean energy — ₹2.88 lakh crore of cleared projects addresses both cost and sustainability. - Investment attraction — the pipeline is large and includes India’s single largest FDI commitment.

Not yet working - Conversion of MoUs into commissioned plants. Commitments have consistently exceeded delivered capacity; execution is the binding constraint, not attraction. - Regional dispersal — despite Orvakal and Kopparthy, investment still clusters on the coast. - Skill supply — the literacy deficit is a decade-scale problem that industrial policy cannot solve. - Policy continuity — successive governments have restructured flagship policies and projects; the AP Land Titling Act, 2022 was repealed in 2024, and the capital question has been reopened. Investors price political risk.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s industrial challenges are structural rather than policy-made — the loss of a metropolitan anchor, low urbanisation, a thin supplier base and India’s lowest literacy. Its strategies are correspondingly well-targeted: corridors

and nodes to substitute for agglomeration, ports to substitute for location, procedural certainty to substitute for scale, and MSME parks to substitute for dispersal that markets will not provide. What remains is execution — converting a ₹13.25 lakh crore pipeline into commissioned capacity, and closing the skills gap that determines whether that capacity can be staffed.

P4-Q11b:
## Introduction

The Marginal Cost Pricing Rule states that a public utility should set price equal to the marginal cost of producing one additional unit — that is, P = MC. The rule derives from welfare economics: when price equals marginal cost, the value consumers place on the last unit exactly equals the cost of producing it, so allocative efficiency is achieved and social welfare is maximised.

The logic of the rule

- **P > MC** — Consumers who value the good above its production cost are priced out — output is too low, and there is a deadweight welfare loss
- **P < MC** — Units are consumed whose value is less than their production cost — output is too high, and resources are wasted
- **P = MC** — Output is exactly optimal; welfare is maximised

Public utilities — electricity, water, railways, gas, public transport — are the classic application because they are natural monopolies: a single supplier can serve the whole market at lower cost than several, so competition cannot be relied upon to set an efficient price. The State must therefore set it by rule.

Problems associated with the rule

## The financial deficit problem — the fundamental objection

Public utilities are characterised by very high fixed costs and low marginal costs. Once a transmission network, a dam or a railway line is built, the cost of serving one more consumer is small. Under decreasing average cost, the average cost curve lies above the marginal cost curve throughout — so pricing at marginal cost means:

P = MC < AC → the utility makes a loss on every unit.

The loss must be covered by a government subsidy, financed from taxation — which itself creates distortions elsewhere in the economy (the “excess burden” of taxation). The rule therefore purchases efficiency in one market at the cost of inefficiency in others.

- Measurement difficulty Marginal cost is hard to compute in practice. Which marginal cost — short-run (excluding capacity) or long-run (including it)? Utilities produce jointly (electricity and steam; passenger and freight rail) and face peak and off-peak demand with very different marginal costs. Costs are also lumpy: adding capacity is a discrete jump, not a smooth increment.
- No incentive for cost control If losses are automatically met from the budget, the utility has little incentive to minimise cost. Inefficiency is absorbed by the subsidy rather than penalised by the market — the standard critique of public enterprise pricing.
- Distributional objections Marginal cost pricing is efficiency-focused and distribution-blind. Efficient electricity or water tariffs may be unaffordable for poor households, and the subsidy that funds the deficit is drawn from general taxation, which may be regressive. Equity requires a different rule.
- Investment signalling failure If the utility persistently runs deficits, it cannot generate internal resources for capacity expansion, maintenance or modernisation — the pattern visible in Indian electricity distribution and irrigation.
- Political capture Once prices are set administratively rather than by the market, they become political instruments. Tariffs are held below even marginal cost, revised late, or waived — as with free agricultural power in several States.
- Externalities are ignored Private marginal cost excludes environmental cost. Pricing groundwater or electricity at private marginal cost encourages over-extraction and over-consumption, which is exactly what has happened with subsidised farm power and groundwater depletion.

Alternatives to pure marginal cost pricing

- **Average cost pricing (P = AC)** — Ensures the utility breaks even, but sacrifices allocative efficiency
- **Two-part tariff** — A fixed charge covering capacity cost plus a variable charge equal to marginal cost — the most widely used practical solution, applied in electricity and telecom
- **Peak-load pricing** — Higher tariffs at peak demand, reflecting the true marginal cost of capacity; used in electricity and increasingly in transport
- **Ramsey pricing** — Mark-ups above marginal cost that are inversely proportional to demand elasticity, minimising welfare loss while covering costs
- **Cross-subsidisation** — Higher tariffs for industrial and commercial users subsidise domestic and agricultural consumers — the dominant Indian practice
- **Lifeline tariff / rising block tariff** — A minimum quantity supplied cheaply, with rates rising for higher consumption — reconciles equity with conservation

Indian application

- Electricity: the Electricity Act, 2003 requires State Electricity Regulatory Commissions to set tariffs on cost-reflective principles and to progressively reduce cross-subsidies. In practice, agricultural power is supplied free or at nominal rates — Andhra Pradesh budgets about ₹11,000 crore in agricultural power subsidy benefiting 22.5 lakh farmers, plus ₹890 crore for aquaculture tariff subsidy. The result is the well-documented financial stress of distribution companies, which the 16th Finance Commission has addressed by recommending discom privatisation with a special purpose vehicle to warehouse legacy debt, linked to the release of capital-investment assistance.
- Irrigation water: charges recover a small fraction of operation and maintenance cost, leading to under-maintenance of canals and inefficient water use.
- Railways: passenger fares are held below cost and cross-subsidised by freight — the classic Indian example of distributional pricing overriding efficiency.

## Conclusion

The marginal cost pricing rule is theoretically compelling and practically incomplete: it maximises allocative efficiency but guarantees a deficit in exactly those industries — natural monopolies with high fixed costs — where it is meant to apply. Real utility pricing therefore uses hybrid instruments, chiefly the two-part tariff and peak-load pricing, combined with lifeline rates for equity. The Indian experience adds a further lesson: when tariffs are set politically rather than by rule, the outcome is neither efficient nor equitable but simply unsustainable — visible in discom losses, deferred maintenance and groundwater depletion.

## Value addition
- Definitions: Marginal cost — the addition to total cost from producing one more unit. Natural monopoly — an industry in which a single firm can supply the market at lower cost than two or more, because of large economies of scale.
- Intellectual lineage: the rule derives from the Pareto optimality conditions of welfare economics; the deficit problem was analysed by Harold Hotelling (1938), who argued for financing the deficit from general taxation; Frank Ramsey (1927) provided the second-best alternative.
- Regulatory framework in India: the Electricity Act, 2003; Central and State Electricity Regulatory Commissions; the UDAY scheme (2015) for discom financial restructuring; the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme.
- AP context: agricultural power subsidy of about ₹11,000 crore for 22.5 lakh farmers and ₹890 crore for aquaculture

— an explicit choice of distributional over efficiency pricing, with the fiscal consequences that follow.

## Introduction

Keyword discipline: “Give recommendations” means the recommendations carry the marks. State the problems concisely and devote the answer to what should be done.

A Public-Private Partnership is a long-term contract between a government authority and a private party for the provision of a public asset or service, in which the private party bears significant risk and management responsibility, with remuneration linked to performance. India has one of the world’s largest PPP programmes, and given a National Infrastructure Pipeline requirement far beyond what the exchequer can fund, PPPs are a necessity rather than a preference.

- The problems — stated concisely
- **Risk allocation** — Risk assigned to the party least able to manage it; the private partner bearing traffic, land and clearance risks it cannot control
- **Contractual** — Rigid, one-sided contracts with no provision for renegotiation when circumstances change over a 20-30 year concession
- **Financial** — Aggressive bidding producing unviable projects; the twin-balance-sheet problem as stressed banks and over-leveraged developers stalled projects; absence of long-tenure finance to match 25-year assets
- **Land and clearances** — Delays in acquisition and environmental clearance — the single largest cause of cost and time overrun; the LARR Act, 2013 raised compensation and consent requirements
- **Dispute resolution** — Protracted arbitration and litigation; disputes running for years while assets lie idle
- **Capacity** — Weak project preparation by public authorities; poor feasibility studies; inadequate contract management skills in government
- **Sectoral concentration** — PPPs concentrated in roads, ports and airports; thin in social sectors, water and urban services
- **Regulatory gaps** — Independent regulators absent or under-empowered in several sectors
- **Equity concerns** — User charges pricing out the poor in health, water and transport

- Recommendations — the future plan of action
- Rebalance risk — the foundational reform

The governing principle must be that each risk is borne by the party best able to manage it: - Government should bear land acquisition, clearances, right-of-way and political or regulatory change risk — risks it alone controls. - The private party should bear construction, operation, maintenance and technology risk. - Demand risk should be shared or transferred, since a developer cannot forecast traffic over thirty years. The Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM) — in which the government funds 40% during construction and pays the balance as annuity — was designed precisely for this and has revived road-sector participation. Extend the HAM principle to other sectors.

- Reform contracts — build in flexibility
- Adopt model concession agreements that permit renegotiation on defined, transparent triggers rather than treating any renegotiation as a failure. The Kelkar Committee (2015) was explicit that a 30-year contract cannot be written to anticipate every contingency.
- Provide for structured exit so that a developer may transfer the asset after construction, freeing capital for new projects.
- Include termination payment clauses that are clear and bankable.
- Build the institutional architecture — the Kelkar recommendations

The Committee on Revisiting and Revitalising the PPP Model (2015), chaired by Vijay Kelkar, recommended three institutions that remain the standard reform agenda: - An Infrastructure PPP Project Review Committee (IPRC) to review stressed projects and recommend resolution; - An Infrastructure PPP Adjudication Tribunal (IPAT) for swift, specialised dispute resolution; - 3PI, an institute to build PPP capacity, develop model contracts and disseminate best practice.

The Committee also recommended that PPPs not be used for small projects, and warned against treating them as a source of revenue rather than of efficiency.

- Strengthen project preparation
- Fund high-quality feasibility, traffic and demand studies through the India Infrastructure Project Development Fund (IIPDF) — poor preparation is the origin of most later disputes.
- Complete land acquisition and clearances before bidding, so the developer bids on a known risk.
- Standardise appraisal through the PPP Appraisal Committee (PPPAC).
- Deepen long-term financing
- NaBFID (2021) as the dedicated development finance institution for infrastructure.
- Deepen the corporate bond market — at about 15-16% of GDP against Korea’s 79%, it cannot yet supply long-tenure infrastructure finance.
- Expand InvITs and REITs to recycle capital from completed assets into new ones.
- Revamped Viability Gap Funding for socially necessary but commercially marginal projects.
- Encourage pension, insurance and sovereign wealth funds into operating assets, whose risk profile suits them.
- Dispute resolution and enforcement
- Institutional arbitration with fixed timelines, in place of ad hoc arbitration.
- Conciliation committees for pre-arbitration settlement.
- Timely payment of undisputed amounts by public authorities during a dispute, so that a contractor’s cash flow does not collapse while the dispute is heard.
- Build public sector capacity
- Dedicated PPP cells in ministries and States with trained contract managers — a PPP is managed for thirty years after it is signed, and government capacity is usually weakest in that phase.
- Continuity of officials handling a project, since frequent transfers destroy institutional memory.
- Transparent, publicly accessible performance monitoring of concessions.
- Extend PPPs into new sectors, with safeguards
- Social infrastructure — health, education, skilling — using availability-based or outcome-based payments rather than user charges, so that access is not rationed by price.
- Urban services — water supply, sewerage, solid waste, urban transport — where the deficit is largest.
- Asset monetisation through TOT, InvITs and NMP 2.0 (₹10 lakh crore, 2025-30), which is politically easier than privatisation because ownership is retained.
- Protect equity and the user
- Independent, adequately empowered regulators with tariff-setting powers in every sector where a PPP creates a monopoly — without this, a public monopoly simply becomes a private one.
- Lifeline tariffs and cross-subsidy for essential services.
- Service-level obligations written into the concession and enforced with penalties.
- Transparency
- Publish concession agreements, performance data and renegotiation decisions; a PPP spends public money and creates public obligations, and should be visible to the public accordingly.

## Conclusion

India’s PPP problems stem from a common root — risk was allocated by bargaining power rather than by capability, and contracts were written as if a thirty-year future could be foreseen. The way forward is therefore to rebalance risk (the HAM principle), make contracts renegotiable on transparent triggers, build the Kelkar institutions (IPRC, IPAT and 3PI), prepare projects properly before bidding, and deepen long-term finance. PPPs remain indispensable — the infrastructure requirement exceeds what any exchequer can fund — but they succeed only where the State is a capable partner rather than merely a contracting authority.

## Value addition
- The key committee: the Committee on Revisiting and Revitalising the PPP Model (2015), chaired by Vijay Kelkar — recommended IPRC, IPAT and 3PI, cautioned against using PPPs for small projects, and stressed that PPPs should be pursued for efficiency, not revenue.
- PPP models to name: BOT (toll and annuity), Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM) — 40% government funding during construction plus annuity, Toll-Operate-Transfer (TOT), DBFOT, EPC and the Swiss Challenge method.
- Institutional support: PPPAC for appraisal, IIPDF for project development, VGF scheme, NaBFID (2021), and

InvITs/REITs for capital recycling.

- Andhra Pradesh illustrations: ports at Krishnapatnam, Gangavaram and Kakinada; Bhogapuram airport (97% complete); 10 new medical colleges under the PPP model; and Dr NTR Vaidya Seva, itself a PPP in health insurance delivery.

## Introduction

Keyword discipline: this question asks for initiatives — the programme architecture and what has actually been built — and then challenges. Q.252 asked for a critical evaluation; keep this answer descriptive-analytical rather than evaluative.

The Smart Cities Mission, launched in June 2015, selected 100 cities through a competitive City Challenge and remains the centrepiece of India’s urban infrastructure programme. It was designed to work alongside a family of complementary missions rather than in isolation, since a city cannot be “smart” while lacking water, sanitation or housing.

- The Mission’s architecture
- **Competitive selection** — 100 cities chosen through a two-stage City Challenge, where cities competed with their own proposals — a departure from formula-based allocation
- **Two-pronged strategy** — Area-based development — retrofitting, redevelopment or greenfield in a defined part of the city; and a pan-city solution applying technology city-wide
- **Implementation vehicle** — A Special Purpose Vehicle for each city under the Companies Act, with a full-time CEO and State-municipal equity
- **Funding pattern** — Central and State assistance, with the balance to come from convergence, PPP, municipal bonds and own resources

- Initiatives taken — what has actually been built
- Integrated Command and Control Centres — the Mission’s signature output ICCCs bring CCTV surveillance, traffic management, solid waste tracking, emergency response, utility monitoring and disaster management onto a single platform. Their versatility was demonstrated during COVID-19, when many were converted overnight into pandemic war rooms for contact tracing, ambulance dispatch and supply coordination.
- Urban mobility Intelligent transport systems, adaptive traffic signalling, smart parking, bus fleet tracking with public information displays, non-motorised transport corridors and cycle-sharing schemes.
- Water and sanitation SCADA-based water supply monitoring, smart water metering, leak detection, sewage treatment plants and rejuvenation of water bodies.
- Solid waste management GPS-tracked collection vehicles, segregation at source, transfer stations, waste-to-energy and compost plants, and underground bins with fill sensors.
- Energy and sustainability LED street lighting retrofits, rooftop solar on public buildings, green building norms, urban forests and electric bus fleets.
- Public and heritage spaces Riverfront and lakefront development, smart roads with utility ducts, pedestrianised precincts, and heritage conservation under HRIDAY.
- Digital governance Municipal e-governance portals, single-window building approvals, digital payment of taxes and utility bills, grievance redressal systems, and GIS-based property mapping — which has improved property tax collection.
- Housing and social infrastructure Convergence with PMAY-Urban for affordable housing and in-situ slum

redevelopment; smart classrooms and health facilities.

- Complementary missions — the wider architecture
- **AMRUT and AMRUT 2.0** — Universal water supply and sewerage in all statutory towns — the basic services layer
- **Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban and 2.0** — Sanitation, open-defecation-free status and solid waste management
- **PMAY-Urban and 2.0** — Affordable housing, credit-linked subsidy and in-situ slum redevelopment
- **HRIDAY** — Heritage city development and augmentation
- **National Urban Digital Mission** — Digital governance standards across cities
- **PM e-Bus Sewa** — Electric bus fleets for cities
- **Metro rail expansion** — Across a growing number of cities, now among the world’s largest networks
- **Assessment frameworks** — Ease of Living Index, Municipal Performance Index, Climate Smart Cities Assessment Framework, and the Swachh Survekshan rankings — introducing competitive federalism among cities

- Highlighting the challenges
- **Financing** — The largest challenge. PPP participation fell far short of projection; municipalities lacked creditworthiness and own-source revenue; only a handful issued municipal bonds
- **Coverage of area-based development** — Investment concentrated in a small proportion of each city’s area and population, leaving peripheries and slums largely untouched — with the risk of making cities more unequal, not less
- **Governance and the 74th Amendment** — SPVs with appointed CEOs effectively bypassed elected municipal corporations, raising a constitutional objection under the 74th Amendment, which was enacted to devolve urban governance to elected bodies
- **Municipal capacity** — Shortage of staff with project management, procurement and contract-management skills; heavy dependence on consultants
- **Land acquisition** — Delays and litigation, particularly for greenfield and redevelopment projects
- **Definitional ambiguity** — “Smart city” was never precisely defined, so cities interpreted it differently and outcomes are not comparable
- **Technology over basic services** — Command centres and smart signalling were funded while water, drainage and sanitation deficits persisted in the same cities
- **Operation and maintenance** — Assets created require recurring expenditure that municipal budgets cannot sustain — sensors and cameras have short replacement cycles
- **Timeline extensions** — Completion deadlines were repeatedly extended
- **Climate resilience** — Urban flooding in Chennai, Mumbai, Hyderabad and Bengaluru exposed that drainage and resilience received less attention than surveillance
- **Data privacy and surveillance** — Extensive CCTV and data collection without a fully operational privacy framework until the DPDP Act, 2023
- **Inclusion** — Slum residents, informal workers and street vendors were rarely central to planning, though they form a large share of urban populations

- The current direction

Urban policy has moved from individual cities to regional agglomerations: - Budget 2026-27 introduced City Economic Regions, focused on Tier-II, Tier-III cities and temple towns, with seven High-Speed Rail “Growth Connectors” — Mumbai-Pune, Pune-Hyderabad, Hyderabad-Bengaluru, Hyderabad-Chennai, Chennai-Bengaluru, Delhi-Varanasi and Varanasi-Siliguri. - UIDF — with Andhra Pradesh availing ₹4,000 crore over two years — and the Urban Challenge Fund. - The 16th Finance Commission’s dedicated Special Infrastructure (wastewater) component for million-plus cities, with Visakhapatnam and Vijayawada qualifying in Andhra Pradesh, alongside ULB

basic grants of ₹9,727 crore (2026-31).

## Conclusion

The Government of India’s initiatives to build smart cities have delivered command and control centres, digitised municipal services, improved mobility and public spaces, and better property tax collection — real gains, achieved through a genuinely innovative competitive selection process. The challenges are equally clear and largely structural rather than technical: municipal finance, governance capacity and incomplete devolution under the 74th Amendment. The shift toward City Economic Regions and agglomeration-scale planning correctly recognises that India’s urban problem is one of scale and institutions, not of technology.

## Value addition
- The Mission’s numbers: launched June 2015; 100 cities selected through the City Challenge; delivery through

SPVs under the Companies Act; Integrated Command and Control Centres as the signature asset.

- The complementary missions: AMRUT/AMRUT 2.0, Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban, PMAY-Urban, HRIDAY, PM e-Bus Sewa, and the National Urban Digital Mission.
- The assessment frameworks: Ease of Living Index, Municipal Performance Index, Climate Smart Cities Assessment Framework and Swachh Survekshan — competitive federalism applied to cities.
- The constitutional issue to name: the 74th Amendment (1992) and the Twelfth Schedule’s 18 functions — SPV-led delivery sits uneasily with elected municipal government.

## Introduction

Note: the operative document was the Andhra Pradesh Industrial Development Policy, 2015-20, notified in the first full year after bifurcation. Q.237 addresses its incentive framework; this answer covers its vision, objectives and sectoral strategy.

The Andhra Pradesh Industrial Development Policy 2015-20 was the residuary State’s first industrial policy after bifurcation, framed at a moment when Andhra Pradesh had lost Hyderabad and possessed almost no large-industry base outside a handful of coastal locations. Its explicit aim, as recorded by the ADB in its assessment of the corridor programme, was to “establish state-of-the-art infrastructure, promote manufacturing, enhance inclusivity, foster innovation, and create employment opportunities across sectors.”

- The context that shaped it
- Loss of Hyderabad and with it the State’s industrial headquarters, IT base and skilled labour market.
- A structural revenue deficit — ₹24,194 crore in 2014-15 — limiting the State’s own capacity to invest.
- An economy still heavily agrarian, with agriculture contributing an unusually high share of GSVA.
- The need to establish credibility with investors who had no reason to choose a new State over established alternatives.
- Vision and objectives
- **Growth** — Position Andhra Pradesh among India’s leading industrial destinations, with high double-digit industrial growth
- **Investment attraction** — Compete with Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Gujarat and Maharashtra for large manufacturing investment
- **Employment** — Create large-scale employment, particularly for the State’s youth
- **Ease of doing business** — Make AP the easiest State in India in which to establish and operate a business — an explicit and measurable ambition
- **Balanced regional development** — Spread industry beyond the coastal belt into Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra
- **Inclusivity** — Special support for SC, ST, women and backward-class entrepreneurs
- **Innovation** — Encourage technology-intensive and sunrise sectors rather than only traditional industry
- **Sustainability** — Promote clean production and energy efficiency

- Focus sectors identified

The policy identified thrust sectors matching the State’s endowment: - Agro and food processing — building on the State’s leadership in aquaculture, horticulture and chillies; - Textiles and apparel; - Automobiles and auto components; - Petroleum, chemicals and petrochemicals — the PCPIR at Visakhapatnam-Kakinada; - Pharmaceuticals and biotechnology; - Electronics and IT hardware; - Aerospace and defence; - Mineral-based industries — cement, steel; - Leather, gems and jewellery; - Renewable energy.

- Institutional and procedural reforms — the policy’s most distinctive element
- **Single Desk Policy** — Statutory single-window clearance with defined timelines and deemed approval if a department did not respond — the policy’s signature reform, and among the most far-reaching in India at the time
- **Self-certification** — Reduced routine inspection under labour and environmental laws
- **Land bank** — APIIC maintained a bank of developed and developable land, with online allotment
- **Investment facilitation** — A dedicated agency for handholding investors from proposal to commissioning
- **Grievance redressal** — Escalation mechanism for delayed clearances

- Infrastructure strategy
- Port-led development, using the 974-km coastline and existing ports at Visakhapatnam, Gangavaram, Kakinada and Krishnapatnam.
- Industrial corridors — the Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor, for which the ADB prepared a

Conceptual Development Plan and Regional Perspective Plan, and which the ADB explicitly linked to this policy.

- Industrial parks, clusters and dedicated zones under APIIC.
- Power capacity addition to assure competitive industrial tariffs.
- Assessment — what the policy achieved

Achievements - Ease of doing business: AP rose to the top of the national Business Reform Action Plan rankings in successive years — a genuine and externally verified achievement, and the policy’s clearest success. - The Single Desk became a model cited by other States. - Corridor development: the policy provided the framework on which the ADB approved US$631 million for VCICDP in September 2016, with State counterpart funding of US$215 million. - Anchor investments in automobiles (Kia at Anantapur), electronics and food processing followed. - Institutional credibility was established with multilateral lenders and large investors — no small achievement for a new State.

Shortfalls - Employment generation lagged investment announcements; several large projects were capital-intensive. - Regional imbalance persisted — investment concentrated in the coastal belt and around Sri City and Anantapur. - Fiscal strain — incentive commitments and delayed disbursement created arrears that affected investor confidence. - Policy discontinuity — successive governments restructured policies and flagship projects, and the capital-city question remained unsettled, raising political risk. - The State’s human capital constraint — literacy at 72.6%, the lowest in India — was not addressed with comparable urgency.

- The transition to the current framework

The 2015-20 policy has been succeeded by the AP Industrial Development Policy 4.0 (2024-29), which retains the same architecture — single-window clearance, sectoral thrust, port-led development, fiscal incentives — while raising the targets to ₹30 lakh crore investment, US$10 billion FDI, 5 lakh jobs and 175 industrial parks, and adding 175 MSME parks, one per assembly constituency, as an explicit dispersal instrument.

## Conclusion

The Industrial Policy 2015-20 was the foundational document of the residuary State’s industrial strategy — and its principal contribution was procedural rather than fiscal. By making clearance statutory, time-bound and subject to deemed approval, it gave a new State the one thing it could offer that others could not easily match: certainty. Its limitations were those of the State itself — a weak fiscal position, a thin skills base and political discontinuity — and these remain the constraints on its successor.

## Value addition
- The external validation: the ADB’s project rationale for VCICDP cites the AP Industrial Development Policy (2015) as its basis — the policy attracted US$631 million in ADB support approved in September 2016, with US$215

million in State counterpart funding.

- The signature reform: the Single Desk Policy with statutory timelines and deemed approval — the mechanism by which AP topped national ease-of-doing-business rankings.
- The anchor investment: Kia Motors at Anantapur, which demonstrated that a Rayalaseema location could attract a global manufacturer.
- The successor: AP Industrial Development Policy 4.0 (2024-29) — ₹30 lakh crore investment, US$10 billion FDI, 5 lakh jobs, 175 industrial parks.

## Introduction

give the vision targets for the sector. (APPSC, 2020)

Andhra Pradesh has an installed capacity of approximately 24,854 MW, drawing on thermal, hydro and a rapidly growing renewable base. The State has cleared 55 clean-energy projects worth ₹2.88 lakh crore since June 2024 under its Integrated Clean Energy Policy. Its challenges, however, are less about generation capacity than about distribution finance, policy credibility and the integration of intermittent renewables.

- Challenges faced by the energy sector
- Distribution company financial stress — the central challenge AP’s DISCOMs carry accumulated losses and payment arrears. The cause is structural: tariffs do not cover the cost of supply for large consumer categories, and the gap is met by subsidy that arrives late or incompletely. The 16th Finance Commission has recommended DISCOM privatisation with a special purpose vehicle to warehouse legacy debt, with capital investment assistance linked to progress — an acknowledgement that the problem cannot be solved incrementally.
- Subsidy burden The State budgets about ₹11,000 crore in agricultural power subsidy for 22.5 lakh farmers and

₹890 crore in aquaculture tariff subsidy. These are politically necessary and economically consequential: free or near-free farm power makes groundwater extraction costless at the margin, which is a principal cause of water table decline in Rayalaseema. Energy subsidy and water depletion are the same problem.

- Cross-subsidy raising industrial tariffs Because agricultural and domestic consumers pay below cost, industrial and commercial consumers pay above it. This directly undermines the State’s industrial competitiveness — an energy-intensive manufacturer comparing Andhra Pradesh with Vietnam or Gujarat is comparing tariffs.
- Policy discontinuity — the most damaging challenge The State has experienced a documented “flip-flop” in renewable energy policy between administrations, producing Power Purchase Agreement review controversies, payment delays to developers and grid integration disputes. Retrospective review of signed contracts is the single most expensive signal a State can send, because it raises the cost of capital for every future project, not only those affected.
- Payment delays to generators Delayed payments raise developers’ financing costs, which are passed back in higher bid tariffs — so delay is not a saving but a deferred and amplified cost.
- Renewable intermittency and storage Solar generates in daylight while demand peaks in the evening. The Economic Survey 2025-26 identifies Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and Pumped Storage Projects (PSP) as essential to address variability, ensure grid stability and manage peak load. Without storage, further renewable addition yields diminishing system value.
- Grid integration and evacuation Renewable generation is concentrated in specific zones — Anantapur, Kurnool, Kadapa for solar and wind — while demand is dispersed. Green Energy Corridor transmission has lagged generation, causing curtailment.
- Baseload adequacy The Economic Survey cautions — citing the Dutch case, where 14,000 companies await grid connection — that energy transitions must be grounded in baseload adequacy and system reliability. AP must add renewables without compromising firm supply.
- Transmission and distribution losses Technical and commercial losses, though improved, remain above the levels achieved by the best-performing States.
- Demand growth Industrial expansion — the Integrated Steel Plant at Anakapalli, the Bulk Drug Park at Nakkapalli, the Orvakal semiconductor facility, Green Aluminium at Kakinada and Google’s US$15 billion data centre at Visakhapatnam — will raise demand sharply. Data centres in particular require reliable, round-the-clock power, which intermittent renewables alone cannot supply.
- Coal and fuel supply Thermal capacity depends on coal linkages and transport; AP lost Singareni Collieries to Telangana at bifurcation, increasing its dependence on external coal supply.
- Land acquisition for renewables Utility-scale solar and wind are land-intensive; acquisition delays are a recognised national constraint that applies here.
- Vision targets for the sector
- **24×7 quality power for all** — The foundational commitment under the power grid component of the State’s infrastructure strategy
- **Large-scale renewable capacity** — 55 clean-energy projects worth ₹2.88 lakh crore cleared since June 2024 — solar, wind, pumped storage and green hydrogen, under the Integrated Clean Energy Policy
- **Pumped storage leadership** — AP has among India’s largest identified pumped storage potential; storage is the State’s declared route to firm renewable supply
- **Green hydrogen** — Production clusters aligned to the National Green Hydrogen Mission, for which Budget 2026-27 provides ₹25,000 crore for Phase 2; Green Aluminium at Kakinada as an anchor consumer
- **Transmission** — Green Energy Corridor expansion for evacuation from generation zones
- **Distribution reform** — Loss reduction, smart metering, and the structural reform the 16th Finance Commission recommends
- **Industrial competitiveness** — Tariffs competitive with rival States, which requires reducing cross-subsidy
- **Alignment with national targets** — India reached non-fossil sources at 51.93% of installed capacity by December 2025 — surpassing the 50% NDC target five years early — with total renewables at 253.96 GW and solar at 135.81 GW, a 45-fold rise from 3 GW in 2014
- **Swarna Andhra @2047** — Energy as an enabler of the US$2.4 trillion economy target, with clean energy as a growth sector in its own right

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s energy challenges are financial and institutional rather than technical: the State can add generation capacity — as ₹2.88 lakh crore of cleared clean-energy projects demonstrates — but it cannot yet price power at cost, pay generators on time, or guarantee policy continuity. Its vision targets of 24×7 supply, large-scale renewables, pumped storage and green hydrogen are achievable and well matched to the State’s endowments. Achieving them depends on distribution reform, honouring existing power purchase agreements, and building storage and transmission alongside generation — since capacity that cannot be evacuated or paid for is capacity that does not exist.

## Value addition
- AP’s position: installed capacity approximately 24,854 MW; 55 clean-energy projects worth ₹2.88 lakh crore

cleared since June 2024; agricultural power subsidy about ₹11,000 crore and aqua tariff subsidy ₹890 crore.

- The national context: renewables 253.96 GW (November 2025); solar 135.81 GW (December 2025) from 3 GW in 2014; non-fossil at 51.93% of installed capacity, achieved five years ahead of the NDC target; record 34.56 GW non-fossil addition in the first eight months of FY26.
- The reform recommended: the 16th Finance Commission urges DISCOM privatisation with an SPV to warehouse legacy debt, with capital investment assistance released against progress.
- The technical priority: Battery Energy Storage Systems and Pumped Storage Projects — identified by the Economic Survey 2025-26 as essential to address renewable variability, ensure grid stability and manage peak load.

## Introduction

India Vision 2020 was prepared by a Committee of the Planning Commission chaired by Dr. S.P. Gupta (report submitted 2002), with intellectual impetus from Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam’s work on technology-led national development. Written when agriculture still employed around 60% of the workforce, it treated the sector’s transformation as the precondition for everything else the country hoped to achieve by 2020.

Major agricultural initiatives proposed

- A second Green Revolution — extending it geographically The first Green Revolution had been confined to irrigated wheat and rice belts. Vision 2020 called for extending productivity gains to eastern and rain-fed India, and to crops other than wheat and rice — a “Rainbow Revolution” spanning food (green), milk (white), oilseeds (yellow), fisheries (blue), horticulture and fruits, and eggs and poultry.
- Diversification toward high-value agriculture A deliberate shift from cereals to horticulture, floriculture, livestock, dairy, poultry and fisheries, recognising that small holdings can generate viable incomes only from high-value output.
- Water security and irrigation efficiency Watershed development, rainwater harvesting, micro-irrigation (drip and sprinkler), participatory irrigation management and the modernisation of existing systems — with an emphasis on efficiency rather than only on new capacity.
- Dryland and rain-fed farming Explicit focus on the roughly 60% of cultivated area that is rain-fed, through drought-resistant varieties, soil and moisture conservation and appropriate cropping systems.
- Agro-processing and value addition Food processing was identified as the route to rural employment and higher farm-gate prices, with cold chains, storage and agro-industrial estates near production centres.
- Marketing reform Reform of APMC regulation, direct marketing, contract farming and better market information — recognising that production gains without marketing reform simply depress prices.
- Technology and biotechnology Application of biotechnology, precision farming, IT-based extension and information systems to raise productivity.
- Rural infrastructure and connectivity Roads, electrification, telecom and storage — later given expression through Bharat Nirman (2005) and PMGSY.
- Credit and risk management Expansion of institutional credit and crop insurance to reduce dependence on moneylenders.
- Sustainability Soil health, balanced fertiliser use, watershed management and organic farming — the environmental dimension of agricultural growth.

Assessment with hindsight — what was realised and what was not

- **Rainbow Revolution / diversification** — Substantially realised. Horticulture output (362.08 MT in 2024-25) now exceeds foodgrain output; livestock GVA rose about 195% between FY15 and FY24; fisheries grew 8.8% a decade
- **Second Green Revolution in the east** — Partly realised — eastern States improved rice productivity, but the regional gap persists
- **Micro-irrigation and water efficiency** — Partly realised through PMKSY; groundwater depletion continues
- **Agro-processing** — Growing — the sector expanded 7.3% annually (2015-2022); processed food’s share of agri-exports rose from 13.7% (2014-15) to 20.4% (2024-25)
- **Marketing reform** — Weakest area. e-NAM covers 1,656 mandis (March 2026); APMC reform remains incomplete and politically contested
- **Credit expansion** — Achieved — institutional credit rose from ₹8.5 lakh crore (2014-15) to ₹25.48 lakh crore (2023-24), with small and marginal farmers’ access up from 57% to 76%
- **Rural infrastructure** — Substantially achieved through PMGSY, Saubhagya, Jal Jeevan Mission and BharatNet
- **Reducing agricultural dependence** — Not achieved — about 46.1% of the population still depends on agriculture

The overall verdict: Vision 2020 correctly identified diversification and value addition as the route forward, and that is precisely where India has performed best — decadal agricultural growth of 4.45% (FY16-FY25), the highest in fifty years, driven by allied sectors rather than crops. Where it under-delivered was in marketing reform and structural transformation of the workforce — the two areas requiring political consensus rather than technical solutions.

## Conclusion

Vision 2020’s agricultural agenda was analytically sound and remarkably prescient: its emphasis on diversification, allied sectors and value addition has been vindicated by the growth pattern of the last decade. Its shortfall lay in the areas it could not command — agricultural marketing, which is a State subject requiring political consensus, and the movement of labour out of farming, which depends on industry rather than agriculture. Those two remain the core of the agenda now carried forward under Viksit Bharat @2047.

## Value addition
- The Rainbow Revolution: Green (foodgrain), White (milk — Operation Flood), Yellow (oilseeds), Blue (fisheries), Golden (horticulture and honey), Silver (eggs and poultry), Pink (prawn/onion), Red (meat and tomato), Brown (leather and cocoa), Grey (fertiliser), Black (petroleum), Round (potato).
- Related visions: Andhra Pradesh Vision 2020 (1999) was a State-level parallel document; the current successors are Viksit Bharat @2047 nationally and Swarna Andhra @2047 in the State.
- Where the diversification argument now stands: horticulture contributes about 33% of agricultural GVA; allied sectors (livestock 7.1%, fisheries 8.8%) outgrow crops (3.5%) by a wide margin.
- Unfinished marketing agenda: Model APMC Act (2003), Model APLM Act (2017), Model Contract Farming Act (2018) — all requiring State adoption, since agricultural marketing is a State subject.

## Introduction

The Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP) is a credit-linked subsidy scheme launched in 2008-09 by merging the erstwhile Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana (PMRY) and the Rural Employment Generation Programme (REGP). A Central Sector Scheme of the Ministry of MSME, it is implemented by the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) as the single nodal agency at the national level.

Objectives

- Generate self-employment by helping individuals set up new micro-enterprises in the non-farm sector, in both rural and urban areas.
- Shift the young from job-seeking to job-creating — targeting traditional artisans, unemployed youth and first-generation entrepreneurs.
- Arrest rural-to-urban migration by creating sustainable local livelihoods.
- Raise the wage-earning capacity of artisans and contribute to the growth of the rural and urban non-farm economy.
- Promote inclusive entrepreneurship, with enhanced support for SC, ST, OBC, minorities, women, ex-servicemen, persons with disabilities and those in hill and border areas.

Institutional structure

- **National nodal agency** — KVIC, a statutory body under the Ministry of MSME
- **State implementation** — State KVIC offices, State Khadi and Village Industries Boards (KVIBs), District Industries Centres (DICs), and the Coir Board
- **Allocation ratio** — KVIC : KVIB : DIC = 30 : 30 : 40
- **Credit delivery** — Public sector banks, RRBs, cooperative banks and SIDBI; subsidy routed by KVIC through the nodal bank

Benefits received under the scheme

## Financial benefits — the margin money subsidy
- **Category** — Urban · Rural
- **General** — 15% · 25%
- **Special (SC/ST/OBC, minorities, women, ex-servicemen, PwD, hill and border areas)** — 25% · 35%

- Maximum project cost: ₹50 lakh for manufacturing and ₹20 lakh for the service or business sector (raised from

₹25 lakh and ₹10 lakh in 2021).

- Own contribution: 10% for general category, 5% for special category; the bank finances 90-95% as term loan plus working capital.
- Repayment: 3 to 7 years after an initial moratorium.
- Second loan for upgradation: well-performing existing units may access up to ₹1 crore (manufacturing) or ₹25 lakh (service) at a 15% subsidy.
- Non-financial benefits - Entrepreneurship Development Programme (EDP) training before disbursement. - Handholding on project preparation through Rural Industrial Consultancy Services and Udyami Mitras. - Marketing support through exhibitions and Khadi/village-industry retail linkages. - Online application, a scoring model (score card) for objective appraisal, and an application tracking system — reducing discretion.
- Eligibility, in brief Any individual above 18 years; at least Class VIII pass for projects above ₹10 lakh (manufacturing) or ₹5 lakh (service); only new units are eligible; only one person per family (self and spouse). Activities on the negative list — meat processing, intoxicants such as beedi, pan and cigarettes — are excluded.

Performance

- Since inception in 2008-09, about 8.37 lakh micro-enterprises have been assisted with margin money of roughly

₹20,775 crore, generating estimated employment for about 68 lakh persons.

- Over 80% of units are in rural areas, and about 50% are set up by SC, ST and women entrepreneurs — a genuinely inclusive delivery record.
- Continuation was approved with an outlay of ₹13,554.42 crore for 2021-22 to 2025-26, aligned with the 15th Finance Commission cycle.

Limitations

- Bank-dependent: sanction rates vary widely by region and by lender’s risk appetite; many applications are rejected at the branch level.
- Survival rate concerns: units often lack market linkage and working capital beyond the first cycle.
- Skill gap: short EDP training is insufficient for genuine enterprise capability.
- Employment estimates are notional, derived from project projections rather than verified job counts.

## Conclusion

PMEGP has become India’s principal instrument for converting credit into self-employment, with a strong rural and social-inclusion bias. Its next stage must move beyond disbursement to enterprise survival — cluster linkages, market access through GeM and e-commerce, mentoring, and integration with PM Vishwakarma, MUDRA and the Employment Linked Incentive Scheme (₹99,446 crore), so that a subsidised loan becomes a lasting business rather than a one-time transfer.

## Value addition
- Revised MSME classification (from 1 April 2025): Micro — investment up to ₹2.5 crore, turnover up to ₹10 crore; Small — ₹25 crore / ₹100 crore; Medium — ₹125 crore / ₹500 crore.
- Complementary schemes: PMMY (MUDRA) — Shishu, Kishore, Tarun; Stand-Up India for SC/ST and women entrepreneurs; PM Vishwakarma for traditional artisans; PM SVANidhi for street vendors; SFURTI for traditional industry clusters.
- Credit context: among unincorporated manufacturing units, formal credit use rose from 48% (2021-22) to 51% (2023-24), with commercial bank borrowing up 6 percentage points.
- Andhra Pradesh link: 175 MSME parks, one in each assembly constituency, under the AP MSME & Entrepreneur Development Policy 4.0 (2024-29) — the State-level counterpart to PMEGP’s objective.

## Introduction

Keyword discipline: “Explain briefly” signals a structured, economical answer. Name the four pillars clearly, explain each with substance, and resist the temptation to write a general IT-policy essay.

Bifurcation in 2014 removed Hyderabad — HITEC City, Cyberabad and the entire IT ecosystem — from Andhra Pradesh. The residuary State had to rebuild an IT sector from a very low base, and its strategy rests on four pillars: human capital, infrastructure, incentives and good governance. The design logic is that no single pillar suffices: talent without infrastructure emigrates, infrastructure without incentives stands empty, and incentives without governance are not credible.

Pillar 1 — Human Capital

The rationale: IT is the most talent-dependent of all industries. A firm locates where it can recruit, not where the rent is cheapest.

- **Higher education base** — Over 82.5% of the State’s higher education institutions are private, producing a large annual output of engineering graduates; AP students are disproportionately represented in national technical admissions
- **Skilling** — AP State Skill Development Corporation; Skill Development allocation of ₹1,232 crore in Budget 2026-27; government ITIs with MoUs with 167 industry partners, 9,188 trainees in in-plant training and 98% placement or apprenticeship
- **Industry-linked curriculum** — Finishing schools and employability training, continuing the logic of the earlier Jawahar Knowledge Centres, which addressed employability rather than qualifications
- **Higher education reform** — Learning Excellence in Andhra Pradesh as a KG-to-PG framework; NEP 2020 alignment; the Academic Bank of Credits and National Credit Framework
- **The binding constraint** — AP’s literacy of 72.6% (PLFS 2023-24) is the lowest among Indian States — the State produces skilled graduates from a narrow base, and widening that base is the deeper task

Pillar 2 — Infrastructure

The rationale: IT requires connectivity, power and space — and, increasingly, data-centre-grade power and cooling.

- **Connectivity** — APSFL (AP State FiberNet Limited) providing broadband up to 100 Mbps to every village; high tele-density; 5G rollout
- **IT parks and campuses** — IT parks at Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada, Tirupati and Kakinada; plug-and-play built-up space to reduce a firm’s set-up time
- **Data centres** — Google’s US$15 billion AI data centre at Visakhapatnam — the largest single FDI commitment in the country; data-centre parks under IT & GCC Policy 4.0
- **Deep-tech clusters** — Amaravati Quantum Valley; the Ratan Tata Innovation Hub; Drone City at Orvakal
- **Power** — Assured supply, with 55 clean-energy projects worth ₹2.88 lakh crore cleared since June 2024 — significant because data centres require round-the-clock reliable power
- **Air connectivity** — Alluri Sitaramaraju International Airport, Bhogapuram — 97% complete — essential, since IT and GCC business depends on executive travel
- **Urban liveability** — Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada-Amaravati and Tirupati developed as liveable centres, since IT professionals choose cities as much as employers

Pillar 3 — Incentives

The rationale: AP competes against Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai and Pune, all with established ecosystems. Incentives are the compensation for a thinner ecosystem.

- **Policy framework** — AP IT & GCC Policy 4.0 (2024-29), alongside the Industrial Development Policy 4.0 targeting ₹30 lakh crore investment and US$10 billion FDI
- **Capital and rental subsidy** — Support for built-up space, particularly for firms establishing in Tier-II locations
- **Power tariff reimbursement** — A significant cost item for data centres
- **SGST reimbursement** — Improving working capital
- **Stamp duty and land conversion reimbursement** — Reducing entry cost
- **Recruitment and training assistance** — Reimbursement of training cost for local recruits — linking the incentive to the human capital pillar

Pillar 4 — Good Governance

The rationale: An IT firm’s principal concern is predictability. Incentives can be matched by any State; certainty cannot be easily matched.

- **Single Desk Policy** — Statutory single-window clearance with defined timelines and deemed approval — if a department does not act, approval is deemed granted

The four are mutually reinforcing rather than additive: skilled graduates attract firms; firms justify infrastructure; infrastructure and incentives make location viable; and governance makes the commitment credible. The weakest pillar determines the outcome — which is why AP’s literacy rate, rather than its incentive package, is the real constraint on the sector’s growth.

Andhra Pradesh’s four-pillar IT strategy — human capital, infrastructure, incentives and good governance — is a coherent response to the loss of Hyderabad. Its strongest pillars are governance and infrastructure, evidenced by the Single Desk, village broadband and the Visakhapatnam data centre commitment; its weakest is human capital, since a State with India’s lowest literacy cannot indefinitely supply a talent-intensive industry. Strengthening that pillar is what will determine whether the other three deliver.
