## Introduction

Life expectancy at birth is the average number of years a newborn would live if the age-specific mortality rates prevailing at the time of birth remained constant throughout its life. The conditional clause matters: it is a snapshot of current mortality conditions, not a prediction about any individual or generation. Global life expectancy rose from roughly the low 30s in 1900 to about 73 years today, one of the most significant changes in human history.

- narrower base, thicker top (ageing) . Beneath, note: The doubling came mainly from deaths that stopped happening in the first five years.

## The single most important insight — why the average doubled

Life expectancy at birth is an average, so it is extraordinarily sensitive to deaths in infancy. A child dying at one contributes 1 to the average; an adult dying at seventy contributes 70. In 1900, a very large share of children died before their fifth birthday, dragging the average far below the age most surviving adults actually reached. The doubling therefore reflects mainly the collapse of child mortality, not a doubling of the human lifespan. An adult in 1900 who survived childhood could expect to live into their sixties. Stating this distinguishes a strong answer from one that simply lists causes.

## Factors contributing to the improvement
- 1. Control of infectious disease — the largest single contributor. Vaccination (smallpox eradicated in 1980, polio near-eliminated), antibiotics from the 1940s, oral rehydration therapy for diarrhoeal disease, and antiretrovirals for HIV. India’s programmes: the Universal Immunisation Programme, Mission Indradhanush and U-WIN; India was certified polio-free in 2014. Infectious disease killed disproportionately in childhood, which is why its control moved the average so sharply.
- 2. Water, sanitation and hygiene — often the underrated driver. Piped water, sewerage and sanitation reduced cholera, typhoid and diarrhoeal deaths before most modern medicine existed. Historians of public health generally attribute more of the nineteenth- and early twentieth-century mortality decline to sanitary engineering than to clinical medicine. India’s instruments: Swachh Bharat Mission and Jal Jeevan Mission for household tap water.
- 3. Nutrition and food security. Higher agricultural productivity — the Green Revolution in India’s case — reduced famine and chronic undernutrition, which had amplified mortality from ordinary infections. Undernourished children die of measles and diarrhoea that well-nourished children survive. India’s programmes: PDS and the National Food Security Act, POSHAN 2.0, ICDS and PM POSHAN.
- 4. Maternal and child health services. Institutional delivery, skilled birth attendance, antenatal care and neonatal intensive care. India’s instruments: Janani Suraksha Yojana, Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram, LaQshya and the ASHA network — India has recorded substantial declines in maternal and infant mortality.
- 5. Rising incomes, education and social development. Higher income improves nutrition, housing and healthcare access. Female education is particularly strongly associated with child survival, through better nutrition, hygiene practice, immunisation uptake and care-seeking. This is why education is a health intervention, not merely a social one.
- 6. Medical technology and financial protection. Imaging, surgery, cardiac and cancer care extend life at older ages — the source of most recent gains, as against the earlier gains from child survival. India’s AB-PMJAY provides Rs. 5 lakh cover to about 12.37 crore families, and Jan Aushadhi supplies affordable generics.

## India’s position within the global picture

India’s life expectancy at birth stands at about 68.5 years for males and 72.5 years for females (SRS Abridged Life Tables 2019-23, Office of the Registrar General of India), up from under 50 in the early 1970s — a faster improvement than the global average over the same period, reflecting how much scope for gain existed.

## The emerging complication — worth adding

Rising life expectancy produces population ageing and an epidemiological transition from communicable to non-communicable diseases — cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancer and respiratory illness — which are chronic, expensive and require lifelong management rather than cure. India faces the additional difficulty of a double burden: NCDs rising while infectious disease and undernutrition persist. Progress in longevity therefore shifts the health system’s task rather than completing it, and healthy life expectancy (years lived in good health) becomes the more meaningful measure than life expectancy alone.

## Conclusion

Life expectancy at birth measures current mortality conditions rather than individual prospects, and its doubling since 1900 reflects above all the collapse of child mortality — achieved through vaccination, sanitation, nutrition and maternal care rather than through any extension of the maximum human lifespan. India has compressed this transition into a few decades. The next frontier is different in kind: managing non-communicable disease and ageing, where the objective shifts from adding years to life toward adding health to those years.

## Value addition
- India’s data: life expectancy at birth about 68.5 years (male) and 72.5 years (female) — SRS Abridged Life Tables 2019-23, ORGI; birth rate 18.4 per 1,000 in 2023 and infant mortality at a record low (SRS Bulletin 2023).
- Related demographic measures to distinguish:life expectancy at birth versus life expectancy at age 60 (which has risen far less); healthy life expectancy (HALE) — years lived in good health; infant mortality rate, under-five mortality rate and maternal mortality ratio; total fertility rate, with India now at or below replacement level.
- The demographic and epidemiological transitions: the demographic transition moves societies from high birth and death rates to low; the epidemiological transition shifts the disease burden from communicable and maternal-nutritional causes to non-communicable diseases — the “double burden” being India’s distinctive position.
- Global context: global life expectancy around 73 years, with wide variation — over 84 in Japan and Switzerland, under 55 in the worst-affected countries; COVID-19 caused a temporary global decline in 2020-21, since substantially recovered.
- Programmes underpinning India’s gains: Universal Immunisation Programme and Mission Indradhanush; U-WIN; JSY and JSSK; POSHAN 2.0 and PM POSHAN; Swachh Bharat Mission and Jal Jeevan Mission; AB-PMJAY and Ayushman Vay Vandana for those aged 70+; the National Programme for Prevention and Control of NCDs.

## Introduction

The Unique Identification Authority of India is a statutory authority under the Aadhaar Act, 2016, functioning under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. It issues Aadhaar — a 12-digit number linked to minimal demographic and biometric data — and operates the authentication infrastructure behind it. Aadhaar's significance lies not in identity itself but in de-duplicated, verifiable identity, which converts welfare from an entitlement claimed on paper into one authenticated in real time.

Beneficiary

1. What is UIDAI

Established as a statutory authority under the Aadhaar Act, 2016, UIDAI manages enrolment, updation, authentication and e-KYC services. Under Section 7 of the Act, Aadhaar may be required for receipt of subsidies and benefits financed from the Consolidated Fund of India, giving it legal grounding as the identity layer of welfare

delivery.

2. How UIDAT has harnessed IT for targeted delivery (DBT)

- Authentication at the point of delivery: Aadhaar-linked bank accounts and biometric authentication ensure that the person receiving a subsidy is the person entitled to it — eliminating ghost and duplicate beneficiaries that plagued paperbased rolls.
- The JAM trinity as a delivery rail: Aadhaar establishes identity, Jan Dhan accounts receive funds, and mobile confirms receipt; the Aadhaar Payment Bridge routes bulk transfers while the Public Financial Management System tracks fund flow from treasury to beneficiary.
- Measured fiscal outcome: Cumulative DBT transfers had crossed %43.95 lakh crore by May 2025, and DBT has generated cumulative savings of about ¥3.48 lakh crore by plugging leakages — with food subsidies alone accounting for =1.85 lakh crore (53%) through Aadhaar-linked ration-card authentication, 742,534 crore under MGNREGS, and %22,106 crore under PM-KISAN by removing 2.1 crore ineligible beneficiaries (PIB, April and November 2025). Subsidies as a share of total government expenditure roughly halved.
- APinstance: Andhra Pradesh's NTR Bharosa social security pensions are delivered at the doorstep on the 1st of each month against Aadhaar-based verification, and the state's Mana Mitra WhatsApp platform now offers 1,126 services across 35 departments to 58.2 lakh citizens (2026) — showing Aadhaar authentication extended from cash transfer into full service delivery.

3. How Aadhaar helps in financial transactions

- Aadhaar Enabled Payment System (AePS): allows cash withdrawal, deposit, balance enquiry and fund transfer using only the Aadhaar number and a fingerprint, through Business Correspondents — effectively creating a bank branch wherever a microATM exists. This is the single most important instrument for banking the last mile.
- e-KYC: instant paperless verification for opening bank accounts, mutual fund folios and telecom connections, collapsing onboarding time from days to minutes and cutting compliance costs.
- Aadhaar Pay: enables merchants to accept payments through biometric authentication from customers who possess neither a debit card nor a smartphone.

4. Factors that improved life expectancy

India's life expectancy at birth stands at about 68.5 years for males and 72.5 years for females (SRS Abridged Life Tables 2019-23, Office of the Registrar General of India), up from under 50 years in the early 1970s. Key contributors:

- Reduced infant and child mortality: the largest single driver, since deaths in infancy pull the average down disproportionately. India's infant mortality rate reached a record low and the birth rate fell to 18.4 per 1,000 in 2023 (SRS Bulletin 2023, ORGI).

Universal immunisation — from the Expanded Programme (1978) to Mission Indradhanush and U-WIN today — underpins this.

- Maternal health and institutional delivery: Janani Suraksha Yojana and Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram shifted births from home to facility, cutting maternal and neonatal deaths.
- Nutrition and food security: PDS, POSHAN 2.0, ICDS and PM POSHAN reduced the undernutrition that amplifies mortality from ordinary infections.
- Water, sanitation and hygiene: Swachh Bharat Mission and Jal Jeevan Mission cut the diarrhoeal and infectious disease burden — the classic pathway by which sanitation, not medicine, raises longevity.
- Financial protection and access: AB-PMJAY's %5 lakh cover for about 12.37 crore families, Jan Aushadhi generic medicines and expanded emergency care reduced deaths caused by treatment being unaffordable rather than unavailable.

## Conclusion

UIDAT illustrates how a single, well-designed digital public good can restructure

governance: Aadhaar converted welfare delivery from a discretionary, intermediarydependent process into an authenticated, auditable transaction, and simultaneously became the gateway to banking for the previously excluded. Combined with sustained gains in immunisation, nutrition, sanitation and financial protection, these reforms explain India's rise in life expectancy from under 50 to over 70 years within a single lifetime. The remaining task is to ensure that biometric failure never becomes a cause of exclusion.

- Legal and institutional anchors: Aadhaar Act, 2016; Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2018) upheld Aadhaar for welfare under Section 7 while restricting private mandatory use; UIDAI provides exception-handling and grievance redressal for biometric failure.

## Introduction

Cybercrime is any illegal act in which a computer, smartphone, network or digital data is the target, tool or setting of the offence — ranging from data theft and financial fraud to harassment and ransomware attacks that disrupt essential services. As digital adoption has deepened, India has built a multi-layered victim-support system combining rapid reporting, technical response, awareness and legal remedy.

(i) Phishing

- What it is: a deception technique in which the attacker impersonates a trusted entity — a bank, tax department, e-commerce platform or government portal — to induce the victim to disclose credentials, card details or OTPs, or to click a malicious link.
- Variants to name:phishing (email), smishing (SMS), vishing (voice call), and spear phishing (targeted at a specific individual using researched personal details, which is why it succeeds against sophisticated victims).
- Why it works: phishing exploits human trust, not technical vulnerability. No amount of network security prevents a user from voluntarily entering an OTP on a convincing fake page — which is why awareness is the primary defence.
- Indian context: CERT-In has repeatedly issued alerts on phishing campaigns impersonating government bodies and financial institutions, redirecting victims to spoofed websites to harvest credentials. Phishing is the entry point for the bulk of the financial fraud reported through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal.

(ii) Ransomware

- What it is: malicious software that encrypts data or locks systems and demands payment — usually in cryptocurrency — for restoration. Modern variants use double extortion: the data is both encrypted and exfiltrated, so the victim is threatened with publication even if backups exist.
- Why it is systemically serious: ransomware against hospitals, utilities or financial-services vendors converts a data crime into a service failure affecting people who were never the target. An attack on a shared software vendor can cascade across many institutions simultaneously.
- Indian response:CERT-In is the national incident response agency and its 2022 Directions require reporting of specified cyber incidents within a fixed window and retention of logs; NCIIPC protects critical information infrastructure in banking, energy, telecom, transport and health. Official guidance is consistently not to pay the ransom, since payment neither guarantees restoration nor prevents repetition, and to rely instead on offline backups and rapid reporting.

the system | prevention = backups + patching . It shows you understand that different offences need different defences.

How the government helps victims of cybercrime

1. Report — the golden hour - National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in): enables reporting of financial fraud and of crimes against women and children, with an anonymous reporting option for the latter. - Helpline 1930, operated under I4C, for immediate reporting of financial fraud. -CFCFRMS — the Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting and Management System — connects banks, payment intermediaries and police so that a reported transaction can be frozen mid-transfer. Through it, more than Rs. 7,130 crore has been saved across over 23.02 lakh complaints (MHA, reply in Lok Sabha, 2 December 2025). The value of reporting falls sharply with every hour of delay.

2. Recover and disrupt - I4C’s Suspect Registry, with banks and financial institutions, holds over 18.43 lakh suspect identifiers and 24.67 lakh Layer-1 mule accounts, and has helped block fraudulent transactions of about Rs. 8,031.56 crore. - Blocking of instruments used in fraud: over 9.42 lakh SIM cards, 2,63,348 IMEIs, 3,962 Skype IDs and 83,668 WhatsApp accounts (PIB, 2025).

3. Technical and institutional support - I4C (MHA) provides forensic and analytical support to State cyber cells and runs the Cyber Fraud Mitigation Centre. - CERT-In (MeitY) issues advisories and coordinates incident response; NCIIPC secures critical sectors. - Cyber forensic laboratories and CyTrain build investigative capacity among police, prosecutors and judicial officers.

4. Awareness and prevention - Cyber Surakshit Bharat, Cyber Dost and I4C’s national campaigns — including the caller-tune campaign with the Department of Telecommunications and the weekly Cyber-Alert programme with DD News — target the behaviours that phishing and digital-arrest scams exploit. The Prime Minister’s Mann Ki Baat address of 28 October 2024 on “digital arrest” is the clearest instance of prevention through mass communication. - Cyber-safety modules in school curricula and Budget 2025-26’s Rs. 782 crore allocation for cybersecurity projects.

5. Legal remedy - IT Act, 2000: Sections 43 (damage to computer systems), 66 (computer-related offences), 66C (identity theft), 66D (cheating by personation using a computer resource), 66E (violation of privacy), and the 67 series (obscene and sexually explicit material, with 67B covering child sexual abuse material). - Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (in force 1 July 2024, replacing the IPC): covers cheating, forgery, stalking, criminal intimidation and organised crime, including where committed by electronic means. Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 governs the admissibility of electronic evidence. - DPDP Act, 2023 places obligations on data fiduciaries to protect personal data and provides recourse through the Data Protection Board.

## Conclusion

India’s cyber-victim support system is genuinely multi-layered — a single national helpline, a transaction-freezing mechanism that has saved over Rs. 7,130 crore, forensic support to State police, and a modernised legal framework under the IT Act and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. Its effectiveness, however, depends on something the government cannot supply: the victim reporting within the golden hour. Awareness is therefore not a supplement to enforcement in cybercrime — it is the enforcement mechanism that works fastest.

- The four offences in one line each, for whichever pair the paper asks:cyberbullying — repeated humiliation or threat through digital platforms,

disproportionately affecting minors and women, now aggravated by AI-morphed images; cyberstalking — persistent online monitoring, tracking or intimidation, often using location sharing or spyware and frequently overlapping with physical stalking; phishing — impersonation to extract credentials; ransomware — encryption of data for extortion.

- Institutional map:I4C (MHA — coordination, NCRP, 1930, CFCFRMS, Suspect Registry); CERT-In (MeitY — incident response and advisories); NCIIPC (critical information infrastructure); National Cyber Coordination Centre (threat awareness); State cyber cells.

- Protections for women and children: anonymous reporting on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal; Section 67B of the IT Act on child sexual abuse material; the POCSO Act; and takedown obligations on intermediaries under the IT Rules, 2021 as amended in 2026.

- A sharp closing line: in most crime, reporting begins the investigation; in cyber-financial fraud, reporting is the recovery — which is why the 1930 helpline and the golden hour matter more than any subsequent enforcement step.

## Introduction

The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), formed in 1969 and headquartered at Bengaluru, is India’s national space agency, functioning under the Department of Space (created 1972). It grew from the Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR), established in 1962 under Dr. Vikram Sarabhai, whose founding conviction was that a developing country must apply advanced technology to the real problems of its people rather than pursue prestige.

## A brief history
- Origins (1962-69). INCOSPAR was set up in 1962; the Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station (TERLS) in Kerala was chosen for its position near the magnetic equator, and India’s first sounding rocket was launched from Thumba on 21 November 1963. ISRO was formed in 1969, and the Department of Space and Space Commission followed in 1972.
- First satellites (1975-81).Aryabhata (1975), India’s first satellite, was launched by a Soviet vehicle; Bhaskara-I and II pioneered Earth observation; APPLE (1981) demonstrated three-axis-stabilised communication technology. The SITE experiment (1975-76), using NASA’s ATS-6 satellite to broadcast instructional television to some 2,400 villages, established the applications-first philosophy.
- Indigenous launch capability (1980).SLV-3 placed the Rohini satellite in orbit in July 1980, making India the sixth nation capable of independent orbital launch. ASLV followed as a developmental step, then PSLV (first success 1994) and GSLV, with the indigenous cryogenic upper stage proven in January 2014.
- Applications era. The INSAT system (from 1983) transformed telecommunication, broadcasting and cyclone warning; the IRS series (from 1988) built the world’s largest civilian remote-sensing constellation, feeding the National Natural Resources Management System.
- Deep space and the present. Chandrayaan-1 (2008), Mars Orbiter Mission (2013), Chandrayaan-2 (2019), Chandrayaan-3 (2023) and Aditya-L1 (2023); NISAR with NASA (July 2025); Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla’s Axiom-4 flight to the ISS (2025); and the 2020 space reforms creating IN-SPACe and NSIL to open the sector to private enterprise. ISRO is currently chaired by Dr. V. Narayanan.

## Three ISRO centres and their locations
- Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC), Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala — ISRO’s lead centre for launch vehicle design and development: PSLV, GSLV, LVM3, propulsion systems, aerodynamics and materials. Every Indian launch vehicle originates here.
- Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR), Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh — India’s only orbital spaceport, with two operational launch pads and a third approved at Rs. 3,984.86 crore, plus the Solid Propellant Space Booster Plant, vehicle integration facilities and Mission Control. Chosen for its east-coast location, which allows rockets to gain velocity from Earth’s eastward rotation and drop spent stages safely over the Bay of Bengal.
- National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad, Telangana — acquisition, processing, archiving and dissemination of satellite data; operates the Bhuvan geoportal and supports disaster management and resource applications nationally.

## A note on the Chandrayaan missions
- Chandrayaan-1 (2008, PSLV-C11): India’s first lunar mission; provided spectral evidence of water on the Moon, redirecting global lunar exploration toward the poles.
- Chandrayaan-2 (2019, GSLV Mk III): orbiter fully successful and still operational, supplying the imagery later used to validate Chandrayaan-3’s landing site; the Vikram lander hard-landed.
- Chandrayaan-3 (2023, LVM3-M4):soft landing near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023, making India the fourth nation to soft-land on the Moon and the first at the south pole. The Pragyan rover confirmed sulphur in situ; the site was named Shiv Shakti Point and 23 August declared National Space Day.
- Alternatively, Mangalyaan (MOM, 2013): India became the first nation to reach Mars orbit on its maiden attempt, at about Rs. 450 crore, with a spacecraft designed for six months that operated for roughly eight years.

## Conclusion

ISRO’s trajectory — from a sounding rocket carried to a Thumba fishing village to a soft landing at the lunar south pole and an Indian astronaut aboard the ISS — reflects a deliberate strategy: master each capability indigenously, and justify each mission by its application. With Gaganyaan, the Bharatiya Antariksh Station and Chandrayaan-4 ahead, and a private sector now entering under IN-SPACe, the organisation is shifting from being India’s space programme to being its anchor.

## Introduction

A satellite’s orbit is dictated by its job. Orbital altitude determines period, coverage area, signal delay and resolution, and every orbit represents a trade-off among these. India uses four principal orbital regimes — LEO, MEO, GEO and SSO — each matched to a class of mission.

Diagram 1 — draw concentric circles around Earth, to scale by label:Earth --> LEO (160-2,000 km) --> MEO (~20,000 km) --> GEO (35,786 km, equatorial) , with a separate near-vertical ellipse through the poles labelled SSO (polar, ~600-900 km) .

Diagram 2 — for GEO, draw Earth rotating with an arrow and a satellite above the equator with a matching arrow, annotated period = 24 hrs -->

appears fixed .

## Low Earth Orbit (LEO) — 160 to 2,000 km
- Period: roughly 90-120 minutes, so a satellite circles Earth many times daily.
- The trade-off: proximity gives high spatial resolution and low signal delay, but each pass covers a narrow strip and the satellite is visible from any ground point for only minutes — so continuous coverage requires a constellation.
- Uses and Indian examples: Earth observation and imaging (Cartosat, RISAT/EOS), scientific missions, and human spaceflight — Gaganyaan targets about 400 km. Atmospheric drag at these altitudes means orbits decay, which is also why LEO debris eventually re-enters.

## Medium Earth Orbit (MEO) — roughly 2,000 to 35,786 km
- Typical navigation altitude: about 20,000-23,000 km, with periods of roughly 12 hours.
- Why navigation uses it: a MEO satellite is visible from a large fraction of Earth’s surface at once, so a modest constellation of 24-30 satellites guarantees that at least four are visible from anywhere — the minimum a receiver needs.
- Examples: GPS (USA), GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (EU).NavIC does not use MEO — see below.

## Geostationary Orbit (GEO) — 35,786 km above the equator
- The physics: at this altitude the orbital period exactly equals Earth’s rotation period, so a satellite above the equator appears stationary in the sky.
- Why that matters: a fixed household dish or VSAT terminal never has to track the satellite — the entire economics of DTH television and satellite broadband depends on this.
- The trade-off: continuous coverage of about a third of Earth’s surface from one satellite, but at the cost of a signal round-trip delay of roughly a quarter of a second, and coverage that degrades at high latitudes.
- Indian examples:INSAT and GSAT communication satellites; INSAT-3D/3DR meteorological satellites; CMS-03 (2025) for naval communication.
- Where NavIC actually sits: NavIC’s constellation comprises three satellites in geostationary orbit and four in inclined geosynchronous orbit (GSO), all at geosynchronous altitude. The inclined satellites trace a figure-of-eight ground track over the Indian region rather than remaining fixed. This design gives good elevation angles over India specifically — the deliberate choice of a regional rather than global system.

## Sun-Synchronous Orbit (SSO) — a near-polar LEO, typically 600-900 km
- The mechanism: the orbital plane is inclined slightly beyond 90deg so that it precesses at the same rate as Earth’s revolution around the Sun — about one degree per day.
- The consequence: the satellite crosses any given latitude at the same local solar time on every pass, so illumination and shadow conditions are consistent from one image to the next.
- Why this is indispensable: without it, an apparent change between two images could simply be different sun angles. Consistent lighting is what makes change detection — deforestation, urban sprawl, crop growth, glacier retreat — scientifically valid.
- Indian examples:Resourcesat, Oceansat/EOS-06, Cartosat, and NISAR, placed in SSO near 747 km by GSLV-F16 in July 2025.

## Note on PSLV and GSLV launches
- PSLV — ISRO’s workhorse, four-staged with alternating solid and liquid propulsion, optimised for LEO and SSO. Its restartable fourth stage permits multi-orbit deployment; PSLV-C37 released 104 satellites in one mission. It also launched Chandrayaan-1, the Mars Orbiter Mission and Aditya-L1, using Earth-orbit-raising manoeuvres to compensate for limited launch energy.
- GSLV — three-staged with a cryogenic upper stage, built to reach Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit for heavy communication satellites. The indigenous cryogenic stage flew successfully in January 2014. LVM3, the heaviest variant, launched Chandrayaan-2 and Chandrayaan-3 and, as HLVM3, will carry Gaganyaan. GSLV-F16 also placed NISAR into a sun-synchronous polar orbit in July 2025, showing the vehicle is no longer confined to GTO.
- Both launch from SDSC-SHAR, Sriharikota, where a third launch pad has been approved at Rs. 3,984.86 crore.

## Conclusion

Orbit selection is the first design decision in any space mission, and each regime embodies a trade-off: LEO buys resolution at the cost of coverage, GEO buys permanence at the cost of delay, MEO balances the two for navigation, and SSO buys the consistent illumination that makes change detection meaningful. India’s ability to reach all four — through PSLV for low and Sun-synchronous orbits and GSLV/LVM3 for geosynchronous and beyond — is what makes it a full-spectrum space power rather than a specialist one.

## Value addition
- The NavIC orbit point stated plainly: NavIC uses 3 GEO + 4 inclined GSO satellites at geosynchronous altitude, not MEO. GPS, GLONASS and Galileo use MEO. This is a frequently confused distinction and stating it correctly is a visible marker of accuracy.
- Orbit facts worth memorising: GEO altitude 35,786 km; GEO period 23 h 56 m (a sidereal day); LEO period 90-120 minutes; MEO navigation altitude about 20,200 km for GPS; SSO inclination slightly above 90deg (typically ~98deg ) to achieve precession.
- Other orbits to name:Molniya (highly elliptical, for high-latitude coverage); polar orbit (passes over both poles); Lagrange points — Aditya-L1 operates in a halo orbit around the Sun-Earth L1 point about 1.5 million km from Earth, which is not an Earth orbit at all; graveyard orbit above GEO for retired satellites.
- Launch vehicles by orbit: SSLV and PSLV for LEO/SSO; GSLV Mk II and LVM3 for GTO; HLVM3 for human spaceflight; NGLV under development for about 30 tonnes to LEO with partial reusability.
- Why Sriharikota: near-equatorial east-coast siting gives a velocity bonus from Earth’s rotation and safe drop zones over the Bay of Bengal — the reason India’s spaceport is in Andhra Pradesh.
- A quick check that avoids the common error:communication and weather –> GEO; navigation –> MEO (except NavIC, which is GEO/GSO); imaging –> SSO; human spaceflight and space stations –> LEO.

## Introduction

Nuclear energy is the energy released from the nucleus of an atom — through fission, the splitting of heavy nuclei such as uranium-235 or plutonium-239, which powers all commercial reactors; or fusion, the joining of light nuclei, which powers the Sun and remains experimental, with India participating in ITER. Fission releases roughly a million times more energy per unit mass than chemical combustion and produces no carbon dioxide during operation.

## Updating the question’s premise

The seven reactors under construction at the end of 2019 form part of a programme that has since expanded considerably. India today operates around 25 commercial reactors with 8.78 GW installed (MNRE, March 2026), targets 22,480 MW by 2031-32, and under the Nuclear Energy Mission for Viksit Bharat announced in Budget 2025-26, aims for 100 GWe by 2047, with Rs. 20,000 crore for developing at least five indigenous Small Modular Reactors by 2033.

## Advantages of nuclear energy in India
- Dispatchable low-carbon baseload — the property renewables lack. Nuclear generates continuously regardless of sun or wind, at capacity factors above 80%. As solar and wind rise toward half of installed capacity, the system needs a clean source that can serve the evening peak; nuclear is the principal candidate. Kudankulam contributes materially to southern grid stability.
- Very low land intensity. A nuclear plant requires a small fraction of the land needed for equivalent solar or wind output — significant in a densely populated country where land acquisition is a primary constraint on renewable expansion.
- Energy density and fuel logistics. A small mass of fuel yields enormous energy, so fuel transport and storage burdens are trivial compared with coal.
- Indigenous capability and long-term security. The three-stage programme — PHWR –> Fast Breeder –> thorium — is designed around India’s modest uranium and very large thorium reserves; the PFBR at Kalpakkam marks entry into Stage II. Indigenous 700 MWe PHWRs demonstrate technological self-reliance.
- Industrial decarbonisation.Bharat Small Reactors and SMRs such as BSMR-200 and SMR-55 are designed for brownfield sites — repurposing retiring coal plants and supplying captive power to hard-to-abate industries like steel and cement.

## Disadvantages and challenges
- High capital cost and long gestation. Indian nuclear projects have historically taken around a decade against a global best of roughly six years, and delays — as at Jaitapur — compound financing costs.
- Radioactive waste. Spent fuel requires cooling, reprocessing and vitrification, with deep geological disposal as the eventual solution. India’s closed fuel cycle mitigates this by reusing plutonium and uranium, but high-level waste remains.
- Safety and public acceptance.Chernobyl (1986) and Fukushima (2011) shape public perception; siting attracts local opposition over land, displacement and perceived risk.
- Fuel constraints and technology access. Domestic uranium is limited; access to international fuel and technology was restricted for decades by India’s NPT status, and thorium utilisation remains technically distant.
- Capital requirement of the 2047 target. Reaching 100 GW implies investment of the order of several lakh crore rupees — which is precisely why private participation became necessary.

## The NPT and its impact on India — in brief

The NPT (drafted 1968, in force 1970) seeks to prevent proliferation, promote peaceful nuclear use and advance disarmament. India has not signed it, regarding the 1 January 1967 cut-off defining nuclear-weapon states as discriminatory, and objecting that Article VI disarmament obligations have gone unfulfilled. The consequence was three decades of technology denial from 1974. This was substantially resolved by the 2008 India-US Civil Nuclear Agreement, the India-specific IAEA safeguards agreement and the NSG waiver, which restored fuel access without requiring signature. India is a member of the MTCR, Wassenaar Arrangement and Australia Group, but not of the NSG.

Countries not party to the NPT: India, Pakistan, Israel and South Sudan — with North Korea having announced withdrawal in 2003.

The current legislative position: the SHANTI Act, 2025, enacted December 2025, repealed the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010, opening the sector to private and foreign participation.

## Conclusion

Nuclear energy occupies a specific and increasingly important position in India’s mix: it is the only mature, dispatchable, low-carbon, land-efficient source available at scale, which makes it complementary to rather than competitive with renewables. Its constraints — cost, gestation, waste and public acceptance — are real but addressable, and the SHANTI Act, 2025 has removed the liability barrier that stalled investment for fifteen years. Whether the 100 GW target by 2047 is met will depend on execution speed rather than on law or technology.

## Value addition
- Current status: about 25 commercial reactors, 8.78 GW installed (MNRE, March 2026); 22,480 MW targeted by 2031-32; 100 GWe by 2047 under the Nuclear Energy Mission; Rs. 20,000 crore for five indigenous SMRs by 2033; roadmap of about 54 GW from NPCIL and 46 GW from other public, private and joint-venture participants.
- The three stages: Stage I PHWRs on natural uranium producing plutonium; Stage II Fast Breeder Reactors using that plutonium and breeding more fuel than consumed (PFBR, Kalpakkam); Stage III thorium-based reactors using U-233. Conceived by Homi Bhabha around India’s resource profile.
- Institutions: Department of Atomic Energy; NPCIL (operations); BHAVINI (breeder reactors); BARC (research); IGCAR Kalpakkam; AERB (independent regulation); Nuclear Fuel Complex, Hyderabad; UCIL for uranium mining.
- Reactor types to distinguish: PHWR (natural uranium, heavy water moderator — India’s indigenous mainstay, now at 700 MWe); LWR/VVER (enriched uranium, imported — Kudankulam); FBR; BSMR-200 and SMR-55 for brownfield and captive use.
- Fuel reserves: uranium at Jaduguda and Turamdih (Jharkhand) and Tummalapalle, Kadapa district, Andhra Pradesh — among the world’s larger deposits; thorium as monazite in the coastal sands of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, among the world’s largest reserves.
- Waste management terms: cooling pools –> reprocessing (closed fuel cycle) –> vitrification in borosilicate glass –> engineered surface storage –> deep geological repository.

## Introduction

Clean energy is energy produced with minimal or no emission of greenhouse gases and air pollutants. The term is broader than “renewable”: nuclear power is clean but not renewable, since uranium is finite, while a renewable source such as traditional biomass burning is not necessarily clean. India, committed under the Paris Agreement to net zero by 2070, has made clean energy central to its development strategy.

CARBON , overlapping A and additionally containing nuclear . The overlap is the point of the diagram.

## Sources of clean energy and how they work
- Solar.Photovoltaic cells convert sunlight directly into electricity through the photovoltaic effect, in which photons excite electrons across a semiconductor junction. Solar thermal systems concentrate sunlight to heat a fluid, raise steam and drive a turbine. India receives about 300 sunny days a year and 4-7 kWh per square metre per day.
- Wind. Moving air turns turbine blades; the rotor drives a generator through a gearbox. Power output rises with the cube of wind speed, which is why siting and hub height matter far more than turbine count.
- Hydropower. Falling or flowing water turns a turbine. Large hydro provides dispatchable generation and pumped storage — pumping water uphill using surplus power and releasing it at peak — makes it a storage technology as well as a generation one.
- Biomass and bio-CNG. Organic material — crop residue, animal waste, municipal waste — is combusted, gasified or anaerobically digested to produce heat, electricity or compressed biogas. It is carbon-neutral in principle because the carbon released was recently absorbed by the plant.
- Geothermal. Heat from the Earth’s interior raises steam to drive turbines. India’s potential is concentrated in identified provinces such as Puga Valley (Ladakh), Tattapani (Chhattisgarh) and Manikaran, but commercial generation remains negligible.
- Tidal and wave. Tidal barrages or turbines convert the kinetic and potential energy of tides. India’s estimated potential is around 8,000 MW along the Gulf of Khambhat, Gulf of Kutch and the Sundarbans, essentially untapped.
- Nuclear. Controlled fission of uranium releases heat that raises steam. It is low-carbon and dispatchable, providing baseload power — the property renewables lack.
- Green hydrogen. Water is split by electrolysis using renewable electricity, producing a storable fuel for sectors that cannot be directly electrified — steel, fertiliser, refining and heavy transport.

## Which are widely used in India
- Widely used: solar (150.26 GW), wind (56.09 GW), large hydro (51.41 GW), bio-power (11.75 GW) and small hydro (5.17 GW) — together 274.68 GW of renewable capacity as on 31 March 2026, within non-fossil capacity of 283.46 GW including nuclear at 8.78 GW (MNRE).
- Growing rapidly: rooftop and distributed solar under PM Surya Ghar and PM-KUSUM, which together contributed 16.3 GW in 2025-26; green hydrogen under the National Green Hydrogen Mission.
- Negligible in practice: geothermal and tidal remain at pilot or exploratory stage despite assessed potential — worth stating, since an honest answer distinguishes potential from deployment.
- Standing: India ranks third globally in renewable installed capacity (IRENA, 2026) and crossed 50% non-fossil capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of target.
- AP instance: Andhra Pradesh’s Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024 targets over 160 GW, including 78.5 GW solar, 35 GW wind and 22 GW pumped storage; the State hosts the Kurnool and NP Kunta Ultra Mega Solar Parks.

## Conclusion

Clean energy in India is now dominated by solar and wind, supported by hydro, with nuclear providing low-carbon baseload and green hydrogen emerging for hard-to-abate sectors. Geothermal and tidal, though technically available, remain untapped — a reminder that resource potential and commercial deployment are different things. The transition’s next phase depends less on adding new sources than on adding storage, which alone allows clean energy to serve demand when the sun sets.

## Value addition
- The definitional triad:renewable (naturally replenished); clean/low-carbon (renewable plus nuclear); green (renewable with minimal environmental impact). Nuclear is clean but not renewable; traditional biomass burning is renewable but not clean.
- PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana (15 February 2024): rooftop solar for 1 crore households with up to 300 free units per month; subsidy of 60% of system cost up to 2 kW and 40% of additional cost for 2-3 kW, capped at 3 kW; Model Solar Village in each district; incentive of Rs. 1,000 per rooftop installation to ULBs and Gram Panchayats.
- PM-KUSUM: three components — decentralised solar plants on barren land, standalone solar pumps, and solarisation of grid-connected pumps — allowing farmers to sell surplus power.
- Geothermal and tidal potential sites to name: Puga Valley and Chumathang (Ladakh), Tattapani (Chhattisgarh), Manikaran (Himachal Pradesh); Gulf of Khambhat and Gulf of Kutch (Gujarat) and the Sundarbans for tidal.
- Pumped storage as the bridge technology: it is both generation and storage, and India’s 22 GW target in Andhra Pradesh alone signals its centrality to firming variable renewables.
- SDG linkage: SDG 7 (affordable and clean energy) and SDG 13 (climate action); India co-founded the International Solar Alliance, headquartered at Gurugram.

## Introduction

The Sustainable Development Goals — 17 goals with 169 targets — were adopted by all UN member states in September 2015 under the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, succeeding the Millennium Development Goals. Their organising principle is “leave no one behind”. India’s position is decisive for global attainment: given its population, the SDGs cannot be met globally unless they are met in India.

## Four goals and India’s route to them

SDG 1 — No Poverty - Requirement: end poverty in all forms; implement nationally appropriate social protection systems. - India’s instruments: MGNREGA (guaranteed rural wage employment), PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana and the National Food Security Act, PM Awas Yojana (housing), PM Jan Dhan Yojana with DBT — cumulative transfers crossing Rs. 43.95 lakh crore by May 2025 with savings of about Rs. 3.48 lakh crore from plugged leakages (PIB), Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY protecting about 12.37 crore families from catastrophic health expenditure, and PM Vishwakarma and livelihood missions. - Route forward: multidimensional poverty has fallen sharply, but the task is now consolidating gains — portable entitlements for migrants, and social protection for informal workers registered on e-Shram.

SDG 4 — Quality Education - Requirement: inclusive, equitable quality education and lifelong learning. - India’s instruments:NEP 2020; Samagra Shiksha; NIPUN Bharat for foundational literacy and numeracy by Grade 3; PM POSHAN (mid-day meals) addressing both nutrition and attendance; DIKSHA, PM e-VIDYA with 200 DTH channels, and SWAYAM; ULLAS for adult literacy; PM SHRI model schools. - Route forward: enrolment is near-universal; the deficit is learning outcomes, which is why NIPUN Bharat targets foundational competence rather than attendance. Teacher quality and vacancy remain the binding constraint.

SDG 7 — Affordable and Clean Energy - Requirement: universal access to affordable, reliable, modern energy; substantially increase the renewable share. - India’s instruments:Saubhagya for household electrification; Ujjwala for clean cooking fuel; PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana (1 crore rooftop households); PM-KUSUM; the National Solar Mission and National Green Hydrogen Mission. - Progress:non-fossil capacity reached 283.46 GW as on 31 March 2026, with renewables at 274.68 GW; India crossed 50% non-fossil installed capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of its NDC target, and ranks third globally in renewable installed capacity (IRENA, 2026). - Route forward: the constraint has shifted from generation to storage and distribution finance.

SDG 13 — Climate Action - Requirement: strengthen resilience and adaptive capacity; integrate climate measures into national policy. - India’s instruments:NAPCC with eight missions and State Action Plans; Panchamrit commitments; net zero by 2070; Mission LIFE for demand-side action; Carbon Credit Trading Scheme; NDMA and the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure, co-founded by India. - Route forward: adaptation finance for agriculture and coastal zones, and heat action plans for cities — India’s adaptation need exceeds its mitigation need in the near term.

(Other goals that make strong alternative choices: SDG 2 with PM-POSHAN and natural farming; SDG 3 with Ayushman Bharat and eSanjeevani; SDG 6 with Jal Jeevan Mission and Swachh Bharat; SDG 5 with Beti Bachao Beti Padhao and women’s reservation.)

## India’s monitoring architecture — the distinctive contribution
- NITI Aayog is the nodal body for SDG coordination; MoSPI maintains the National Indicator Framework.
- The SDG India Index, first published in 2018, ranks States and UTs — the world’s first sub-national SDG index of its kind. Its 2023-24 edition covered 16 goals and 113 indicators, with India’s composite score rising to 71 from 66 in 2020-21; SDG 13 (Climate Action) showed the sharpest improvement, from 54 to 67.
- India has presented Voluntary National Reviews to the UN High-Level Political Forum (2017 and 2020).
- Localisation: SDGs are being mapped to Gram Panchayat Development Plans through the Localisation of SDGs framework and the nine themes of the Panchayat Development Index, so the goals reach the village level.

Challenges: inter-State and intra-State disparity; financing gaps; data availability and lag at district level; and the tension between growth and environmental targets.

AP relevance: Andhra Pradesh performs strongly on several SDG India Index parameters, particularly clean energy and infrastructure, while its literacy indicators remain below the national average — making SDG 4 the State’s most binding constraint. The State’s APCNF natural farming programme is a nationally cited contribution to SDGs 2, 13 and 15.

## Conclusion

The SDGs translate an abstract commitment into 17 measurable goals, and India’s approach — through the SDG India Index and localisation to panchayats — has converted a global agenda into a federal and eventually local one. Progress on clean energy has exceeded targets, while learning outcomes and nutrition remain the hardest goals. With the 2030 deadline approaching, the priority is not new schemes but convergence of existing ones and reliable district-level data to direct them.

## Value addition
- The 17 SDGs — worth knowing in groups:people (1-5: poverty, hunger, health, education, gender); planet (6, 12-15: water, consumption, climate, oceans, land); prosperity (7-11: energy, work, industry, inequality, cities); peace (16); partnership (17). The five Ps framing is a quick structuring device.

- The distinction worth making: MDGs (2000-15) were eight goals directed at developing countries; SDGs are 17 goals universally applicable to all countries, including developed ones — a shift from aid to shared responsibility.

## Introduction

An earthquake is the sudden release of accumulated elastic strain energy in the Earth’s crust, radiating as seismic waves. India’s exposure is substantial: about 59% of its land area is vulnerable to moderate to severe seismic hazard, spanning Zones II to V under IS 1893. The essential policy insight is that earthquakes cannot be prevented or predicted — but their consequences are almost entirely a function of construction quality and preparedness, both of which are controllable.

## Causes of earthquakes
- Tectonic — the dominant cause. Lithospheric plates move relative to one another; friction locks them at boundaries while stress accumulates, until it exceeds the rock’s strength and the fault slips suddenly. The Himalayan seismic belt results from the ongoing convergence of the Indian and Eurasian plates at roughly 5 cm per year, making it among the world’s most seismically active continental zones. Boundary types: convergent (Himalaya), divergent (mid-ocean ridges) and transform (San Andreas).
- Intraplate. Earthquakes also occur far from plate boundaries within stable continental regions, driven by reactivation of ancient faults — Latur (1993) and Jabalpur (1997) are the Indian examples, and they matter because peninsular India was long assumed to be safe.
- Volcanic. Magma movement generates tremors, often preceding eruptions; not significant in mainland India, but relevant at Barren Island in the Andamans.
- Collapse. Cave-ins in caverns and mine workings produce shallow, low-magnitude events.
- Human-induced or triggered.Reservoir-triggered seismicity — Koyna (1967, M ~6.3) being the world’s most-studied case — fluid injection, deep mining and groundwater extraction. Human activity typically triggers the release of pre-existing tectonic stress rather than creating the energy.

## Can earthquakes be prevented or predicted?
- Prevention: no. Plate motion is driven by mantle convection and cannot be arrested. What can be prevented is the disaster: “earthquakes do not kill people; buildings do.” Seismic-resistant construction, retrofitting, land-use zoning and enforcement of IS 1893 and IS 13920 determine casualty numbers far more than magnitude does.
- Prediction: no — and the distinction matters.Prediction means specifying the time, place and magnitude of a future earthquake within narrow limits. This has never been reliably achieved and is not currently considered scientifically feasible. Precursors that have been investigated — radon emission, groundwater level changes, foreshocks, electromagnetic anomalies, animal behaviour — are inconsistent and produce unacceptable false-alarm rates.
- What is achievable:

Seismic hazard zonation — probabilistic mapping of expected ground shaking, expressed in India as Zones II to V under IS 1893. This is long-term forecasting of where, not when. Long-term probabilistic forecasting — statements of the probability of an event exceeding a given magnitude in a region over decades, based on fault slip rates and historical seismicity. The concept of a seismic gap — a segment of an active fault that has not ruptured recently and has therefore accumulated strain — identifies the central Himalayan seismic gap as a region of particular concern. Earthquake Early Warning (EEW) — the practical achievement. It does not predict; it detects the earthquake as it begins and exploits the fact that fast-travelling, low-damage P-waves arrive before slower, destructive S-waves and surface waves. This yields seconds to tens of seconds of warning — enough to halt trains, shut gas pipelines, stop lifts at the nearest floor and trigger drop-cover-hold responses. India has an operational system in Uttarakhand, and the National Center for Seismology is developing wider capability.

## Relief agency actions after an earthquake

Common to both settings — the first 72 hours: - Rapid damage and needs assessment using satellite imagery, drones and field teams; activation of the Incident Response System under NDMA. - Search and rescue by NDRF and SDRF, prioritising collapsed structures with survival probability; the “golden hours” concept, since survival falls sharply after 72 hours under rubble. - Medical triage, field hospitals, trauma and crush-injury management (crush syndrome requiring dialysis capability), and blood supply. - Restoration of lifelines — water, sanitation, power, telecom — and temporary shelter with attention to women, children, the elderly and persons with disabilities. - Aftershock preparedness, since aftershocks collapse already-weakened structures and are a major cause of secondary casualties among rescuers and returning residents. - Epidemic prevention, dead body management with dignity and identification, and psychosocial support.

Additional priorities in an INLAND region: - Landslide and rockfall risk, particularly in Himalayan terrain, blocking access roads and isolating villages —

requiring air-lifted relief and route clearance as a first priority. - Landslide-dammed lakes, which can burst catastrophically days later; these require immediate aerial reconnaissance and controlled breaching. - Dam and reservoir safety inspection for structures near the epicentre. - Extended logistics chains over damaged mountain roads; helicopter-dependent access. - Livestock relief and fodder, given the rural economy of most inland seismic zones.

Additional priorities in a COASTAL region: - Immediate tsunami evacuation — the decisive difference. A coastal earthquake may generate a tsunami arriving within minutes for a near-field source. Relief agencies must move people inland and to higher ground before assessing structural damage — the opposite of inland sequencing. The Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (ITEWC) at INCOIS, Hyderabad, issues warnings within about 10 minutes of an undersea earthquake. - Do not return until the all-clear, since later tsunami waves are frequently larger than the first. - Port, harbour and fishing fleet damage assessment; recovery of stranded fishermen at sea using NavIC and coastal radio. - Saltwater contamination of wells and farmland, requiring alternative drinking water supply. - Liquefaction in saturated coastal and alluvial soils, causing buildings to tilt or sink even without direct shaking damage — a distinct engineering assessment. - Coastal protection structures, embankments and industrial installations (refineries, chemical plants, ports) inspected for secondary hazard.

## Conclusion

Earthquakes cannot be prevented or predicted, but this is far less limiting than it sounds: seismic zonation tells us where, building codes determine who survives, and early warning systems now provide seconds that can stop a train or a lift. Relief must then be differentiated by geography — inland response is dominated by landslides and access, coastal response by the imperative of tsunami evacuation within minutes. India’s institutional architecture, from NDMA and NDRF to the ITEWC, is designed around exactly this distinction.

- Seismic zonation: India divided into Zones II-V under IS 1893; Zone V includes the North-East, Kutch, Andaman & Nicobar and parts of the Himalaya; about 59% of India’s land area is prone to moderate-to-severe seismic hazard. Andhra Pradesh lies largely in Zones II-III.

## Introduction

Solid waste is any discarded solid material arising from human activity — household, commercial, industrial, agricultural or institutional. Its systematic classification matters operationally, because the treatment route is determined by the waste’s source and composition: organic waste goes to composting, hazardous waste to secure disposal, inert waste to landfill.

## Classification by source
- Municipal solid waste — residential, commercial and institutional: food waste, packaging, paper, textiles.
- Industrial waste — manufacturing processes: chemicals, solvents, sludge, process residues, often hazardous.
- Bio-medical waste — hospitals, clinics and laboratories: contaminated dressings, sharps, anatomical waste, expired pharmaceuticals.
- Agricultural waste — crop residue, husk, spoiled grain, animal manure.
- E-waste — discarded electrical and electronic equipment.
- Construction and demolition waste — concrete, brick, wood, metal, largely inert but high in volume.
- Radioactive waste — from nuclear facilities, hospitals and research, governed separately by AERB.

## Classification by type or composition
- Biodegradable — decomposes biologically: food, garden and paper waste.
- Non-biodegradable — plastics, glass, metals, synthetic materials.
- Hazardous — toxic, corrosive, reactive, flammable or infectious: batteries, solvents, sharps, pesticides.
- Inert — chemically unreactive: concrete, sand, rubble.

non-biodegradable / hazardous / inert) on the other, showing that the two classifications are independent and cross-cutting.

## Steps in solid waste management — following the waste hierarchy

The governing principle is the hierarchy: Reduce –> Reuse –> Recycle –> Recover –> Dispose, with landfilling the last resort.

- Generation and storage at source. Segregated storage under the SWM Rules, 2016: green bins for wet/biodegradable, blue for dry/recyclable, and black or red for domestic hazardous waste. Segregation at source determines the value of everything downstream.
- Collection and transportation. Door-to-door collection in covered vehicles; GPS-enabled fleets and GIS route optimisation in cities including Indore and Visakhapatnam; transfer stations for large cities.
- Segregation and sorting.Material Recovery Facilities (MRFs) separate dry waste into paper, plastic grades, metal and glass; waste-picker integration improves recovery rates at low cost.
- Processing and treatment.Composting and vermicomposting and biomethanation for biodegradable waste; recycling for plastics, paper, glass and metal; refuse-derived fuel from high-calorific rejects; incineration for biomedical and specified hazardous waste; bio-mining for legacy dumpsites.
- Final disposal. Only inert and non-recoverable residue to engineered sanitary landfills with liners, leachate collection and treatment, gas capture and daily cover.

## Advantages and disadvantages of landfills
- **Advantages** — Disadvantages
- **Low cost per tonne for large volumes in the short term** — Leachate contamination of groundwater and soil where liners and collection fail
- **Handles all residual fractions, including what cannot be recycled or composted** — Methane emissions — a greenhouse gas roughly 28 times more potent than CO2 over a century
- **Compaction reduces volume, maximising land use** — Land requirement and permanence — land is effectively sterilised for decades
- **Landfill gas recovery can generate energy from captured methane** — Public opposition (NIMBY) and siting difficulty
- **Simple technology, requiring less operational skill than WTE or composting** — Odour, vectors and fires; risk of slope failure at overloaded dumps

A necessary distinction: an engineered sanitary landfill — with liner, leachate treatment, gas capture and daily cover — is a legitimate final-disposal facility. An open dump is not a landfill at all. Most of India’s 2,452 dumpsites fall in the second category, which is why the disadvantages above are so visible in practice.

## Conclusion

Solid waste classification is not academic — it determines the treatment route, and misclassification at the household bin propagates through the entire system. The management sequence works only if segregation holds at source. Landfills remain necessary for inert residue, but should be engineered rather than improvised, and minimised through recovery: India’s shift toward bio-mining legacy dumps and processing organic waste locally reflects a move from disposal-led to recovery-led waste management.

## Introduction

Soil erosion is the detachment, transport and deposition of topsoil by water, wind, gravity or ice. Its severity follows from a simple fact of timescale: soil forms at a rate of the order of a centimetre over several centuries, while erosion can remove that depth in a single season. Erosion is therefore effectively irreversible on human timescales, which is why prevention matters far more than remediation.

## Agents of soil erosion
- Water — the most widespread agent in India. Rainfall impact, surface runoff, rivers and waves detach and transport particles, especially where vegetation cover is sparse and slopes are steep.
- Wind — dominant in arid and semi-arid regions such as Rajasthan and parts of Gujarat, lifting and transporting fine, dry, loose particles through suspension, saltation and surface creep.
- Gravity — mass movement including landslides, slumps and soil creep, significant in the Himalaya and the Western Ghats.
- Glaciers — abrasion and plucking in the high Himalaya.
- Human activity — deforestation, overgrazing, shifting cultivation, mining, construction and unsuitable tillage act as accelerating agents rather than independent ones.

## Stages of erosion — the progression that matters

1. Splash erosion — raindrop impact detaches individual soil particles and forms a surface crust. This is the initiating stage, and preventing it — through vegetative or residue cover that intercepts raindrops — is the cheapest possible intervention. 2. Sheet erosion — uniform removal of a thin layer of topsoil across the surface. The most damaging stage in aggregate and the least visible, because the field looks unchanged while its most fertile layer is removed. Detected by exposed subsoil colour, exposed plant roots and pedestalled stones. 3. Rill erosion — runoff concentrates into small channels a few centimetres deep, still removable by normal ploughing. 4. Gully erosion — rills deepen and widen into channels that cannot be crossed by farm machinery, permanently removing land from cultivation. 5. Ravine formation — advanced, deep and branching gullies, as in the Chambal ravines of Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, which have taken large areas out of use.

The policy conclusion from the sequence: intervention cost rises by orders of magnitude at each stage — from a cover crop at the splash stage to gully plugging and mechanical structures at the fourth. Erosion control is therefore an early-stage intervention or an expensive one.

Wind erosion has its own stages: surface creep (large particles rolling), saltation (medium particles bouncing — the dominant transport mode) and suspension (fine particles carried long distances).

## Effects of soil erosion
- Loss of topsoil fertility — the eroded layer is the one containing organic matter and nutrients, so the loss is disproportionate to the depth removed.
- Declining agricultural productivity and rising fertiliser requirement to compensate.
- Reduced water-holding capacity, increasing drought vulnerability.
- Siltation of reservoirs, canals and river beds — shortening reservoir life, reducing irrigation and hydropower capacity, and raising flood levels.
- Water pollution — sediment carrying nutrients and pesticides causing turbidity and eutrophication.
- Land degradation, gullying and desertification, permanently removing land from production.
- Loss of biodiversity and soil microbial life.
- Economic and social consequences — falling farm incomes, indebtedness and distress migration from degraded rainfed regions.
- Carbon loss — soil organic carbon oxidised and released, so erosion is also a climate issue.

## Factors affecting soil erosion

Natural: - Rainfall erosivity — intensity matters far more than total amount; a short, intense downpour erodes more than the same volume falling gently over a day. - Soil erodibility — texture, structure, organic matter content and infiltration capacity; silty soils with low organic matter are most erodible. -Slope — both gradient and length; erosion increases sharply with both. - Vegetation cover — the single most protective factor, intercepting raindrops, binding soil with roots and slowing runoff. - Climate and wind velocity.

Human-induced: - Deforestation and removal of vegetative cover. - Overgrazing, preventing regeneration and compacting soil. - Shifting cultivation with shortened fallow cycles. - Unsuitable tillage — ploughing up and down the slope rather than along the contour. - Monocropping and residue removal, reducing organic matter. - Mining, quarrying and construction exposing bare soil. - Faulty irrigation causing waterlogging and salinisation.

## Measures for soil conservation — matched to the erosion type

Agronomic (vegetative) — the first line - Contour cropping — cultivating along the contour so each furrow acts as a small barrier. - Strip cropping — alternating erosion-permitting and erosion-resisting crops in strips. - Cover crops, mulching and residue retention, addressing splash erosion at the source. - Crop rotation with legumes, restoring organic matter and structure. - Agroforestry and alley cropping; vetiver hedges as vegetative barriers, valued for their deep, dense binding roots.

Mechanical (engineering) — for later stages - Contour bunding and graded bunding on gentle slopes. - Terracing on steep slopes, converting a long slope into a series of level steps. - Gully plugging, check dams and gabion structures to arrest advanced erosion. - Percolation tanks and farm ponds to detain runoff and recharge groundwater.

For wind erosion - Shelterbelts and windbreaks of trees planted perpendicular to prevailing wind. - Sand dune stabilisation with micro-windbreaks and grasses. - Strip cropping perpendicular to wind direction; stubble mulching.

Institutional and programmatic - WDC-PMKSY 2.0 (2021-26) — watershed treatment on the ridge-to-valley principle, with 49.50 lakh ha target and Rs. 8,134 crore outlay, monitored through Srishti and Drishti. - MGNREGA water and soil conservation works, providing the labour finance. - Soil Health Card Scheme; National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture; National Mission on Natural Farming; National Agroforestry Policy, 2014. - Green India Mission and CAMPA for afforestation on degraded land. - Research institutions:ICAR-IISWC, Dehradun (soil and water conservation); CAZRI, Jodhpur (arid zone); CSSRI, Karnal (salinity); NBSS&LUP, Nagpur (soil survey). - AP instance:APCNF covers over 1.77 million farmers with practices — permanent soil cover, diverse cropping, minimal disturbance — that directly address splash and sheet erosion at source, with reported water savings up to 50%; and Neeru-Chettu linking water conservation with plantation.

## Conclusion

Soil erosion progresses through identifiable stages, and its central practical lesson is that the cheapest intervention is the earliest: a cover crop preventing splash erosion costs a fraction of the gully plugging required three stages later. Because soil regenerates over centuries while erosion works in seasons, conservation is not restoration but prevention. India’s watershed programmes apply this correctly through ridge-to-valley treatment; the gap is in maintaining treated watersheds beyond the project period.

## Value addition

- Wind erosion transport modes:surface creep (large particles), saltation (medium particles bouncing — the dominant mode), suspension (fine particles over long distances).
- Soil formation rate: of the order of a centimetre over several centuries — the fact that makes erosion effectively irreversible and prevention non-negotiable.
- Degradation data: the Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas of India (ISRO/SAC) provides the national assessment; the Wastelands Atlas of India, 5th edition (2019) records wasteland at about 55.76 million ha (16.96%); India has committed to restore 26 million hectares by 2030 (UNCCD COP14, New Delhi, 2019).
- The ridge-to-valley principle: watershed treatment must begin at the highest point; a check dam built before the ridge is treated silts up. This is the single most examinable technical point in soil and watershed questions.
- Programmes and institutions:WDC-PMKSY 2.0 with Srishti and Drishti; MGNREGA; Soil Health Card; NMSA; National Mission on Natural Farming; National Agroforestry Policy 2014; ICAR-IISWC Dehradun; CAZRI Jodhpur; CSSRI Karnal.

The three terms are not interchangeable. Gene therapy is a clinical purpose — correcting a disease-causing gene in a patient. Transgenesis is a cross-species outcome — inserting foreign DNA to create a new heritable trait. Genome editing is a technique — making a targeted change at a chosen genomic address, which may or may not introduce foreign DNA. Gene enhancement is neither a purpose nor a technique but an intent — using these tools beyond the restoration of normal function. Conflating them is the commonest error in this question; the ethical weight of each falls at a different point.

1. Gene therapy — the therapeutic frontier and its equity problem. India now has two flagship examples. More recently, PIB (19 November 2025) reported the launch of BIRSA 101, India’s first indigenous CRISPR-based gene therapy for sickle cell disease, developed at CSIR-Institute of Genomics and Integrative Biology on its engineered enFnCas9 platform and transferred to the Serum Institute of India for scale-up.Ethical concern: the dominant issue is distributive justice, not safety — imported CRISPR therapies have been priced at Rs. 20-25 crore per patient, placing a cure beyond a public health system; the indigenous route is the ethical response. Secondary concerns are long-term uncertainty (India’s 2019 guidelines mandate follow-up of at least five years, extendable to ten post-commercialisation) and the risk of false hope in trial recruitment. 2. Transgenic organisms — ecological and socio-economic ethics.Bt cotton, carrying cry1Ac from Bacillus thuringiensis, was approved by GEAC in 2002 and remains India’s only commercially cultivated GM crop. Ethical concerns: resistance evolution has already materialised — pink bollworm resistance to Bt cotton validated the objection that a single-toxin monoculture creates selection pressure; gene flow to wild relatives threatens landraces; and proprietary seed raises questions of farmer autonomy, partially answered by the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act, 2001, which uniquely preserves the Indian farmer’s right to save and exchange seed. The contested nature of transgenesis in food crops was underlined when the Supreme Court delivered a split verdict on GM mustard DMH-11 in Gene Campaign v. Union of India on 23 July 2024, while unanimously directing the Union to frame a National Policy on GM crops through stakeholder consultation. 3. Genome editing and enhancement — consent and equity at the germline. The He Jiankui episode (China, 2018), in which embryos were edited for HIV resistance, remains the defining ethical failure: an embryo cannot consent, the edit is heritable by all descendants, and off-target effects are irreversible across generations. Enhancement compounds this — editing for height, musculature or cognition converts a medical technology into a positional good, so that genetic advantage tracks purchasing power and inequality becomes biologically inscribed. India has pre-empted this: the National Guidelines for Gene Therapy Product Development and Clinical Trials (ICMR-DBT, 2019) prohibit germline gene therapy, and the National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants (ICMR, 2017) confine research to somatic-cell interventions. 4. When genome editing can be considered ethical — a five-test checklist. Infographic 2 — draw as a five-rung ladder, ethical only if all rungs are met:

## Test Requirement

Somatic only Edit confined to the patient’s own cells; not heritable

Therapeutic necessity Serious disease with unmet need — not enhancement

Informed consent Competent, voluntary, documented; no consent is possible at embryo stage

Proportionality and evidence Benefit demonstrably outweighs off-target risk; long-term follow-up mandated

Equity and oversight Affordable access; approval by IBSC/RCGM, CDSCO under NDCT Rules 2019, and institutional ethics review

To these, global instruments add a floor: the UNESCO Universal Declaration on the Human Genome and Human Rights (1997) treats the human genome as the heritage of humanity, and the WHO governance framework and recommendations on human genome editing (2021) calls for a public registry of all human genome-editing research and rejects germline clinical use in the present state of knowledge.

Andhra Pradesh anchor: Sickle cell disease burden in AP is concentrated in tribal districts such as Alluri Sitharama Raju and Parvathipuram Manyam, which are covered by the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (launched 2023, targeting elimination by 2047) — making BIRSA 101 directly relevant to the state. On the manufacturing side, the Andhra Pradesh MedTech Zone (AMTZ), Visakhapatnam, India’s first medical device park, and the co-located Kalam Institute of Health Technology, supported by DBT, position the state within the cell-and-gene therapy device and diagnostics ecosystem.

## Conclusion

The distinction between these approaches is not semantic but moral: gene therapy repairs, transgenesis creates, genome editing enables, and enhancement exceeds. Ethical evaluation must therefore attach to intent and heritability, not to the tool.

India’s architecture — somatic-only permission, a germline ban, CDSCO oversight and an indigenous, affordability-first innovation model exemplified by NexCAR19 and BIRSA 101 — offers a defensible middle path between prohibition and permissiveness. Genome editing becomes ethical precisely when it heals a specific person, with their consent, at a price a public health system can bear, under independent scrutiny — and stops being ethical the moment it is used to buy an advantage for a lineage.

## Introduction

The 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna for developing CRISPR-Cas9 as a method of genome editing. Its origin, however, is not in a laboratory but in an evolutionary arms race: CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) is an adaptive immune system that bacteria and archaea evolved against bacteriophages. The insight that transformed biology was that this bacterial memory system could be reprogrammed to cut any chosen DNA sequence — converting a microbial defence into a universal editing tool.

1. How CRISPR functions in nature. When a bacteriophage injects its DNA, the bacterium excises a short fragment and files it as a spacer between palindromic repeats in its CRISPR array — a heritable molecular memory of past infection (adaptation). On re-infection the array is transcribed and processed, with the help of trans-activating crRNA, into mature crRNA guides that load onto Cas proteins (expression). The guide then scans invading DNA for a complementary sequence; critically, Cas9 will only cut if the target is flanked by a short Protospacer Adjacent Motif (PAM), which is present in the virus but absent in the bacterium’s own CRISPR array — this is how the system avoids attacking itself. On a match, Cas9’s two nuclease domains cleave both DNA strands (interference).

2. How it was adapted as a research tool. The engineering breakthrough was to fuse crRNA and tracrRNA into a single guide RNA (gRNA), whose 20-nucleotide sequence can be synthesised to match any genomic address. Cas9 then functions as programmable molecular scissors. The cell’s repair machinery determines the outcome: error-prone non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) creates small insertions or deletions that knock out a gene (SDN-1), while homology-directed repair (HDR) with a supplied template makes a precise substitution (SDN-2/SDN-3). Newer derivatives — base editing and prime editing — rewrite single letters without a double-strand break, reducing off-target damage. 3. Clinical application — and India’s arrival at the frontier. Globally, Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel) became the first regulator-approved CRISPR therapy in 2023 (UK MHRA and US FDA) for sickle cell disease and transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia. India’s own entry followed: PIB (19 November 2025) reported the launch of BIRSA 101, India’s first indigenous CRISPR-based gene therapy for sickle cell disease, developed at CSIR-IGIB using its engineered enFnCas9 platform, with a technology transfer and collaboration agreement signed with the Serum Institute of India for affordable scale-up. Its significance is economic as much as scientific — it targets a fraction of the Rs. 20-25 crore per-patient cost of imported CRISPR therapy, and directly serves the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023), which aims at a sickle-cell-free India by 2047. 4. Agricultural application — India as first mover. In May 2025 ICAR released DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala) and Pusa DST Rice 1, the world’s first genome-edited rice varieties, developed with CRISPR-Cas at ICAR-IIRR Hyderabad and ICAR-IARI New Delhi respectively. Because these carry no foreign DNA, they fall outside the GMO route. ICAR reports a 19% yield increase, about 20% lower greenhouse gas emissions and a saving of 7,500 million cubic metres of irrigation water; the programme is backed by the Rs. 500 crore allocation for genome editing in agricultural crops made in the Union Budget 2023-24. 5. Diagnostic application.FELUDA (FnCas9 Editor Linked Uniform Detection Assay), developed by CSIR-IGIB and approved by DCGI in 2020, used a CRISPR-based paper-strip readout for SARS-CoV-2 — demonstrating that CRISPR is not only a scalpel but also a highly specific sensor, with obvious extension to tuberculosis and sickle-cell screening.

Andhra Pradesh anchor: The genome-edited rice varieties are built on AP genetics — Kamala from Samba Mahsuri (BPT 5204), bred at ANGRAU’s Bapatla station, and Pusa DST Rice 1 from MTU 1010 (Cotton Dora Sannalu), bred at ANGRAU’s Regional Agricultural Research Station, Maruteru — and both are notified for Zone VII, which includes Andhra Pradesh (ICAR, May 2025).

## Conclusion

CRISPR’s trajectory illustrates how basic microbiology becomes national capability. A bacterial memory of past viral attack has, within a decade of the 2020 Nobel, become an approved medicine, a released crop variety and a diagnostic strip. For India, the significance is that it has crossed from adoption to origination — indigenous platforms such as enFnCas9 and FELUDA, and the first genome-edited rice varieties in the world, place the country among originators rather than licensees. The remaining task is governance: off-target risk, the germline prohibition and equitable pricing must be enforced with the same rigour that produced the science.

- Terminology to deploy precisely: spacer, protospacer, PAM, crRNA, tracrRNA, sgRNA, NHEJ, HDR, SDN-1/2/3, off-target effect. Using PAM correctly distinguishes a strong answer from a memorised one.
- Regulatory point: by an Office Memorandum of March 2022, MoEFCC exempted SDN-1 and SDN-2 genome-edited plants free of exogenous DNA from Rules 7-11 of the Rules, 1989 under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, followed by DBT’s Guidelines for Safety Assessment of Genome Edited Plants (May 2022).
