## Introduction

Communicable diseases still account for roughly one-fourth of India’s total disease burden, even as non-communicable diseases dominate (ICMR–NIS, India: Health of the Nation’s States framework, MoHFW). Their significance lies not only in mortality but in their capacity to trigger outbreaks that disrupt livelihoods — a cholera cluster shuts a market, an encephalitis season empties a paddy belt, and a single H5N1 detection can freeze an entire poultry economy. Of the five diseases listed, cholera, Japanese encephalitis and avian influenza are selected here as the three most operationally live in the Andhra Pradesh context.

## Cholera
- Cause: An acute secretory diarrhoeal illness caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae (toxigenic serogroups O1 and O139), transmitted by the faeco-oral route through faecally contaminated water and food. The cholera toxin activates adenylate cyclase in intestinal cells, causing massive isotonic fluid loss — which is why death is from dehydration, not from the organism itself. Coastal Andhra’s cyclone-and-flood cycle, which contaminates open wells and disrupts piped supply, is a classic outbreak setting.
- Treatment:Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT) is the mainstay and can cut case-fatality below 1%; intravenous Ringer’s Lactate is used in severe dehydration, with doxycycline/azithromycin to shorten shedding. Zinc supplementation is added for children under five, per MoHFW’s standard case-management protocol.
- Prevention: Chlorination and Field Test Kit based water-quality surveillance under the Jal Jeevan Mission; sanitation under Swachh Bharat Mission-Grameen Phase II (ODF Plus); Oral Cholera Vaccine (OCV) deployment in hotspot pockets; and outbreak detection through the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP)/IDSP run by NCDC.

## Encephalitis (Japanese Encephalitis)
- Cause: Inflammation of the brain parenchyma; in India the leading vaccine-preventable cause is the Japanese Encephalitis virus (JEV), a flavivirus transmitted by Culex tritaeniorhynchus mosquitoes that breed in paddy fields, with pigs as amplifying hosts and ardeid water-birds as reservoirs. Per NCVBDC (MoHFW), JE/AES has been reported from 355 districts across 24 States/UTs, and Andhra Pradesh is a listed endemic State — its paddy-and-piggery landscape supplies exactly the ecology JEV needs.
- Treatment:No specific antiviral exists — management is supportive: airway protection, control of seizures and raised intracranial pressure, and early referral to Encephalitis Treatment Centres. This is precisely why prevention carries the entire burden.
- Prevention:Two doses of live-attenuated SA 14-14-2 JE vaccine under the Universal Immunisation Programme (at 9–12 months with measles, and at 16–24 months with the DPT booster), now covering 343 of 357 endemic districts; the indigenously developed JENVAC (ICMR–Bharat Biotech) is used for adult vaccination in 44 high-incidence districts. Vector control, pig-shed relocation away from habitation, and physical rehabilitation under the National Programme for Prevention and Control of JE/AES (2012) complete the package.

## Avian Influenza (Bird Flu)
- Cause: Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) influenza A viruses, principally H5N1, maintained in wild migratory waterfowl and spilling into commercial poultry; human infection is rare and follows direct contact with infected birds or contaminated environments, not properly cooked poultry. This is directly consequential for Andhra Pradesh — India’s largest egg-producing State — where H5N1 outbreaks were confirmed in poultry in the Annamayya and Chittoor districts during the 2025-26 season, following earlier detections in Nellore (2024) and East Godavari.
- Treatment: Neuraminidase inhibitors — oseltamivir — given early, plus intensive supportive care for respiratory failure. Human cases in India remain sporadic.
- Prevention: India follows a “detect-and-cull” policy under the DAHD National Action Plan for Prevention, Control and Containment of Avian Influenza — culling within a 1 km infected zone, 10 km surveillance zone, movement restrictions and disinfection. DAHD (PIB, April 2025) approved commercial use of the H9N2 low-pathogenic vaccine developed by ICAR-NIHSAD, Bhopal, and farm-level biosecurity plus PPE for cullers remains the frontline defence.
- **Cholera** — Japanese Encephalitis · Avian Influenza
- **Agent** — V. cholerae (bacterium) · JE virus (flavivirus) · Influenza A H5N1 (virus)
- **Route** — Faeco-oral (water) · Culex mosquito; pig amplifier · Bird-to-human contact
- **Treatment** — ORS / IV fluids + antibiotic · Supportive only · Oseltamivir + supportive

- **Prevention** — Safe water, OCV, sanitation · Vaccine (SA 14-14- 2/JENVAC) · Culling + biosecurity

A single arrow beneath, labelled “Water — Vector — Zoonosis”, shows the examiner you have chosen one disease from each transmission class deliberately.

## Conclusion

The three diseases chosen illustrate three distinct control logics: cholera is defeated by engineering (water and sanitation), Japanese encephalitis by immunisation, and avian influenza by veterinary containment. Their common thread is that none can be solved by the health department alone — which is the rationale for the National One Health Mission, approved to integrate human, animal and environmental health surveillance. For Andhra Pradesh, with its cyclone-exposed coast, paddy-piggery ecology and the country’s largest poultry economy, all three risks are simultaneous, making integrated district-level preparedness not optional but essential.

## Value addition
- AP as poultry capital: Andhra Pradesh is India’s leading egg producer; the National Egg Coordination Committee was founded at Hyderabad and the Sri Venkateswara Veterinary University (SVVU), Tirupati provides the State’s diagnostic backbone alongside ICAR-NIHSAD, Bhopal (the national HPAI reference laboratory).
- Cholera specifics for a bonus mark:V. cholerae O1 has two biotypes (Classical, El Tor) and two serotypes (Ogawa, Inaba); the current pandemic is the seventh, driven by El Tor. Robert Koch identified the organism in 1884 in Kolkata.
- JE landmark: India’s first JE outbreak was reported from Vellore (1955); the catastrophic eastern Uttar Pradesh outbreak of 2005 (>6,000 cases, ~1,500 deaths) triggered the introduction of mass JE vaccination — a useful example of an outbreak driving policy.
- Avian influenza reservoir logic: Wild waterfowl are the natural reservoir; the Central Asian Flyway brings migratory birds into Indian wetlands each winter, which is why Indian outbreaks cluster in December–March.
- Institutional map worth naming: NCDC (outbreak response), ICMR-NIV Pune (virology), ICMR-NIMR (malaria), ICMR-NIHSAD Bhopal (animal disease), and ICMR-NIN, Hyderabad for the nutrition dimension.

## Introduction
**Recombinant DNA (rDNA) technology** combines DNA from different sources to create new genetic combinations with desired traits. Developed in the 1970s, it is the foundation of modern biotechnology, medicine and agriculture.

## What is recombinant DNA?
- Artificially constructed DNA formed by joining segments from different organisms; when introduced into a host cell, the foreign gene expresses a desired protein or trait.

## Schematic process of creating rDNA
1. **Isolation of the target gene** from a donor (e.g., the human insulin gene).
2. **Cutting with restriction enzymes**: restriction endonucleases (e.g., **EcoRI**, recognising GAATTC) act as molecular scissors, creating complementary "sticky ends" on both gene and vector.
3. **Insertion into a vector**: the fragment is ligated (by **DNA ligase**) into a vector such as plasmid pBR322 or a phage — forming the recombinant molecule.
4. **Transformation into a host**: the recombinant vector is introduced into a host (usually *E. coli*) by heat shock or electroporation.
5. **Selection and expression**: transformed cells are identified via selectable markers (e.g., antibiotic resistance) and cultured so the gene is expressed and the protein harvested.

## Roles of restriction enzymes and vectors
- **Restriction enzymes**: make site-specific cuts, enabling precise gene splicing.
- **Vectors** (plasmids/phages): carry the gene into the host and provide an origin of replication, selectable marker and cloning site — ensuring transfer, replication and stable maintenance.

## Example
- **Human insulin (Humulin)** — the first recombinant drug, produced (1982) in *E. coli* by Eli Lilly. Others include **Bt cotton** and the **recombinant Hepatitis-B vaccine**.

## Conclusion
rDNA technology — using restriction enzymes and vectors — enables the manufacture of life-saving products like insulin and underpins modern medicine, agriculture and industry; recombinant biopharmaceuticals now form a large share of new drug approvals.

## Introduction

Intellectual Property (IP) refers to creations of the human mind - inventions, literary and artistic works, designs, symbols and names - over which the law grants time-bound exclusive rights so that creators can appropriate the value of their effort. Internationally, IP is divided into industrial property (patents, trademarks, designs, GIs) governed by the Paris Convention, 1883, and copyright governed by the Berne Convention, 1886, with minimum standards harmonised by the TRIPS Agreement, 1995 under the WTO. India’s IP filings crossed 6.89 lakh in 2024-25 (PIB, July 2025), reflecting the practical stakes of these distinctions.

Rights of an inventor - a bundle, not a single right. - Right to exclude: to prevent others from making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing the invention during the patent term - the core negative right. - Right to exploit: to manufacture, licence (exclusive or non-exclusive), assign or mortgage the patent, generating royalty income; assignments must be recorded with the Controller. - Right to sue: to seek injunctions, damages or account of profits for infringement before the appropriate court. - Moral and attribution rights: under Section 57 of the Copyright Act, 1957, authors retain paternity and integrity rights even after assigning economic rights; in patents, the Certificate of Inventorship introduced by the Patents (Amendment) Rules, 2024 formally acknowledges inventor contribution.

How rights are gained globally. Patents are territorial - there is no world patent. Protection is obtained either by filing separately in each country or through the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT), which India joined in 1998, allowing a single international application to preserve priority in over 150 states for up to 30/31 months. Trademarks use the Madrid Protocol, which India acceded to in 2013, permitting a single application designating multiple countries. Micro-organism deposits for biotech patents are handled under the Budapest Treaty (India, 2001).

How rights are enforced globally.TRIPS sets minimum substantive and enforcement standards binding on WTO members, and disputes between states are heard by the WTO Dispute Settlement Body - the only IP treaty with binding inter-state enforcement. WIPO administers the Paris, Berne, PCT and Madrid systems and offers arbitration and mediation. Actual enforcement, however, remains national: in India through civil suits, criminal provisions of the Trade Marks and Copyright Acts, and customs border measures that allow seizure of counterfeit consignments at ports such as Visakhapatnam and Krishnapatnam.

## Conclusion

Copyright, patent and trademark are not interchangeable labels but responses to three different market failures - under-supply of expression, under-disclosure of invention, and consumer confusion. An inventor’s rights are consequently a bundle of exclusion, exploitation and remedy, acquired territorially and coordinated internationally through PCT, Madrid and TRIPS. For India, the strategic task is to use TRIPS flexibilities - Section 3(d), compulsory licensing, and the public-order exclusions - so that a strong IP regime attracts investment without pricing essential medicines and technologies beyond the reach of citizens.

## Introduction

A patent is an exclusive right granted by the state for an invention that is novel, involves an inventive step and is capable of industrial application, conferred for 20 years from the date of filing under the Patents Act, 1970. It embodies a bargain: the inventor discloses the invention fully to the public, and in return receives a temporary right to exclude others. India’s patent system has scaled rapidly - filings rose from 24,326 in 2020-21 to 68,176 in 2024-25, and 1,03,057 patents were granted in FY 2023-24 (PIB, 2024; November 2025).

Examples of patents (Indian and global). - Rotavac - India’s indigenously developed rotavirus vaccine (Bharat Biotech, with DBT support), now in the Universal Immunisation Programme. - ZyCoV-D - the world’s first approved human DNA vaccine, an Indian patent-protected platform. - Semiconductor chip architectures and telecom standard-essential patents (Ericsson, Qualcomm) that drive global licensing revenue. - Pharmaceutical molecules such as Sildenafil and Sorafenib (Nexavar), and low-cost devices such as IISc’s artificial heart valve. - Not patentable in India: scientific principles, mathematical or business methods, computer programmes per se, plants and animals (except micro-organisms), methods of treatment, and inventions contrary to public order or morality.

The safeguards that survived the 2005 shift - the analytical core. India did not adopt product patents unconditionally. Section 3(d) denies patents to new forms of known substances unless they show significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy, a provision upheld by the Supreme Court in Novartis AG v. Union of India (2013) when rejecting the Glivec (imatinib mesylate) application - the world’s most cited anti-evergreening precedent. Additionally, Sections 84-92 permit compulsory licensing; India issued its first in 2012, allowing Natco to manufacture Bayer’s Nexavar at a fraction of the price on grounds of affordability and non-working. Together these preserve public-health space within a product-patent regime.

How GI tags relate to patents. A Geographical Indication, registered under the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, is a sibling right within IPR, not a species of patent. Both are statutory exclusive rights, both are territorial, and both are recognised under TRIPS (GIs under Article 22). The differences are decisive:

Andhra Pradesh illustrates the collective model: Araku Valley Arabica coffee, grown organically by tribal communities at 900-1,100 m in the Eastern Ghats, is one of only five GI-tagged Indian regional coffees (Coffee Board; PIB, November 2025); Etikoppaka lacquer toys (GI 2017, Anakapalli district) and Kondapalli Bommalu (GI 2006, NTR district) sustain thousands of artisan households, with GST on toys reduced from 12% to 5% to widen the market (PIB, September 2025). Others include Bandar Laddu, Tirupati Laddu, Banaganapalle mangoes, Dharmavaram and Venkatagiri sarees, Bobbili Veena and Budithi brassware.

## Conclusion

A patent rewards the new; a GI protects the inherited. India’s IPR architecture deliberately uses both - product patents to attract innovation-led investment after 2005, and Section 3(d) with compulsory licensing to prevent that monopoly from becoming exploitative. For a state such as Andhra Pradesh, whose comparative advantage lies as much in Araku coffee and Etikoppaka lacquerware as in pharmaceutical R&D, the GI route is the more immediately transformative instrument,

converting geography and inherited skill into legally defensible market premium for entire communities.

## Introduction

Solar energy is the most abundant renewable resource and, following a decade of steep cost decline, the cheapest source of new electricity in most markets including India. Global solar capacity has grown exponentially, and India — with 150.26 GW installed as on 31 March 2026 (MNRE) — has become one of the three largest solar markets in the world.

Global status

- Global solar capacity has grown several-fold in a decade, driven by an approximately 85%+ fall in module prices since 2010 — the steepest cost decline of any energy technology in history.
- China dominates both installed capacity and manufacturing, followed by the United States, the European Union and India. China’s share of global module, cell and polysilicon manufacturing exceeds 80%, which is itself a strategic concern for every other market.
- Growth areas globally: utility-scale parks, distributed rooftop, floating solar, agrivoltaics, and the pairing of solar with battery storage — increasingly bid as a single “firm renewable” product.

Status in India

- Installed solar capacity: 150.26 GW as on 31 March 2026 (MNRE), within total renewable capacity of 274.68 GW and non-fossil capacity of 283.46 GW. India ranks third globally in solar power capacity and has overtaken Japan to become the world’s third-largest solar electricity generator.
- Composition: ground-mounted utility-scale plants dominate, with grid-connected rooftop, hybrid and off-grid systems making up the remainder. Distributed renewable energy contributed 16.3 GW of the 44.61 GW added in 2025-26, including 8.7 GW rooftop and 7.6 GW under PM-KUSUM.
- Major solar parks:Bhadla (Rajasthan), Pavagada (Karnataka), Rewa (Madhya Pradesh), and Kurnool and NP Kunta (Andhra Pradesh).
- Policy drivers: the National Solar Mission (2010, under NAPCC); PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana (2024) for 1 crore rooftop households; PM-KUSUM for agricultural solarisation; Solar Park Scheme; PLI for High Efficiency Solar PV Modules; ALMM for domestic content; ISTS charge waiver; 100% FDI under the automatic route.
- Manufacturing: India’s module manufacturing capacity has expanded rapidly under PLI, though cell, wafer and polysilicon capacity remains the gap — assembly has been indigenised faster than the upstream value chain.

Factors hindering solar utilisation

- Intermittency and the evening peak. Solar generates nothing after sunset, precisely when demand peaks. Until storage scales, every unit of solar capacity requires backup capacity — the single most fundamental constraint.
- Storage cost. Battery costs have fallen but remain the binding economic constraint on firm renewable supply; pumped storage is currently India’s most bankable large-scale option.
- Land requirement. Utility-scale solar needs large contiguous parcels — roughly 4-5 acres per MW — raising acquisition cost, delay and competition with agriculture. Floating solar and agrivoltaics are the responses.
- Grid integration and evacuation. Curtailment occurs where transmission lags generation; Green Energy Corridors and REMCs address this but unevenly.
- DISCOM finances and offtake risk. Delayed payments and renegotiation of power purchase agreements deter investment irrespective of tariff competitiveness.
- Supply chain dependence. Imported cells, wafers and polysilicon, and dependence on concentrated sources for critical minerals used in storage.
- Rooftop-specific barriers: split incentives between landlord and tenant, roof ownership in multi-storey buildings, net-metering policy variation across States, and upfront cost for households despite subsidy.
- End-of-life waste. Module and battery disposal is an emerging problem; the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 and Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 provide EPR frameworks, but module recycling capacity remains limited.

## Conclusion

India has moved from a marginal to a leading position in global solar — third in capacity, third in generation, with the 50% non-fossil milestone achieved five years early. Cost, once the principal hindrance, is largely resolved. The binding constraints are now storage, which determines whether solar can serve the evening peak, land, which determines how much utility-scale capacity can be built, and upstream manufacturing, which determines whether solar independence is real or merely assembled.

## Introduction

The pandemic exposed a delivery problem rather than a content problem: India’s curriculum was rapidly digitised, but a large share of households had no reliable internet to receive it. Satellite broadcast solves precisely this, since a DTH signal reaches a household with a set-top box and no connectivity at all — which is why India’s principal educational response was built on satellite television rather than on streaming.

(internet) | Radio & community radio (lowest barrier) , all feeding into NCERT/CIET content .

## Satellite broadcast — the channel that reaches the unconnected
- SWAYAM PRABHA, inaugurated on 7 July 2017, runs educational DTH channels 24x7 using two transponders on GSAT-15, uplinked from BISAG, Gandhinagar, with the portal maintained by INFLIBNET. Content is supplied by NPTEL, the IITs, UGC, CEC, IGNOU, NCERT and NIOS.
- PM e-VIDYA, launched on 17 May 2020 in direct response to the pandemic, unified digital, online and on-air education. Its flagship component, “One

Class, One Channel”, began with 12 DTH channels for Classes 1-12 carrying NCERT curriculum content and has since been expanded to 200 channels, allowing States and UTs to telecast content in their own languages and curricula.

- Why this is the right technology for the problem: a DTH broadcast is one-to-many and connectivity-independent. Its cost does not rise with the number of viewers, and it works where no tower reaches. For the households the digital divide actually excludes, satellite television — not an app — is the accessible medium.
- Accessibility as design: PM e-VIDYA DTH channel 31 for Indian Sign Language was launched in December 2024, positioning ISL both as a medium and as a subject — reaching learners excluded by hearing impairment, not only by geography.

## The honest historical record — and why it matters

India’s satellite-education lineage is genuine but must be stated accurately: - SITE (1975-76), using NASA’s ATS-6, broadcast instructional television to some 2,400 villages — at the time the largest sociological communication experiment ever conducted. - EDUSAT (GSAT-3), launched 2004, was the world’s first satellite dedicated exclusively to education, running tele-education networks for schools and universities. It was decommissioned in 2010, and its functions were absorbed into the GSAT fleet and into SWAYAM PRABHA. - The lesson is not that satellites failed but that the delivery layer evolves: the concept EDUSAT proved is now executed by GSAT-15 transponders and DTH, at far greater scale and lower cost per learner.

## Complementary internet-based delivery

Where connectivity exists, satellite communication supports the backhaul: DIKSHA (curriculum-linked content in multiple Indian languages), SWAYAM and NPTEL (higher education), ePathshala (digital textbooks), and e-PG Pathshala. BharatNet extends fibre to Gram Panchayats, with satellite links serving locations fibre cannot economically reach.

## Inspiring the next generation — the programme as curriculum
- YUVIKA (Yuva Vigyani Karyakram), ISRO’s Young Scientist Programme, gives school students exposure to space science and technology, built explicitly on a “catch them young” rationale.
- ISRO’s collaboration with NESTS supports STEM education and teacher training in Eklavya Model Residential Schools for tribal students.
- National Space Day (23 August), marking Chandrayaan-3’s landing, has become a national science-outreach occasion.

## What satellites cannot do — the necessary qualification
- Broadcast is one-way. Television cannot assess a student, answer a question or detect who has stopped watching. Learning loss during the pandemic was concentrated among children who had access to content but no interaction, and satellite delivery does not fix that.
- Household barriers persist: a set-top box, a functioning television, electricity, and — critically — a shared device in a household where a girl’s access is often subordinated.
- Teacher capacity determines whether broadcast content is integrated into learning or merely transmitted.

## Conclusion

India’s space programme addresses one specific, important part of the educational access problem: it delivers curriculum content to households that no internet connection reaches, through 200 PM e-VIDYA channels riding on GSAT-15. That is a genuine and scalable contribution, and its extension to Indian Sign Language shows the model can be widened. But broadcast is one-way, and restoring education after the pandemic requires what satellites cannot supply — assessment, interaction and teachers. The space programme’s role is to guarantee that no child is excluded for want of a signal; closing the learning gap itself remains a classroom problem.

P5-Q11a:
## Introduction

The National e-Governance Plan (NeGP), approved in 2006, was India’s first attempt to give coherence to scattered departmental computerisation. Its vision was to make government services “accessible to the common man in his locality, through common service delivery outlets, and ensure efficiency, transparency and reliability at affordable costs”. Chronologically it preceded Digital India (2015), and was subsequently restructured as e-Kranti — NeGP 2.0, forming one of Digital India’s nine pillars.

## NeGP’s architecture
- 31 Mission Mode Projects (MMPs) in three categories: Central (Income Tax, Passport, MCA21, Banking, Insurance), State (land records, road transport, e-District, agriculture, treasuries) and Integrated (Common Service Centres, e-Procurement, e-Courts, India Portal).
- Core infrastructure pillars:State Data Centres for hosting, State Wide Area Networks (SWAN) for connectivity, Common Service Centres as the physical front end, and the State e-Governance Service Delivery Gateway for interoperability.
- e-Kranti (2015) added mobile-first delivery, cloud by default, integration of services rather than siloed MMPs, and mandatory security standards.

## Three projects explained

## Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana — the account that makes transfer possible
- The problem it solves: DBT requires a bank account. Before PMJDY (2014), a large share of poor households had none, so subsidy could only be delivered in kind or in cash, both leakage-prone.
- What it does: zero-balance accounts with RuPay debit card, accident insurance cover and overdraft facility, opened at scale including through Business Correspondents.
- Its systemic role: PMJDY is the “J” of the JAM trinity — Jan Dhan (where money goes), Aadhaar (who you are), Mobile (confirmation). Without it, Aadhaar-linked DBT would have had no destination. Cumulative DBT transfers crossed Rs. 43.95 lakh crore by May 2025 (PIB, November 2025).
- Beyond transfers: the accounts became the entry point to formal credit, insurance (PMJJBY, PMSBY) and pension (APY), and the base on which UPI’s rural expansion rests.

## DigiLocker — the end of repeated document production
- The problem it solves: Indian administration required citizens to produce attested copies of the same documents to every department, repeatedly, at their own cost.
- What it does: a cloud-based digital wallet holding issuer-pushed documents — driving licences, vehicle registration certificates, Aadhaar, PAN, school and university certificates, insurance policies — which are legally at par with originals under Rule 9A of the IT (Preservation and Retention of Information by Intermediaries) Rules.
- The key distinction: documents issued directly by the authority into DigiLocker carry legal validity, unlike self-uploaded scans. Transport authorities accept DigiLocker licences and RCs during roadside checks; boards and universities issue results directly into it.
- Integration: DigiLocker is now linked with UMANG, allowing document access and service delivery through a single flow (NeGD, January 2025).

## National Digital Literacy Mission — and its successor
- The problem it solves: infrastructure without capability produces access without use.
- What it did: NDLM and Digital Saksharta Abhiyan trained citizens in operating digital devices, using the internet, and transacting online, with emphasis on rural and semi-urban households.
- Its successor:PMGDISHA (Pradhan Mantri Gramin Digital Saksharta Abhiyan) scaled this to rural households, targeting one certified digitally literate person per household, delivered largely through CSCs.
- Why it matters more now: with household internet access at 86.3% (NSO, CMS: Telecom, 2025), the binding constraint has shifted decisively from access to skills — making digital literacy, not connectivity, the priority intervention.

## Conclusion

NeGP built the plumbing — data centres, networks and service outlets — and Digital India built the platforms on top of it, with e-Kranti as the bridge. The three projects examined illustrate the complete chain: Jan Dhan created the destination for benefits, DigiLocker removed the paperwork friction, and digital literacy programmes address whether citizens can actually use what has been built. The chain is only as strong as its weakest link, and that link is now capability rather than infrastructure.

## Value addition
- e-Bhasha (the option not developed above): promotes digital content and interfaces in Indian languages so that government websites, e-learning material and service portals are usable by non-English speakers. Its current successor in spirit is Bhashini, the National Language Translation Mission, which builds AI translation and speech models across Indian languages — arguably the most consequential inclusion intervention available, since it bypasses both the English filter and print literacy.
- BharatNet (the other option): the world’s largest rural broadband programme, laying optical fibre to Gram Panchayats to enable telemedicine, online education, e-governance and digital payments; the Amended BharatNet Programme (2023) extends it toward village-level connectivity with a ring topology for reliability, implemented through BBNL, BSNL and State agencies such as APSFL in Andhra Pradesh.
- Digital India’s nine pillars: broadband highways; universal access to mobile connectivity; public internet access programme; e-Governance (reforming government through technology); e-Kranti (electronic delivery of services); information for all; electronics manufacturing; IT for jobs; and early harvest programmes.
- PMJDY features to cite: zero-balance account, RuPay card with accident insurance cover, overdraft facility, and linkage to PMJJBY, PMSBY and Atal Pension Yojana — the “financial inclusion stack” built on the account.
- DigiLocker legal point: documents issued directly by the issuing authority into DigiLocker are at par with original physical documents; self-uploaded documents are not.
- AP-specific: APSFL Fibre Grid as the State BharatNet implementing agency; Mana Mitra as a WhatsApp-based service aggregator comparable to UMANG; e-Seva, one of India’s earliest citizen service-centre models.
P5-Q11b:
## Introduction

Biofuels are liquid or gaseous fuels derived from biomass — plants, crop residue, animal and organic waste — used mainly as transport fuel. They are classified by feedstock into 1G (ethanol from sugarcane, molasses and grain; biodiesel from vegetable oils), 2G (ethanol from lignocellulosic residue, bio-CNG), 3G (algae-based fuels, bio-hydrogen) and 4G. For India, importing 85-88% of its crude oil, their importance is primarily economic before it is environmental.

Reduced crude imports --> Forex saved , with a return arrow labelled payments to farmers . The circularity is the economic argument in one diagram.

## Why biofuels matter to India’s economy
- Foreign exchange and the current account — the largest single benefit. Crude oil is India’s biggest import by value. Every litre of ethanol blended displaces a litre of imported petrol, and the achievement of 20% ethanol blending (E20) in 2025-26 (PIB) therefore represents a substantial and recurring reduction in the oil import bill. This directly strengthens the current account and reduces exposure to price and currency shocks.
- Farmer income and price stabilisation. Ethanol creates an alternative demand channel for sugarcane, maize and damaged food grains. Its significance for sugarcane is structural: diverting cane juice and B-heavy molasses to ethanol reduces the chronic sugar surplus that depresses prices and causes mill payment arrears to farmers. Ethanol has become a mechanism for stabilising cane arrears, not merely an energy policy.
- Rural industrial investment. Distillery capacity expansion, grain-based ethanol plants and compressed biogas units are located in agricultural districts rather than metros, creating rural manufacturing investment and employment where alternatives are scarce.
- Waste valorisation.2G ethanol from crop residue converts a disposal problem into a revenue stream and directly addresses stubble burning in Punjab, Haryana and western UP — an air-quality benefit with large avoided health costs. SATAT does the same for organic waste through compressed biogas.
- Energy security. Domestically produced fuel is not subject to shipping disruption, sanctions or supply cartels.
- Employment. The value chain spans cultivation, collection, transport, processing and distribution — labour-intensive at almost every stage.
- Environmental co-benefits: lower carbon monoxide and hydrocarbon emissions from blended fuel, and lifecycle CO2 reduction where feedstock is sustainably sourced.

## The economic costs to acknowledge — a balanced answer states both
- Water intensity. Sugarcane is among the most water-demanding crops; expanding cane-based ethanol in water-stressed regions such as Marathwada transfers an energy gain into a water cost. Grain and 2G routes are less water-intensive.
- Food-versus-fuel risk, managed in policy by restricting food-grain diversion to surplus and damaged stocks with National Biofuel Coordination Committee approval.
- Fiscal cost of differential ethanol pricing and interest subvention for distilleries.

## The National Policy on Biofuels, 2018 — in brief
- Vision: 20% ethanol blending in petrol and 5% biodiesel blending in diesel by 2030, using domestic feedstock — the ethanol target advanced to 2025 by the 2022 amendment and achieved in 2025-26.
- Categorisation: Basic Biofuels (1G) and Advanced Biofuels (2G, 3G), permitting differentiated incentives so that harder technologies receive greater support.
- Feedstock expansion: sugarcane juice, sugar beet, sweet sorghum, corn, cassava and damaged food grains unfit for human consumption, with surplus grain permitted on NBCC approval.
- Viability Gap Funding of Rs. 5,000 crore over six years for 2G ethanol bio-refineries.
- Institutions: National Biofuel Coordination Committee, chaired by the Minister of Petroleum and Natural Gas; Biofuel Steering Committee under the Secretary.
- Related programmes:Pradhan Mantri JI-VAN Yojana for 2G ethanol projects; SATAT for compressed biogas; GOBARdhan for rural biogas; the Global Biofuels Alliance launched at the G20 Summit, New Delhi (2023).

AP relevance: Andhra Pradesh’s sugarcane belt in the Godavari and Krishna districts and its maize cultivation supply ethanol feedstock; the State’s substantial rice production creates a large residue base relevant to 2G ethanol and compressed biogas; Rythu Bharosa Kendras provide the village-level procurement interface.

## Conclusion

Biofuels matter to India’s economy through a rare alignment of interests: they cut the import bill, raise farm incomes, attract investment to rural districts and reduce residue burning. The achievement of E20 in 2025-26, five years ahead of the original target, demonstrates that the policy architecture worked. The next phase — 2G ethanol from crop residue — offers the largest remaining gains, because it converts an environmental liability into fuel without any food-versus-fuel or water trade-off at all.

## Value addition
- Ethanol blending trajectory: under 2% in 2013-14; 10% achieved June 2022, five months early; E20 fuel available from April 2023; 20% achieved in 2025-26 (PIB). Blended fuel meets BIS specifications verified from distillery to retail pump.
- The biofuel generations: 1G (sugar, starch, vegetable oils); 2G (lignocellulosic residue, municipal waste, bio-CNG); 3G (algae, bio-hydrogen); 4G (engineered organisms with carbon capture).
- Programmes to name:Ethanol Blended Petrol Programme; Pradhan Mantri JI-VAN Yojana (2G ethanol); SATAT (compressed biogas); GOBARdhan (rural biogas); Global Biofuels Alliance (G20, New Delhi, 2023) with 24 countries and 12 international organisations.
- The sugar-ethanol linkage — the sharpest economic point: diverting cane juice and B-heavy molasses to ethanol reduces the structural sugar surplus, supports cane prices and helps clear mill arrears to farmers. Ethanol policy is therefore also sugar-sector policy.
- Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF): an emerging biofuel application; India has indicated indicative SAF blending targets for international flights — a forward-looking point that few answers include.
- The water caveat: sugarcane requires very high water input per tonne; expanding cane-based ethanol in water-stressed regions converts an energy gain into a groundwater cost, which is why grain-based and 2G routes are strategically preferable.
- AP-specific: sugarcane in the Godavari and Krishna districts; maize cultivation; rice residue base for 2G ethanol and compressed biogas; Rythu Bharosa Kendras for procurement.

Sources used: MNRE on installed solar and renewable capacity as on 31 March 2026 and the June 2025 non-fossil milestone; IRENA Renewable Energy Statistics 2026 as cited by MNRE; PIB on the Ethanol Blended Petrol Programme and achievement of E20 in 2025-26, and on the Global Biofuels Alliance; Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, National Policy on Biofuels 2018 and the 2022 amendment; MoEFCC E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 with the Second Amendment Rules 2023 and Amendment Rules 2024, and Solid Waste Management Rules 2016; Central Pollution Control Board annual data on municipal solid waste generation, collection, processing and landfilling (2021-22); Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs on Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban 2.0 and legacy waste remediation; International Solar Alliance; Government of Andhra Pradesh Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024, APSPCL and NREDCAP.

## Introduction
Though often used interchangeably, 'forest cover' and 'forest area' are distinct concepts in forestry statistics.

## Difference
- **Forest area (recorded forest area)**: land legally notified/recorded as forest in government records, regardless of whether it has trees.
- **Forest cover**: all land with a tree canopy density of more than 10% and area over one hectare, irrespective of ownership or legal status—measured by satellite (Forest Survey of India).
- Thus forest cover may include trees outside recorded forests, and recorded forest area may include areas without actual tree cover.

## What such a graph typically shows
- Trends in India's forest and tree cover over time—generally a gradual increase in total forest and tree cover as per successive India State of Forest Reports.

## Conclusion
Distinguishing recorded forest area (legal) from forest cover (actual canopy) is important for accurate assessment of India's forests and effective conservation policy.
P5-Q13a:
## Introduction

Climate justice reframes climate change from a technical or environmental problem into a question of ethics, rights and equity. Its central observation is a mismatch: those who contributed least to the accumulated stock of greenhouse gases — the poor, small island states, women, indigenous communities and future generations — bear the greatest harm, while those who benefited most from historical emissions are best insulated from the consequences.

## The three dimensions of climate justice
- Distributive justice — how burdens and benefits are shared. The developed world’s historical emissions occupy most of the atmospheric carbon space, yet developing countries face the largest adaptation costs. This underpins Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC), enshrined in the UNFCCC (1992) and reaffirmed in the Paris Agreement.
- Procedural justice — who participates in decisions. Vulnerable countries and communities are least represented in negotiation and finance decisions that determine their future.
- Intergenerational justice — obligations to those not yet born, who will inherit consequences without having had any voice in the choices producing them.

## Evidence supporting the claim
- Emissions inequality: the global richest decile accounts for a large majority of consumption emissions while the poorest half accounts for a small fraction (Oxfam carbon inequality analyses).
- Mortality asymmetry: the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (2022) found that mortality from floods, droughts and storms in the decade to 2020 was 15 times higher in highly vulnerable regions than in regions with very low vulnerability — the single most citable statistic on this topic.
- Displacement: weather-related disasters displace tens of millions annually, overwhelmingly in developing countries (UNHCR and IDMC data).
- India’s position: among the largest aggregate emitters but with per capita emissions far below the global average, and a substantial population still gaining energy access — the empirical basis of India’s negotiating stance.

## How the media covers climate justice

Rather than cataloguing specific covers, the analytically stronger treatment is how media framing shapes the issue:

- From polar bears to people. Coverage has shifted over two decades from framing climate change as a wildlife and wilderness story to framing it as a story about human livelihoods, migration and inequality — a reframing that made climate justice legible to general audiences.
- Personalisation and the youth frame.Time named Greta Thunberg Person of the Year in 2019, the youngest individual so recognised — a decision that placed intergenerational justice on mainstream front pages. Time runs a dedicated climate vertical (TIME CO2) and an annual climate-focused issue and leaders list, sustaining coverage between summit cycles.
- Frontline reporting. Outlets including The Guardian, National Geographic and, in India, Down To Earth (Centre for Science and Environment) document impacts on specific communities — small island states, delta farmers, pastoralists — converting statistical risk into recognisable human circumstance.
- Language as policy.The Guardian’s editorial shift from “climate change” to “climate emergency” in 2019 illustrates how media vocabulary itself becomes a political intervention.
- Accountability journalism. Investigations into fossil fuel companies’ internal knowledge of climate science, and into the gap between corporate net-zero pledges and actual emissions (“greenwashing”), have influenced litigation and disclosure regulation.
- The limits worth noting critically: coverage remains concentrated around COP summits and disasters, producing episodic rather than sustained attention; reporting capacity is concentrated in the Global North, so affected communities are often depicted rather than heard; and the visual grammar of catastrophe can induce fatalism rather than engagement.

## Measures aligned with climate justice

1. Loss and Damage finance — as grants, not loans. The Loss and Damage Fund, agreed at COP27 (Sharm el-Sheikh, 2022) and operationalised at COP28 (Dubai, 2023), addresses harms beyond adaptation — a submerged island, a salinised delta, a destroyed harvest. The justice principle requires that this be grant-based: financing irreversible loss through loans would compel the least responsible to borrow for damage they did not cause, deepening the inequity the fund exists to correct. India has consistently pressed this position. The complementary demand is the New Collective Quantified Goal on climate finance, replacing the unmet USD 100 billion per year pledge.

2. Community-centred, rights-based adaptation. Adaptation designed with rather than for affected communities: local disaster risk governance; recognition of Community Forest Resource rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006, so that forest-dependent communities control the resources they protect; support for women farmers, who bear disproportionate agricultural risk; and integration of indigenous and traditional ecological knowledge into adaptation planning. APCNF in Andhra Pradesh — a farmer-led, women’s self-help-group-anchored agroecology programme covering over 1.77 million farmers — is a working demonstration of adaptation designed from below rather than imposed from above.

A third measure worth adding:technology transfer and equitable access — concessional access to clean technologies and intellectual property flexibilities, so that developing countries are not required to pay a premium for the means of decarbonisation.

## Conclusion

Climate justice asserts that the distribution of climate burdens is neither natural nor accidental, and must therefore be addressed as a matter of fairness rather than of charity. Media coverage has been decisive in shifting the framing from ecosystems to people and from the future to the present, though it remains episodic and unevenly voiced. Concrete progress depends on two things: grant-based loss and damage finance that does not indebt the victims, and adaptation designed with the participation of those it is meant to protect.

## Value addition
- CBDR-RC: enshrined in the Rio Declaration (1992) and the UNFCCC, reaffirmed with “in the light of different national circumstances” in the Paris Agreement; derived from the notion of the common heritage of mankind; recognises both historical responsibility and differential capacity.
- Climate finance architecture: the unmet USD 100 billion per year pledge (Copenhagen 2009, target 2020); Green Climate Fund; Adaptation Fund; Loss and Damage Fund (agreed COP27, operationalised COP28); the New Collective Quantified Goal agreed at COP29 (Baku, 2024).
- The key statistic: IPCC AR6 (2022) — mortality from floods, droughts and storms was 15 times higher in highly vulnerable regions than in the least vulnerable, 2010-2020.
- India’s climate justice positions: per capita emissions well below the global average; carbon space and equity arguments; Mission LIFE as a demand-side contribution; the International Solar Alliance, Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure and Global Biofuels Alliance as South-oriented institutional contributions.
- Concepts to name:climate refugee (not recognised in international law — a significant protection gap); just transition (protecting workers and regions dependent on fossil industries); carbon colonialism (offsetting arrangements that displace land use in developing countries); polluter pays; intergenerational equity.
- Judicial and civic dimension: climate litigation is growing globally; in India, the Supreme Court in M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (2024) recognised a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change as flowing from Articles 14 and 21 — a strong and current point for any climate justice answer.
- AP-specific: cyclone exposure along the 1,053-km coast; sea-level and salinity risk in the Godavari-Krishna delta; Rayalaseema drought; APCNF as community-led adaptation.

P5-Q14a:
## Introduction

Air pollution is India’s most significant environmental health risk, arising from vehicles, industry, construction, waste burning, agricultural residue burning and — critically indoors — solid cooking fuels. The Air Quality Index (AQI), launched in 2014 under the “Swachh Bharat, Swasth Bharat” initiative, converts complex monitoring data into a single number a citizen can act upon.

## Common and hazardous pollutants, with health effects

## Outdoor (ambient)
- **Pollutant** — Main sources · Principal health hazard
- **PM2.5** — Combustion — vehicles, industry, biomass burning · Penetrates deep into alveoli and enters the bloodstream; ischaemic heart disease, stroke, lung cancer, COPD, low birth weight
- **PM10** — Road and construction dust, industry · Upper respiratory irritation, aggravated asthma and bronchitis
- **NO2** — Vehicle exhaust, power generation · Airway inflammation; increased respiratory infection in children; asthma exacerbation
- **SO2** — Coal combustion, refineries, smelting · Bronchoconstriction, aggravated asthma; precursor of acid rain
- **CO** — Incomplete combustion · Binds haemoglobin in preference to oxygen, reducing oxygen delivery — headache, dizziness, confusion, death at high concentration
- **Ground-level O₃** — Secondary — formed from NOx and VOCs in sunlight · Chest pain, coughing, reduced lung function; also damages crops
- **Pb** — Legacy fuel, batteries, smelting · Neurodevelopmental damage in children, anaemia, kidney damage
- **NH₃** — Fertiliser application, livestock · Precursor of secondary particulate formation

## Indoor (household) — the under-discussed half of the question
- Solid fuel combustion (firewood, dung cakes, crop residue, coal) in poorly ventilated kitchens produces very high concentrations of PM2.5 and CO. The burden falls disproportionately on women and young children, who spend most time near the hearth, causing COPD, acute respiratory infection, low birth weight and eye disease. PMUY (Ujjwala) addresses this by providing LPG connections — an air-pollution intervention as much as an energy one, and the point most answers miss.
- VOCs from paints, adhesives, cleaning agents, air fresheners and furnishings — eye, nose and throat irritation; some are carcinogenic (benzene, formaldehyde).
- Tobacco smoke — the most concentrated indoor carcinogen source.
- Radon — a radioactive gas seeping from soil and building material; a leading cause of lung cancer after smoking.
- Biological contaminants — mould, dust mites, pet dander, causing allergy and asthma.
- Asbestos from older construction — mesothelioma and asbestosis.

## What is the Air Quality Index?
- A single composite number derived from concentrations of eight pollutants — PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O₃, NH₃ and Pb — translating technical data into a colour-coded public health message.
- Six categories:Good (0-50), Satisfactory (51-100), Moderately Polluted (101-200), Poor (201-300), Very Poor (301-400), Severe (401-500), each with an associated health advisory.
- The calculation rule worth stating: AQI is determined by the worst-performing pollutant — the sub-index of the pollutant with the highest value becomes the AQI, and that pollutant is reported as the “prominent pollutant”. A city can therefore have a Severe AQI on the strength of PM2.5 alone.
- Requirement: at least three pollutants must be monitored, one of which must be PM10 or PM2.5, for an AQI to be computed.

## Who monitors AQI in India?

The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), under MoEFCC, in coordination with State Pollution Control Boards and Pollution Control Committees. Data comes from Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Stations (CAAQMS) and manual stations under the National Air Quality Monitoring Programme (NAMP). Real-time AQI is disseminated to citizens through the SAMEER app and the CPCB portal. Standards are set under the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS), 2009.

## Contribution of particulate matter to AQI

PM2.5 is the prominent pollutant determining AQI in most Indian cities, on most days. The reasons are specific: it has multiple sources (vehicles, industry, construction, waste and crop-residue burning, household fuel), it remains suspended for days and travels hundreds of kilometres, and it forms secondarily in the atmosphere from precursor gases — SO2, NOx and NH₃ — so controlling only direct emissions is insufficient. Because AQI reports the worst sub-index, PM2.5 usually is the AQI.

## Conclusion

India’s air pollution burden arises outdoors from combustion and dust, and indoors from solid cooking fuel — with particulate matter, especially PM2.5, dominating both. The AQI has succeeded in making air quality legible to citizens and actionable for administrators. The remaining challenge is that measurement has expanded faster than abatement: NCAP’s focus on PM10 and road dust addresses the most visible fraction rather than the most harmful one, and shifting the programme’s centre of gravity to PM2.5 and its precursor gases is the reform most often urged.

## Value addition
- National Clean Air Programme (NCAP): launched January 2019 by MoEFCC; covers 131 non-attainment and million-plus cities across 24 States/UTs; original target 20-30% PM reduction by 2024 against a 2017 baseline; revised target of up to 40% reduction in PM10 or attainment of NAAQS (60 µg/m³) by 2025-26; city-specific annual targets of 3-15%; performance-linked funding, with additional support through the XV Finance Commission air quality grant; progress tracked on the PRANA portal.
- NAAQS (2009) key limits: PM2.5 annual 40 µg/m³ and 24-hour 60 µg/m³; PM10 annual 60 µg/m³ and 24-hour 100 µg/m³ — both substantially above WHO guideline values, which is itself an examinable point.
- Institutional machinery: CPCB and SPCBs; CAQM (Commission for Air Quality Management in the NCR and Adjoining Areas, statutory since 2021); GRAP (Graded Response Action Plan) for Delhi-NCR; the System of Air Quality and Weather Forecasting and Research (SAFAR).
- Source-control measures:BS-VI fuel and vehicle norms from April 2020 (leapfrogging BS-V); PMUY for clean cooking; FGD installation at thermal plants; PM E-DRIVE for electric mobility; crop-residue management machinery and bio-decomposer for stubble burning; dust control at construction sites.
- Indoor air pollution — the neglected half: household air pollution from solid fuels affects women and children most; PMUY is the principal intervention; improved cookstoves and electric cooking are complementary.
- AP-specific: Visakhapatnam’s industrial corridor and monitoring stations; the Vijayawada-Guntur-Tenali-Mangalagiri urban region; CPCB’s critically polluted area assessments in AP industrial clusters.

## Introduction
**COVID-19** is a respiratory disease caused by the **SARS-CoV-2** virus, first identified in Wuhan in 2019, which led to a global pandemic. Understanding its spread and the role of **immuno-diagnostics** was central to managing it.

## What it is and how it spreads
- SARS-CoV-2 is a single-stranded RNA coronavirus with spike (S), envelope (E), membrane (M) and nucleocapsid (N) proteins; the **spike protein binds ACE2 receptors** in the respiratory tract to enter human cells.
- **Transmission**: mainly through respiratory **droplets** and **aerosols** (especially in poorly ventilated closed spaces), **surface contact**, and **asymptomatic spread** — countered by masks, hand hygiene and distancing.

## Immuno-diagnostic methods in the pandemic
- **Molecular test (RT-PCR)**: detects viral RNA; the **gold standard** for accuracy, scaled across ICMR-approved labs.
- **Antigen tests**: detect viral proteins, giving **rapid results (15-30 min)** for mass screening during outbreaks.
- **Antibody (serological) tests**: detect **IgM/IgG** produced after infection — used in national **sero-surveillance** to estimate population exposure and immunity.

## India's response
- Testing infrastructure scaled rapidly under ICMR and the National Health Mission (thousands of RT-PCR and antigen centres); digital platforms **Aarogya Setu and CoWIN** aided tracking and vaccination; indigenous kits (Feluda, Covisense) advanced self-reliant diagnostics.

## Conclusion
COVID-19 spreads chiefly by respiratory routes, and immuno-diagnostic tools — antigen and antibody tests alongside RT-PCR — were vital for **rapid screening, tracing and epidemiological surveillance**. Continued investment in public-health and biotech infrastructure is key to future pandemic preparedness.
P5-Q15a:
## Introduction

Vaccination works by presenting the immune system with a safe facsimile of a pathogen so that immunological memory forms before any real encounter. Where coverage is high enough, this protection becomes collective, breaking transmission chains altogether. India's record demonstrates both dimensions: full immunisation coverage rose from 62% in 2015 to 98.4% in January 2026 (MoHFW, PIB, March 2026), and the country has both eradicated smallpox and been certified polio-free — outcomes achieved through the global framework of the Global Vaccine Action Plan and the national delivery drive of Mission Indradhanush.

1. Mechanism of action — the five-stage sequence

The antigen is taken up by antigen-presenting cells and displayed to T lymphocytes; helper T cells license B cells to produce high-affinity antibodies while cytotoxic T cells handle infected cells; a subset of both lineages persists as memory. On genuine exposure, memory cells respond in hours rather than the one to two weeks a primary response requires, so infection is aborted or blunted. Above a threshold coverage, the pathogen can no longer find susceptible hosts — herd immunity — which is what converts individual protection into disease elimination.

The two examples the question asks for: smallpox and polio. State the caveat that polio is technically eliminated in India rather than globally eradicated — wild poliovirus still circulates in Afghanistan and Pakistan, which is why India maintains OPV and IPV in the schedule and screens at borders. That caveat is precisely what distinguishes a wellinformed answer.

3. Global Vaccine Action Plan (GVAP), 2011-2020

- Origin and vision: endorsed by the World Health Assembly in 2012 under the "Decade of Vaccines" framework, GVAP set out a vision of a world in which all individuals and communities enjoy lives free from vaccine-preventable diseases.
- Five goals: achieve a polio-free world; meet global and regional elimination targets (measles, rubella, maternal and neonatal tetanus); reach vaccination coverage targets in every region, country and community; develop and introduce new and improved vaccines and technologies; and exceed the Millennium Development Goal 4 target for child mortality reduction.
- Six strategic objectives: country ownership; community demand; equity of access; strong immunisation systems integrated with health systems; sustainable financing; and research and development.
- Accountability: an independent Monitoring and Evaluation framework with annual assessment by the Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE) on immunisation.
- Achievements and shortfalls: GVAP catalysed the introduction of new vaccines — pneumococcal conjugate, rotavirus, HPV — across low- and middle-income countries and raised the political visibility of immunisation. But its own final review concluded that most targets were missed, owing to persistent within-country inequity, weak national ownership and financing gaps.
- Successor: GVAP was replaced by the Immunization Agenda 2030 (IA2030), which shifts emphasis from national coverage averages to reaching zero-dose children — the children who have received no vaccine at all — because averages conceal precisely the populations that outbreaks begin in.

4. Mission Indradhanush — corrected chronology and outcomes

- Launch and rationale: launched on 25 December 2014 by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare under the Universal Immunisation Programme. Between 2009 and 2013 coverage was rising only about 1 percentage point a year; at that rate reaching 90% would have taken a further quarter-century. The Mission replaced incremental routine immunisation with targeted campaign mode.
- Method: identify pockets of low coverage, hard-to-reach terrain, migrant and urbanslum populations; run intensive catch-up rounds for children under two and pregnant women; use head-count surveys and due-lists rather than session-site averages.

- Outcomes: the first two phases alone produced a 6.7 percentage-point rise in full immunisation coverage within a year, and the pace of annual improvement rose from about 1% to roughly 4%. Cumulatively, crores of children and lakhs of pregnant women have been vaccinated across phases.
- Current architecture: delivery is now digitised through U-WIN, an individual electronic immunisation registry modelled on Co-WIN, supported by eVIN for coldchain and stock visibility, so that a child who moves between States is still tracked against a due-list rather than lost.
- Current national push: the National Zero Measles-Rubella Elimination Campaign 2025-26 was launched on 24 April 2025, targeting elimination of both diseases by 2026; MR first-dose coverage stood at 93.7% and second-dose at 92.2% (2024-25 HMIS data), and India recorded a 73% decline in measles cases and 17% reduction in rubella cases in 2024 against 2023 (MoHFW, PIB).

5. Andhra Pradesh dimension

Andhra Pradesh implements the UIP through its network of PHCs, CHCs, sub-centres and Anganwadi outreach sessions, with ASHA workers and ANMsas the delivery backbone. The State participates in the nationwide HPV vaccination campaign launched on 28 February 2026 for girls aged 14 using the indigenous Cervavac vaccine — significant for AP given cervical cancer's burden among Indian women.

## Conclusion

Vaccines succeed by converting a one-time controlled exposure into lifelong immunological memory, and by converting sufficient individual immunity into collective protection. India's eradication of smallpox and elimination of polio, maternal and neonatal tetanus, and yaws prove the model works at continental scale and under genuine logistical difficulty. GVAP 2011-2020 supplied the global architecture and, in its shortfalls, the crucial lesson that national averages conceal unreached populations — a lesson its successor IA2030 has internalised through the zero-dose metric. Mission Indradhanush embodied the corresponding national response, lifting coverage from 62% to 98.4% by January 2026. The task now is not raising the average further but closing the final 0.06% — the zero-dose children in whom every future outbreak will begin.

## Value addition
- The eleven UIP vaccines, free of cost: BCG, OPV, IPV, Hepatitis B, Pentavalent (DPT + HepB + Hib), Rotavirus (RVV), Pneumococcal Conjugate (PCV), Measles-Rubella (MR), DPT, Td, and Japanese Encephalitis (endemic districts only).
- Decade of additions: IPV (2015), Rotavirus (2016), MR (2017) and PCV (2017) were the four major introductions of the last decade — they targeted precisely the leading infectious causes of child death, which is why they were prioritised. ¢ Zero-dose children — children who have not received even a first dose of DTPcontaining vaccine. India's share fell from 0.11% (2023) to 0.06% (2024). This is the single most useful current statistic for any immunisation answer.
- Scale of the programme: the UIP targets roughly 2.7 crore newborns and 2.9 crore pregnant women annually, delivered through over 1.3 crore immunisation sessions, with more than 1.03 million ASHAs working under the NHM (as of April 2025). ¢ Immunization Agenda 2030 (IA2030) — three strategic priorities: leave no one behind (zero-dose focus), immunisation across the life course (not infancy alone), and resilience to outbreaks and pandemics.
- Related national platforms worth naming: Intensified Diarrhoea Control Fortnight, National Deworming Day, and Poshan Abhiyaan — immunisation gains are consolidated by nutrition and sanitation, and saying so shows systems thinking.
- India's supply role: over 200 crore COVID-19 vaccine doses administered domestically, with Indian-manufactured vaccines supplied to more than 200 countries — the empirical basis for the "pharmacy of the world" claim (PIB, 2026).

## Introduction

The 2020 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded jointly to Harvey J. Alter, Michael Houghton and Charles M. Rice for the discovery of the Hepatitis C Virus. Their work resolved the long-standing puzzle of "non-A, non-B hepatitis" transmitted through blood transfusion: Alter demonstrated an unknown agent was responsible, Houghton's team identified its genome by molecular cloning in 1989, and Rice proved that this cloned virus alone could cause the disease. The practical consequence was immediate — blood-

bank screening became possible, effectively ending transfusion-transmitted hepatitis C,

and the identified viral enzymes became the drug targets that later delivered a cure.

1. The virus

- Classification: an enveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA virus of the genus Hepacivirus, family Flaviviridae — related to dengue and Japanese encephalitis viruses. It is hepatotropic, replicating chiefly in hepatocytes.
- Genome: approximately 9.6 kilobases, translated as a single polyprotein and then cleaved into structural proteins (core, E1, E2) and non-structural proteins (NS3/4A protease, NSSA, NSSB polymerase) — the last three being the precise targets of modern direct-acting antivirals.
- Genetic diversity — the crux of the vaccine problem: the NSSB RNA-dependent RNA polymerase lacks proofreading, so replication is extremely error-prone. HCV therefore exists as eight genotypes and around 90 subtypes, and within a single infected person as a swarm of related variants (a quasispecies). Genotypes 1 and 3 predominate in India.

2. The disease

- Acute phase: usually silent. Roughly 70-80% of new infections cause no symptoms at all; where symptoms occur they are non-specific — fatigue, nausea, right-upperquadrant discomfort, occasionally jaundice. This asymptomatic course is why hepatitis C is called a "silent epidemic": most patients are diagnosed only decades later, when liver damage has already occurred.
- Chronic phase: approximately 55-85% of those infected fail to clear the virus and progress to chronic hepatitis. Over 20-30 years, persistent inflammation drives fibrosis > cirrhosis in a substantial minority, and cirrhosis carries an annual risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. HCV is a leading cause of liver transplantation worldwide.
- Extrahepatic manifestations worth naming for depth: mixed cryoglobulinaemia, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, and an association with type 2 diabetes

and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

Burden (WHO Global Hepatitis Report 2024, data for 2022):

- Globally, 50 million people live with hepatitis C, and about 1 million new infections occur annually; some 304 million live with hepatitis B and C combined.
- India carries the second-highest burden after China: approximately 55 lakh (0.55 crore) people with hepatitis C and 2.9 crore with hepatitis B, with about 1.4 lakh new hepatitis C infections in 2022, and viral hepatitis causing roughly 1.23 lakh deaths in India that year.

3. Diagnosis and treatment — the revolution the Nobel work enabled

- Diagnosis is two-step: an anti-HCV antibody test (which indicates exposure, not active infection, since antibodies persist after cure), confirmed by HCV RNA testing by PCR or core-antigen assay to establish current infection. Fibrosis is then staged by transient elastography (FibroScan) or serum indices such as APRI and FIB-4.
- Treatment: Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAAs) — sofosbuvir, daclatasvir, velpatasvir, ledipasvir — inhibit NSSB polymerase, NSSA or NS3/4A protease. Pan-genotypic combinations achieve sustained virological response (cure) in over 95% of patients in 12 weeks of oral therapy, with minimal side-effects. This replaced the older, poorly tolerated pegylated interferon plus ribavirin regimen — a direct link to Q241, since interferon's principal antiviral indication has thus been superseded for HCV.
- India's contribution: Indian generic manufacturers reduced DAA prices from tens of thousands of dollars per course to a small fraction of that, making global elimination financially conceivable.

4.Is there a vaccine? — the direct answer

No licensed vaccine against hepatitis C exists anywhere in the world. Four biological

## obstacles explain why

1. Extreme genetic variability. With eight genotypes, roughly 90 subtypes and an intrahost quasispecies swarm, a vaccine antigen matched to one variant may not neutralise another. The hypervariable region 1 (HVR1) of the E2 envelope protein — the most immunogenic surface target — is also the fastest-mutating.

2. Immune evasion. HCV shields its neutralising epitopes behind a dense glycan shield and host lipoproteins, spreads directly cell-to-cell without entering the bloodstream, and interferes with innate interferon signalling.

3. No reliable natural immunity to imitate. Vaccine design normally copies what happens in people who recover naturally. But spontaneous clearance of HCV does not confer durable protection — reinfection is well documented — so there is no natural template and no established correlate of protection.

4. Limited experimental and commercial pathway. HCV infects only humans and chimpanzees, and chimpanzee research is now ethically foreclosed, leaving no convenient animal model. Once DAAs made cure routine, commercial incentive for

vaccine development fell sharply.

Research nonetheless continues on recombinant E1/E2 glycoprotein and viral-vectored candidates in early-phase trials. Meanwhile, prevention rests entirely on non-vaccine

measures: universal blood-product screening, injection safety and auto-disable syringes,

sterile invasive procedures, harm reduction for people who inject drugs, and — vitally — screen-and-treat, since curing an infected person removes a transmission source. This is what public health calls treatment as prevention.

Contrast to state for marks: a highly effective Hepatitis B vaccine does exist and is given free under India's UIP including a birth dose. The difference is instructive — HBV is a stable DNA virus with a single dominant surface antigen; HCV is a hypervariable RNA virus. Vaccine feasibility is a property of the virus, not of scientific effort.

5. India's response

- The National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme (NVHCP), launched in 2018 under the National Health Mission, is among the world's largest such programmes. It provides free diagnostics and free treatment for hepatitis B and C, integrated with existing health infrastructure rather than run as a vertical programme.
- Goal: countrywide elimination of hepatitis C by 2030, and significant reduction in morbidity and mortality from hepatitis B and C — aligned with SDG target 3.3 and WHO resolution WHA69.22.
- Delivery design: services decentralised from Model Treatment Centres at tertiary level to district Treatment Centres and further to community and primary health centres, improving access in underserved areas; hepatitis A and E are tracked through the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme; patient management runs on the paperless NVHCP-MIS portal.
- Convergence: hepatitis B birth-dose vaccination under the UIP, injection safety and blood-bank screening standards, and harm-reduction linkage with the National AIDS and STD Control Programme together form the prevention arm.
- Andhra Pradesh: the State delivers NVHCP services through its district hospital and Model Treatment Centre network; the BSL-4 biocontainment and advanced R&D facilities of APCARL at Pulivendula (YSR Kadapa) give the State a platform for antiinfective and diagnostic research relevant to bloodborne viral disease.

## Conclusion

The discovery of hepatitis C is one of modern medicine's most complete stories — an unknown agent identified, blood supplies made safe, its enzymes mapped, and a curative oral therapy delivered within three decades. Yet it also demonstrates the asymmetry between cure and prevention: a disease can be curable in 95% of patients and still have no vaccine, because vaccine feasibility depends on viral biology rather than on effort or funding. India's elimination goal for 2030 therefore rests not on immunisation but on the harder work of finding the undiagnosed — screening at scale, treating early, and sustaining injection and blood safety. For a virus whose defining characteristic is silence, the decisive intervention is diagnosis.

## Value addition
- The five hepatitis viruses at a glance: A and E — faeco-oral, usually self-limiting, no chronicity (HEV is dangerous in pregnancy, with high mortality); B — DNA virus, bloodborne and perinatal, chronic, vaccine available; C — RNA virus, bloodborne, chronic, curable but no vaccine; D — defective, replicates only alongside HBV, so the hepatitis B vaccine prevents it indirectly.
- Why the Nobel citation named three people: Alter established that an unknown agent caused post-transfusion hepatitis; Houghton isolated the genome; Rice proved that the cloned virus alone was sufficient to cause disease — discovery, identification and proof of causation.
- WHO 2030 elimination targets for viral hepatitis: 90% reduction in new infections and 65% reduction in deaths against a 2015 baseline, with 90% diagnosed and 80% of the eligible treated.
- Treatment as prevention: because there is no vaccine, each cure permanently removes a transmission source. This makes the cascade of care — screened > diagnosed > linked > treated > cured — the central metric of the NVHCP, not coverage of any single intervention.
- Blood safety in India: mandatory screening of every donated unit for HIV, HBV, HCV, syphilis and malaria under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, regulated by the National Blood Transfusion Council — the direct policy descendant of Alter's discovery.
- Terminology precision: Sustained Virological Response (SVR12) — undetectable HCV RNA twelve weeks after completing therapy — is the formal definition of cure. Using this term rather than "cured" signals technical command. ¢ Related programmes to name: National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme (2018), Universal Immunisation Programme (Hepatitis B birth dose), National AIDS and STD Control Programme, and the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme.
